author: Cooper Quintin
title: The Vulnerability Apocalypse and Why We Should Fund Open Source
content:
If you use the internet at all, you may have noticed that a large percentage of sites suddenly went down earlier this week

—

and all your nerdiest friends were talking about "The Vulnerability Apocalypse” and this thing called PHP that

powers nearly 70% of the websites on the internet

. You may find yourself wondering: what is PHP, what just happened, what is the vulnerability apocalypse, and what do I need to do? 

 


To find out what you can personally do read the

first blog post

 in this series!

 


What Is PHP? 

 


PHP is a programming language used mainly to create interactive websites. Facebook, Wordpress, Wikipedia, Etsy, and other major sites all use or were originally built on PHP. It is a long-established mainstay of web development. But because it is open-source, maintenance of these critical systems depends on a small number of volunteers working on this in their free time. The disaster scenario that happened this past week is the perfect example of why we need more money and people supporting open-source projects. Corporations should be contributing both.

 


What Is the Vulnerability Apocalypse? 

 


Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) are the way that security professionals file reports about vulnerabilities in software. The

National Vulnerability Database

 (NVD), run by NIST, is the official national database of CVEs. In other words, CVE reports managed by NIST are the closest thing we have to a canonical database of security vulnerabilities in software. The NVD currently has around 400,000 CVEs that have been filed and accepted since 1988. In just the month of October, 13,000 new CVEs have been submitted. This means that 3% of critical software security bugs that have ever been officially logged were found in the last month alone. And it's likely that by the end of the year over a quarter of the software vulnerabilities that have ever been found will be from 2026.

 


 

Computer vulnerabilities reported are rising exponentially. Source: CVE Tracker


This research is being driven almost entirely by the cybersecurity capabilities of major AI models from companies like Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google. Historically it has been popularly assumed by cybersecurity experts that finding unknown (zero-day) exploits in any specific project and turning them into exploits was expensive. The knowledge to discover them was not widespread, and it was a hard task even for those initiated into the arcane ways of vulnerability hunting. Google even dedicated

an entire team to it

. 

 


But now thanks to major AI models, vulnerabilities are cheap, and anyone of moderate technical skill with a few dollars and access to a frontier AI model can find vulnerabilities in a few minutes. For example, recent vulnerabilities in PHP were found with a prompt to an AI model that literally said "

find bad vulnerabilities in PHP

."

 


What Happened This Week?

 


In 2024, a potentially severe vulnerability in PHP was

discovered during an external security audit

. PHP’s maintainers couldn’t agree on a solution, but more importantly, they couldn’t find a way to exploit the vulnerability. Because it didn’t seem like an active threat, they ended up deprioritizing a fix in favor of working on more urgent security issues. Then, in August 2026, security researchers working with the latest models from OpenAI and Anthropic independently discovered the vulnerability again, and another one

—

and now, with a way to exploit them.

 


We now know that the vulnerabilities 

were so severe that they would have allowed even moderately inventive hackers to take over any website that uses PHP and then steal customer data, launch further malware attacks, spy on users, take websites offline, or launch a massive denial of service attack.

[

1

]

 


Because of the severity of these vulnerabilities, several of the involved researchers got together with the makers of PHP to patch the vulnerabilities and disclose them in a coordinated manner. The idea was that hopefully everyone would get a chance to quietly release and then apply fixes for the vulnerabilities before the whole world found out about it.

 


But news already started to leak on October 20th. There was a

post on a widely read forum

 “Hacker News” and other posts elsewhere. One of the researchers accidentally published a video early. Companies reported seeing active exploitation of the vulnerabilities going back as far as October 17th. On October 21st, six …

author: Shan Kenshin Ecaldre
title: ‘Release tortured Mangyan organizer’
content:
“He needs immediate medical attention for injuries and trauma allegedly sustained during his detention.”


Release him now!


Indigenous Mangyan farmer and organizer Miguel Magbata was reportedly beaten and tortured while in military custody after his arrest in Bulalacao, Oriental Mindoro, on October 14, prompting human rights groups to call for his immediate release and to hold accountable those responsible.


According to Karapatan Southern Tagalog, Magbata was arrested after a reported armed encounter between the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) and alleged New People’s Army (NPA) members in Sitio Badyang, Barangay San Roque in Bulalacao. He was reportedly subjected to physical abuse and interrogation by the 1st Infantry Battalion (IB) under the command of the 203rd Infantry Brigade (IBde).


After days of uncertainty over his whereabouts, reports emerged that Magbata was transferred to Roxas Municipal Police Station. Defend Mindoro said that he needs immediate medical attention for injuries and trauma allegedly sustained during his detention.


The group also raised concerns over a Facebook post from 203rd Infantry Brigade of Philippine Army about Magbata’s children and family, published without their consent, which it said could compromise their safety.


Despite his reported transfer to police custody, the military reportedly sought to retain custody of Magbata. Defend Mindoro demanded his immediate release and called for accountability from the 203rd IBde led by Brig. Gen. Melencio Ragudo, and the 1st IB, under Lt. Col. Edwin Mirador.


Red-tagging, militarization


Defend Mindoro said that Magbata’s case shows a pattern of harassment and abuses against Indigenous Peoples, farmers, and community organizers in Mindoro where those asserting their rights are often accused of links to the communist armed movement.


The group cited the killings of Indigenous and peasant individuals Jay-el Maligday, Hulyo Agtay, and Juan Sumilhig which it attributed to military abuses. It also stressed the case of Dolores Solangon, an elderly Mangyan-Iraya woman who reportedly endured illegal arrest and nine hours of torture at the hands of elements from the 76th IB.


Maligday, a young Hanunuo-Mangyan, was allegedly killed by soldiers of the 4th IB while sleeping in his home. The same unit was accused of beating another Hanunuo-Mangyan, Minggo, in Mansalay early this year.


For Defend Mindoro, these abuses are inseparable from the land disputes and economic hardships confronting Indigenous communities and farmers.


In Bulalacao, the group said that large-scale mining and renewable energy projects threaten ancestral lands and local livelihoods. These include developments associated with CleanTech Global Renewables and Singapore-based The Blue Circle which is reportedly planning an offshore wind project involving 100 turbines across a proposed 40,050-hectare area.


Meanwhile, drought has exacerbated the farmers’ hardship. In 2024, an estimated 864 hectares of farmland in Bulalacao were damaged, resulting in P87 million (US$1.37 million) in agricultural losses and affecting around 1,000 registered farmers, according to Defend Mindoro. With another severe El Niño episode looming, communities face renewed threats of crop failure and water shortage.


The group criticized the government for prioritizing counterinsurgency operations over addressing rural poverty, landlessness, and the climate crisis. It said that militarization further endangers communities already struggling to protect their livelihoods and ancestral territories.


Accountability


Defend Mindoro demanded an independent investigation into the allegations of torture and illegal detention. Torture is prohibited under international law and civilians must be protected from violence and cruel treatment in situations of armed conflict.


The group held the 203rd IBde and the Marcos Jr. administration accountable for the alleged violations, calling for an end to military harassment of Indigenous Peoples and farmers.


For Defend Mindoro, Magbata’s case underscores the dangers faced by community organizers defending the rights of rural communities. “No allegation of insurgency can justify torture or the denial of due process,” the group wrote in a statement.

(DAA)

author: 张皓翔
title: The Dislocation of Vendémiaire (IV): The Misrecognized Socialism and the Resisters Who Refuse Connection 【葡月的错位（四）被误认的社会主义与拒绝联结的抗争者】 【A commentary on the French riots between September and October】
content:
This essay is the fourth part of The Dislocation of Vendémiaire. Drawing on Karl Marx's famous "sack of potatoes" metaphor from 1851, it contrasts the historical inability of the French peasantry to unite with the contemporary resisters of the 2026 French/European movements who actively "refuse connection." The author argues that while previous struggles centered on physiological survival, modern struggles have shifted to the realm of existential subjectivity—the refusal to be treated as mere interchangeable parts ("elementalization") within social machinery. The essay re-examines the Soviet experience, arguing that it substituted market-based elementalization with a planned one, thereby creating a historical illusion that alienated modern resisters from political organizations. Ultimately, the text critiques the movement's decentralized, anti-party stance as "eating the child with the bathwater," arguing that without the vanguard, organization, and discipline, resisting a highly organized capitalist state machine is impossible.

author: Natascha Elena Uhlmann
title: Mexico Volkswagen Workers Could Soon Strike
content:
In Mexico, at the world’s largest Volkswagen facility outside of Germany, workers are weighing the risks of a possible strike.


The 6,500 workers build the Jetta, Tiguan, and Taos at the company’s Puebla plant. Their union, SITIAVW, is one of Mexico’s most storied independent unions, and is in the midst of the plant’s annual wage reopener negotiations.


Days before the strike deadline of October 22, the company presented two proposals—offering raises of 7.98 percent and 7.95 percent for a one-year duration—which were rejected by the union. Soon afterwards, the company presented another offer: an 8.24 percent increase, of which 3.59 percent is a one-time payment of 12,000 pesos, equivalent to about $641 U.S. The deal would maintain the yearly salary reopener, a cycle the company had tried to lengthen in previous offers. Workers will vote on the offer on October 28, and could strike the next day if a deal is not reached.


On October 15, workers voted down an offer that  would have provided a 13 percent combined increase to wages and benefits over the next two years. The vote was 3,135 against and 2,452 for.


A month earlier, workers had overwhelmingly voted down the previous offer of a 10 percent combined increase. (The union had been pushing for a 17 percent increase earlier in negotiations.) Days before that first agreement was put to a vote, Volkswagen cut one of three shifts in a segment of the plant that produces the Jetta and the Tiguan. About

800 workers

 lost their jobs,

El Financiero

 reported.


Although the union announced that 611 of the workers—those who did not sign voluntary separation agreements—would be eligible for reinstatement when Volkswagen begins production of its Golf compact car at the Puebla facility next April, the damage was done. 5,925 of the company’s 6,440 eligible voters participated in the ratification vote: of them,

73 percent voted to reject the offer

, in what SITIAVW advisor Willebaldo Gómez Zuppa characterized as an expression of anger at the firings. The deal would have also

pushed the next wage reopener

 to 18 months out instead of the yearly cycle, angering workers.


‘NOT AT OUR EXPENSE’


Workers were also frustrated with the company’s efforts to put off their next wage reopener for 18 months rather than a year. The second offer would have pushed the wage reopener out even further, to two years.


“We are not blind to the delicate crisis facing the German automotive industry, nor are we ignoring the global financial challenges Volkswagen cites,” the union

said

 in a statement in September after workers voted down the first offer. “But let it be heard loud and clear, all the way to Wolfsburg: corporate crises will not be resolved at the expense of the sweat, the rights, and the future of the Mexican working class.”


Volkswagen did not respond to requests for comment. In a statement sent to

La Jornada de Oriente

, VW

said

, "We respect the result of the vote... and at the same time, express our deep worry and disappointment. This agreement represents the greatest viable offer from the company, given current conditions.”


GLOBAL LAYOFFS


In September, VW announced plans to eliminate

50,000 jobs

 globally by 2030, alongside another 50,000 already anticipated cuts—together representing the largest culling of jobs ever by a single automaker.


The company noted in September that its European factories have the capacity to produce

500,000 more vehicles per year

 than it can sell. The industry faces

“enormous pressure”

 due to low cost electric vehicles produced in China, Volkswagen's CEO Oliver ​Blume said at the Paris Motor Show in October.  Its restructuring plan calls for eliminating half the models it produces (the less profitable half).


IG Metall, which represents 120,000 Volkswagen workers in Germany and sits on the company’s supervisory board, agreed to accept the closure of four German plants between 2031 and 2034, telling the

Guardian

 that both labor and management had made concessions to stave off “a dangerous escalation of the conflict.”


Workers at VW's only U.S. assembly plant, in Chattanooga, Tennessee, joined the United Auto Workers in 2024 after years of trying, and ratified their first contract earlier this year. So far the cuts have not affected them.


It remains unclear how many more cuts are expected in Puebla. Since 2012, the plant has cut its workforce by 36 percent,

Milenio reported

author: Tam Saavedra
title: ¡Las Directrices de la CDPD de la ONU sobre Interseccionalidad están aquí!
content:
Las Directrices de la CDPD de la ONU sobre Interseccionalidad acaban de cambiar las reglas del juego para los derechos de las personas con discapacidad: Esto es lo que necesitas saber

 


¡Grandes noticias para las mujeres con discapacidad y para todas las personas defensoras, aliadas y organizaciones feministas y con discapacidad en todo el mundo!

 


Durante su 35º Período de Sesiones en agosto de 2026, el

Comité de las Naciones Unidas sobre los Derechos de las Personas con Discapacidad

 (CDPD de la ONU)

 adoptó oficialmente las

Directrices sobre la Identificación y Abordaje de la Discriminación Interseccional Contra las Niñas, Adolescentes, Mujeres y Mujeres Mayores con Discapacidad

.

 


Este hito representa un paso gigante para los derechos de las personas con discapacidad. Por primera vez, los Estados Partes cuentan con orientación explícita y accionable para respaldar sus obligaciones en la intersección entre género y discapacidad.

 


Lee las Directrices oficiales de la CDPD de la ONU aquí

 


¿Qué son las Directrices de la CDPD sobre Discriminación Interseccional?

 


Las Directrices constituyen un marco internacional autorizado, desarrollado por la CDPD de la ONU, para ayudar a los Estados a prevenir, supervisar y abordar de mejor manera la discriminación interseccional.

 


A lo largo de años de procesos de revisión de países por parte de la CDPD de la ONU, el Comité identificó una brecha persistente y crítica:

los derechos humanos específicos de las mujeres con discapacidad y la discriminación interseccional y compleja que experimentan, rara vez son comprendidas o abordadas por los gobiernos.

 


Al celebrar el 20º aniversario de la CDPD de la ONU

, e

stas Directrices fueron emitidas para cerrar esa brecha, garantizando que la convención se aplique a favor de

todas

las mujeres y niñas con discapacidad, y las personas de género diverso con discapacidad a lo largo de sus vidas.

 


¿Por qué estas Directrices cambian las reglas del juego?

 


Los documentos internacionales rara vez se centran de forma explícita en las experiencias de vida y los derechos de las mujeres con discapacidad. Estas Directrices nombran y explican las barreras sistémicas que las mujeres y personas de género diverso con discapacidad enfrentan a diario en todo el mundo, incluyendo:

 


Salud y Derechos Sexuales y Reproductivos (SDSR):

 Abordar y prevenir la esterilización forzada, la anticoncepción forzada, la falta de atención médica accesible, las restricciones al aborto y la falta de atención perinatal, menstrual y menopáusica.

 


Violencia de Género y Basada en la Discapacidad:

 Exponer la violencia institucional, el abuso digital/en línea y la falta generalizada de servicios de apoyo para las víctimas.

 


Reconocimiento de las labores de cuidado:

 Validar a las mujeres con discapacidad como cuidadoras activas y madres, en lugar de tratarlas únicamente como receptoras de cuidados.

 


Exclusión económica y educativa:

 Destacar las barreras en el mercado laboral y la exclusión de la educación durante la pubertad.

 


Respuesta a crisis y cambio climático:

 Combatir la exclusión agravada durante desastres ambientales, emergencias climáticas y esfuerzos de ayuda humanitaria.

 


Por nombrar sólo algunas.

 


7 avances clave en el enfoque de las Directrices

 


Lo que hace que este documento sea un instrumento transformador único es su enfoque estructural y progresista:

 


Inclusión explícita de la diversidad de género:

 Las Directrices abarcan explícitamente los derechos de las personas transgénero, intersexuales, no binarias y de otras diversidades de género con discapacidad, y solicitan una interpretación inclusiva de la diversidad de género de todas las obligaciones descritas.

 


Reconocimiento de las raíces históricas:

 El Comité aborda explícitamente el legado y los impactos continuos del colonialismo y la esclavización, estableciendo que los Estados que se benefician de estos sistemas históricos tienen la responsabilidad particular de reparar sus efectos actuales.

 


Un catálogo abierto de diversidad:

 El texto reconoce que las mujeres con discapacidad pertenecen a comunidades multimarginalizadas —incluidos grupos indígenas, afrodescendientes/negros, dalit, adivasi, refugiados, solicitantes de asilo, minorías religiosas, pastoriles o personas que viven en asentamientos informales, entre otros— dejando espacio para todas las identidades interseccionales.

title: Презентация книги Марии Рахманиновой «Контуры автономии. Черновики к анархистской феноменологии субъекта»
content:
Тбилисский книжный магазин Odradek приглашает на презентацию новой книги Марии Рахманиновой.

28.10 20:00 Odradek Bookstore Dzmebi Zubalashvili, 40

На презентации выступит сама Мария, а также автор одного из предисловий к книге Дмитрий Поляков. Все остальные также приглашаются к дискуссии после вступительных слов — как те, кто уже успел ознакомиться с текстом, так и те, кто познакомится с его содержанием через доклады-сообщения выступающих.

Книга Рахманиновой приглашает к вдумчивому и внимательному вглядыванию в вопрос о том, что есть общее и что есть особенное, обращаясь к классикам анархистской мысли и к наиболее видным и скрытым в тени западным философам современности, чьё внимание также касается этого вопроса.

«Предлагаемые „черновики“ — если не первое, то определённо редкое в русскоязычном пространстве философско-антропологическое высказывание о субъекте, скрупулёзно увязывающее анархизм с научным дискурсом XXI века. Выходя в свет, этот текст выводит с собой из тени и либертарную мысль о личности, то и дело вытесняемую „здравым смыслом“ Левиафана. И в этой очередной реактивации анархистских установок, безусловно, есть нечто обнадёживающее — как минимум, их не изживающая себя актуальность». Дмитрий Поляков.

Книжный магазин Odradek напоминает, что книгу уже можно приобрести и совсем скоро — в других независимых книжных Тбилиси. По поводу доставки и появления книг в других городах и странах Odradek обещает своевременно оповестить.

title: Boğaziçi'nde Nurettin Yıldız protestosu davasında gazeteci Öztürk'e beraat, 14 öğrenciye ceza talebi
content:
Mayıs 2025'te  Boğaziçi Üniversitesi'ndeki protesto sırasında gözaltına alınan 14 öğrenci ve T24 muhabiri Can Öztürk'ün yargılandığı davanın beşinci duruşmasında savcı esas hakkındaki mütalaasını sundu.


Medya ve Hukuk Çalışmaları Derneği'nden (MLSA) Canan Coşkun'un haberine göre İstanbul 69. Asliye Ceza Mahkemesi'ndeki duruşmada savcı, dosyadaki görüntülerde Can Öztürk'ün protestoyu görüntülediğinin anlaşıldığını belirterek suçlamaların kanıtlanamadığını bildirdi.


Mütalaada, Öztürk'ün cezalandırılması için “her türlü şüpheden uzak kesin ve inandırıcı delil” elde edilemediği belirtilerek beraatine karar verilmesi talep edildi.


Öztürk, Mayıs 2025'te Boğaziçi Üniversitesi'ndeki protestoyu takip ederken polisler tarafından gözaltına alınmış, daha sonra yurt dışına çıkış yasağı ve karakola imza verme yükümlülüğüyle serbest bırakılmıştı.


14 öğrenciye dört ayrı suçlama


Savcı, protestoya katılan 14 öğrencinin ise polislerin oluşturduğu güvenlik hattına yüklenerek bazı polislerin inşaat çukuruna düşmesine ve yaralanmasına neden olduğunu ileri sürdü.


Mütalaaya göre olayda bir polisin parmağı kırılmış, diğerleri ise basit tıbbi müdahaleyle giderilebilecek ölçüde yaralanmışlardı. 


Savcı, öğrencilerin 2911 sayılı Toplantı ve Gösteri Yürüyüşleri Kanunu'nun 32. Maddesinde yer alan direnme suçunun yanı sıra Türk Ceza Kanunu'nun 265, 86 ve 87. Maddelerindeki görevi yaptırmamak için direnme, kasten yaralama ve neticesi sebebiyle ağırlaşmış yaralama suçlarından cezalandırılmasını istedi.


Öğrenciler ise suçlamaları reddetti. Daha önceki savunmalarında da öğrenciler, polislerin kendilerini çember içine aldığını ve sıkışıklık nedeniyle nefes alamadıklarını anlatmışlardı.


Avukatlar: "Polislerin sağlık raporları çelişkili"


Duruşmada öğrencilerin avukatı Özge Durdu, müşteki polis amiri Mustafa Ermenek'in sağlık raporları arasında çelişki bulunduğunu ileri sürdü.


Durdu, ilk sağlık raporunda herhangi bir yaralanma tespit edilmemesine rağmen sonraki raporda Ermenek'in basit tıbbi müdahaleyle giderilebilecek şekilde yaralandığının belirtildiğine dikkat çekti.


Ermenek'in dosyasında 26 Haziran 2026 tarihli bir fizik tedavi raporu da bulunduğunu hatırlatan Durdu, raporların birbirini doğrulamadığını savundu.


Öğrencilerin avukatlarından Gamze Serin Şimşek de bu çelişkileri ayrıntılı savunmalarında ele alacaklarını söyledi.


Mahkeme, avukatlara mütalaaya karşı savunmalarını hazırlamaları için süre vererek duruşmayı 11 Ocak 2027 saat 09.30'a erteledi.


6 öğrenci tutuklanmıştı


Dava, çocuk yaşta evliliği meşrulaştıran

açıklamalarıyla

 tepki çeken ilahiyatçı Nurettin Yıldız'ın 13 Mayıs 2025'te Boğaziçi Üniversitesi'ne konuşmacı olarak davet edilmesi üzerine başlayan protestolarla ilgili.


Öğrenciler üniversitede basın açıklaması yapmak isterken polis müdahalesiyle karşılaşmış, 14 öğrenci ve protestoyu izleyen T24 muhabiri gazeteci Can Öztürk gözaltına alınmıştı.


Öğrencilerden 6'sı olaydan hemen sonra tutuklanmış, 8'i adli kontrolle serbest bırakılmıştı.


Boğaziçi'nde 'Nureddin Yıldız'ı protesto eden 6 genç tutuklandı


14 Mayıs 2025


Tutuklu öğrenciler de daha sonra tahliye edildi.


Dava sürerken polislerin şikâyetleri üzerine açılan ikinci dosyanın ilk davayla birleştirilmesi sonucunda öğrenciler yeniden savunma vermek zorunda kalmışlardı.

author: anonym
title: Navigieren auf einer neuen Welle von Unruhen
content:
Jetzt ist es wieder soweit, europäische Regierungen zucken zusammen vor Tausenden Randalierer*innen die in den Metropolen auf die Straße gehen, ohne das sie von den Polizeikräften in Schach zu halten sind. Macron tönt, nicht zum ersten Mal in seiner Amtszeit:


„Wer zerstört hat, muss dafür bezahlen. Wer geplündert hat, muss den Schaden ersetzen. Wer versucht hat, die Republik zu stürzen, wird dafür zur Rechenschaft gezogen.“


Die Papageien der Medien schäumen vor Wut, wie immer wenn die Ohnmacht die Seiten wechselt, und auch die freiwilligen Putzkräfte, die im Sommer 2017 beim G20 in Hamburg mit Bürsten die Bordsteine des Schanzenviertels von Krawallspuren beseitigten sind am Start. Jetzt kratzen sie in Paris geschmolzene Leihräder aus dem Asphalt oder sortieren Mülltonnen in Mailand.


Aber wo sind wir? Überrascht von diesen Wutexplosionen, zu deren entstehen wir wie so oft, nicht viel beitragen konnten. Um nicht den Überblick zu verlieren, eine unvollständige Zusammenfassung der letzten Events,


Brüssel


Am 9. Oktober folgten 30.000 Menschen den Aufrufen von Gewerkschaften gegen die antisozialen Maßnahmen der Regierung. Schüler*innen und Student*innen blockierten Bildungseinrichtungen. Von morgens bis abends kam es im Zentrum, im Bereich der Bahnhöfe zu Zusammenstößen mit den Bullen. Unterbrechung des Konsums, statt die wie eine Pest verbreiteten E-Scooter für eine leicht zu trackende Fortbewegung zu nutzen, werden sie heute von Jugendlichen massenhaft ins Feuer geworfen. Die Spannungen hatten sich schon an den Vortagen und auch in anderen Städten angekündigt.


Am 17. Oktober weitere Krawalle in Brüssel und Lüttich, 195 Festnahmen bei einer Demo gegen die Sparmaßnahmen im frankophonen Bildungswesen, gegen die Polizei und gegen die aktuelle belgische Regierung.


Paris


Nachdem letztes Jahr eine Alles Blockieren Bewegung im September an vielen Orten eskaliert war, wurde deren vermeintliches Ende mit einer lahmen Stimmung eines müden Generalstreiks Anfang Oktober 2025 besiegelt. Um plötzlich mit den diesjährigen Bildungsprotesten und Schulblockaden in eine neue Runde zu gehen. Seit Wochen tut die CRS das, was sie immer macht, sie schießen Demonstrant*innen mit Flash-balls die Augen raus und sprengen Jugendlichen mit Granaten die Hände weg. Aber offenbar war am 17. Oktober die Wut größer als die Angst und Frankreichweit wurden Bullen angegriffen, Geschäfte geplündert, Symbole des Staats zerstört. Trotz jahrzehntelanger Erfahrung mit Aufstandsbekämpfung, gelingt es Politik und Verwaltung bisher nicht, die Allianzen von Schüler*innen, Überresten der Gelb Westen, Banlieue Bewohner*innen, Linken und anderweitig Angepissten zu spalten. Macron, der seine Truppen von Kanaky bis Erbil kämpfen lässt und momentan besonders die Golf Monarchien verteidigen will, kündigt Verhaftungswellen und Ausgangssperren an.


Barcelona


Lange blieb es ruhig in Barcelona aber am 5. Oktober kam es wegen der Wohnungsproblematik zu Riots im Zentrum. 100.000 Menschen beteiligten sich an einer Demo, zu der die Sindicat de Llogateres tenants‘ union aufgerufen hatte, danach Unruhen im Bereich Plaça Catalunya und La Rambla. Bullen setzten wie immer Gummigeschosse ein, 30 Mossos wurden verletzt, Stadtmobiliar lieferte an 28 Stellen das Barrikadenmaterial. Die Sprecherin des Sindicat erklärte als Ziel, das Land zu paralyzieren. Die Regierung hat nach dem Tod von Maricarmen Abascal aufgrund der Zwangsräumung und ihrem Scheitern in der Wohnungspolitik Neuwahlen für den 29. November angekündigt. Anarchist*innen verteilen ein Flugblatt während der disturbios:


„Möge die Wut über alle hinwegfegen. Politische Parteien, Gewerkschaften, Parlamente, alle Organisationen links von der PSOE, Polizei, Richter, Journalisten, Faschisten, jeder einzelne von ihnen ist Teil desselben Apparats zur Kontrolle und Bewältigung unseres Elends. … Unser einziges Ziel ist es, Bündnisse im Kampf und auf der Straße zwischen Gleichen zu knüpfen, unsere Klassenfeinde zu identifizieren und sie mit allen Mitteln anzugreifen.“


Mailand


Am 17. und 18. Oktober erlebte Mailand in seinem kommerziellen Zentrum die Ausschreitungen, die es verdient. Dort drehte sich die Demonstration um die für viele nicht mehr zahlbaren Lebenshaltungskosten. Wie in den anderen Städten auch wurden Bullen angegriffen, Geschäfte geplündert, Banken zerstört und überflüssiges Zeug den Flammen übergeben. Der Bürgermeister Giuseppe Sala befand:

author: Λουκάς Σταμέλλος
title: Ο αντεισαγγελέας ΑΠ Βασίλης Φλωρίδης γίνεται το πρόσωπο της διαφθοράς
content:
Σύνδεσμος δημοσίευσης:

Ο αντεισαγγελέας ΑΠ Βασίλης Φλωρίδης γίνεται το πρόσωπο της διαφθοράς


Ο Βασίλης Φλωρίδης, αντεισαγγελέας Αρείου Πάγου και αδελφός του υπουργού Δικαιοσύνης Γιώργου Φλωρίδη,

δημοσίευσε στην «Καθημερινή» ένα «άρθρο»

 με το οποίο

πέρασε γενεές δεκατέσσαρες τους υφισταμένους του εισαγγελείς


και τα δικαστικά συμβούλια

 γιατί έστειλαν σε δίκη – που

επίκειται

 να φτάσει στο ακροατήριο – 11 άτομα, μεταξύ των οποίων υψηλόβαθμους αξιωματικούς και τον τότε αρχηγό της ΕΛ.ΑΣ.


Το αντικείμενο αυτής της δικογραφίας; Η απόπειρα συγκάλυψης της σύλληψης του γιου του υπουργού (τότε Προστασίας του Πολίτη και νυν Ανάπτυξης) Τάκη Θεοδωρικάκου τον Νοέμβριο του 2021. Η ίδια η σύλληψη μικρή σημασία είχε, καθώς επρόκειτο για το γελοίο «αδίκημα» της κατοχής μικρής ποσότητας κάνναβης. Αυτό που έχει σημασία είναι ότι, κατά τη δικογραφία, φέρεται να κινητοποιήθηκαν «λυτοί και δεμένοι» για να μη γίνει σύλληψη του γιου του υπουργού.

Περισσότερα για την παραπομπή των κατηγορουμένων μπορείτε να διαβάσετε εδώ

.


Με λίγα λόγια, για να γίνει κατανοητό το μέγεθος της ωμής παρέμβασης:


Aδελφός υπουργού χρησιμοποιεί την επιρροή της θεσμικής του ιδιότητας

για να προκαταλάβει το αποτέλεσμα


επικείμενης


ποινικής δίκης

 που αντιμετωπίζει ο γιος ενός άλλου υπουργού. Κι αυτό συνέβη μέσω μιας εφημερίδας – πυλώνα της ελληνικής Δεξιάς, με μεγάλη απήχηση στους δικαστικούς κύκλους.


Η παρέμβαση του Βασίλη Φλωρίδη δεν σχολιάζει κάποια γενικά χαρακτηριστικά υποθέσεων τα οποία δεν μπορούν να συνδεθούν με συγκεκριμένη δικογραφία. Δίνει ουσιαστικά «γραμμή» στους δικαστές που θα κρίνουν την υπόθεση. Κι αυτό το κάνει σχολιάζοντας την ουσία του σκεπτικού των υφισταμένων του εισαγγελέων, με αμετροέπειες όπως:


Και οι τέσσερις εισαγγελείς που αντιστάθηκαν, κατέγραψαν στα δικαστικά τους κείμενα ένα κοινό βασικό δεδομένο: Οτι τα αποδεικτικά στοιχεία που υποτίθεται θεμελίωναν τα εγκλήματα, ήταν σαθρά και δεν μπορούσαν να στηρίξουν τις κατηγορίες. Στη συγκεκριμένη περίπτωση δεν επρόκειτο για έκφραση κρίσης πίσω από την οποία θα μπορούσε να καλυφθεί ο δικαστής. Ηταν κατασκευή κρίσης.


Ο αντεισαγγελέας του Αρείου Πάγου καταλήγει σε λυρικές περιγραφές για «φλέβες διαφθοράς» που «καταλήγουν στην καρδιά του οργανισμού» και «πόρτα της διαφθοράς» που «ανοίγει πάντα από μέσα».


Όλα αυτά επειδή κάποιοι εισαγγελείς και κάποιοι δικαστές στα συμβούλια

δεν θεώρησαν ότι επειδή πρόκειται για γιο υπουργού πρέπει να κάνουν τα στραβά μάτια

 στην απόπειρα συγκάλυψης.


Ευχολόγια οι αντιδράσεις των δικαστικών


Όπως ήταν αναμενόμενο, η πρωτοφανής (

ναι, ακόμα και για την ελλαδική πραγματικότητα είναι πρωτοφανής μια τόσο ωμή


εξωθεσμική


παρέμβαση εν ενεργεία εισαγγελέα στην εξέλιξη μιας ποινικής δικογραφίας

) ακρότητα του Β. Φλωρίδη έχει προκαλέσει αυτό που τα ΜΜΕ αγαπούν να ονομάζουν «θύελλα αντιδράσεων».


Η

Ένωση Δικαστών και Εισαγγελέων στην ανακοίνωσή της

 υπενθύμισε ότι

«Είναι ο ίδιος εισαγγελικός λειτουργός που

σε


παλαιότερο άρθρο του στο Βήμα


έγραφε ότι “οι δικαστικοί λειτουργοί που έχουν συγγενικά πρόσωπα με ενεργή ενασχόληση στην πολιτική πρέπει να απέχουν από τον χειρισμό υποθέσεων στα οποία εμπλέκονται πολιτικά πρόσωπα –οι τιμιότεροι όλων κι αν είναι”

»

. Στην ίδια ανακοίνωση, ωστόσο, η ΕνΔΕ δεν χάνει την ευκαιρία να επιτεθεί και στους… δικηγόρους, για κάποιο λόγο, παρουσιάζοντας μια ιδιότυπη «θεωρία των δύο άκρων».


Ο ίδιος

ο Άρειος Πάγος με δελτίο Τύπου του

 χαρακτήρισε

«θυμική αντίδραση επικοινωνιακού χαρακτήρα»

 το «άρθρο» του αντεισαγγελέα του, σημειώνοντας:

«Τέτοιες δημοσιεύσεις, που αφορούν εκκρεμή υπόθεση ενώπιον του Α΄


βαθμού δικαιοδοσίας και πρόκειται να εκδικασθεί άμεσα, οι οποίες περιέχουν μομφή και καταγγέλλουν αορίστως τους επιληφθέντες δικαστές ως διεφθαρμένους, εκφεύγουν των ορίων της οποιασδήποτε κριτικής των δικαστικών αποφάσεων και βουλευμάτων και πλήττουν την εμπιστοσύνη των πολιτών στο θεσμό της Δικαιοσύνης

»

.


Πρόταση για πειθαρχική αναφορά από την Εναλλακτική Παρέμβαση


Η Εναλλακτική Παρέμβαση Δικηγόρων Αθήνας, με

επιστολή των συμβούλων της προς το Διοικητικό Συμβούλιο του Δικηγορικού Συλλόγου Αθηνών

 επισημαίνει ότι οι ανακοινώσεις αποτροπιασμού δεν αρκούν:


Είναι προφανές ότι απέναντι σε αυτή την κατάπτωση δεν αρκούν οι ανακοινώσεις, σαν και αυτή που εξέδωσε η Ένωση Δικαστών και Εισαγγελέων, πιθανά δε να λειτουργούν και εκτονωτικά. Η τελευταία, την ώρα που κατηγορεί δικηγόρους και διοργανώνει έστω και αποτυχημένη ημερίδα για «ακραίες συμπεριφορές τους κατά δικαστών», έχει σαστίσει …

Ανοιχτό κάλεσμα προς την κοινωνία


Χωρίς τη συλλογική δράση, οι ιδέες κοιμούνται στα κεφάλια και στις βιβλιοθήκες. Η γέννηση της πολιτικής ελευθερίας συμβαδίζει με τον αγώνα για τη συλλογική ιδιοποίηση της θεσμίζουσας αρχής.


Eduardo Colombo


Ως Κοινότητα Κατειλημμένων Προσφυγικών καθ’ όλη τη διάρκεια του πολύμηνου και πολυεπίπεδου αγώνα ενάντια στα τελευταία σχέδια του κράτους και του κεφαλαίου βαδίσαμε και αγωνιστήκαμε πλάι πλάι με τους συντρόφους μας απεργούς πείνας μέχρι θανάτου Αριστοτέλη Χαντζή και Suzon Doppagne και από κοινού με όλους τους ανθρώπους των κινημάτων και της αλληλεγγύης. Ανθρώπους από ευρύτερες κοινωνικές ομάδες που αναγνώρισαν αυτόν τον αγώνα της Κοινότητας ως έναν συλλογικό αγώνα της κοινωνίας που αφορά όλες και όλους, συγκροτώντας ένα ευρύ κοινωνικό μέτωπο.


Και όπως αγωνιστήκαμε συλλογικά, νικήσαμε και συλλογικά!


Έχοντας κλείσει λοιπόν τον πρώτο μεγάλο κύκλο νικηφόρα, είναι ξεκάθαρο πως αυτό που έχουμε να υπερασπιστούμε δεν είναι μόνο αυτή η συγκεκριμένη νίκη ή μια ρωγμή που αποτέλεσε μια στιγμή στον χρόνο ή μια αυτοαναφορική συνθήκη εντός της οποίας βρίσκει τον εαυτό της η Κοινότητα Κατειλημμένων Προσφυγικών. Η παρακαταθήκη αυτού του αγώνα και της νίκης στο παρόν και το μέλλον απλώνεται μπροστά μας αναδεικνύοντας μια τεράστια δυνατότητα: Να ξαναχτίσουμε το συλλογικό φαντασιακό του κόσμου της αλληλεγγύης, της καθημερινής αντίστασης απέναντι στην εξαθλίωση, τον φόβο, την υποταγή, την εξατομίκευση, αντιτάσσοντας την αυτοθέσμιση των κοινωνιών μας και τη συγκρότηση κοινοτήτων, οπουδήποτε οι άνθρωποι αγωνίζονται, στις γειτονιές, σε πόλεις και χωριά, στους χώρους δουλειάς, στα σχολεία και τα πανεπιστήμια, στον δημόσιο χώρο.


Υπό αυτό το πρίσμα καλούμε σε μία διήμερη εκδήλωση στις 24 και 25 Οκτώβρη στις 17.00 στο Πάντειο Πανεπιστήμιο, (Νέο Κτήριο, Αίθουσα Σάκη Καράγιωργα Ι) για να συζητήσουμε πάνω στους κεντρικούς άξονες που δομήθηκε ο αγώνας αυτός, στις διαφορετικές μεθόδους και στα εργαλεία που χρησιμοποιήσαμε, καθώς και να δούμε συλλογικά και συνολικά τα σημεία που οδήγησαν στη νίκη αλλά και τις αδυναμίες, τις αστοχίες και τα λάθη που υπήρξαν. Αλλά κυρίως να εστιάσουμε στη συλλογική δυνατότητα που ανοίχτηκε μέσω αυτού του αγώνα και που πρέπει να διευρύνουμε. Να ενώσουμε τις αντιστάσεις μας για να δημιουργήσουμε τους όρους μιας κοινής δύναμης και να μετατρέψουμε την αλληλεγγύη από αντανακλαστικό σε σταθερή κοινωνική σχέση. Γιατί οι αγώνες κερδίζονται όταν …

author: Ahmed Ismat Ahmed
title: How a child inherits care
content:
We are sitting at Gallal. It’s in Madinaty, on the edge of Cairo where the buildings are all new and the streets are too wide. The tea is too sweet the way Sudanese tea is supposed to be too sweet when someone else makes it for you. Mahmoud is across from me.

I don’t remember either of us standing up. Only the hug itself, which went on long enough that an Egyptian girl at the next table put down her phone and started crying. She didn’t know us. She cried because whatever passed between two men holding on to each other in the middle of that cafe was apparently visible even to a stranger who had no context at all.

Mahmoud went red immediately — a Sudanese man has no idea what to do with a stranger’s tears — so he pulled out his phone, opened Facebook, and muttered that she was probably crying over some relationship, while the screen in his hand played footage of Khartoum burning. We’re good at that silence now. The silence of being physically tethered to one place while completely living inside another. I kept thinking: Does everyone I love do the same? Carry so much that they stop feeling it, until a stranger has to cry for them?

The screen lights up. The wallpaper is a photo of my grandfather’s class in Wadi Halfa, built after the water took Halfa Dagheim. The first time my grandmother told me about it, she didn’t say “displacement.” She said, “We left the house, and the water took it.” Halfa Dagheim was going to drown for the High Dam — a decision made far away by people who would never bear its cost. When they moved to Wadi Halfa, there was only dust. The first shared project families built was a school. The teacher was my grandfather Ahmed, an English teacher. He gathered children under a tree and started. I inherited that before I understood it. Not money. Not land. The habit of starting under a tree when the official map says your town should no longer exist.

The waitress calls me

ya walad

 even though I am 29. That word makes me think of my mother. Her father died during her certificate exams. She carried grief silently and kept studying until she earned admission to veterinary school at the University of Khartoum. She graduated while pregnant with me. I came from that lineage of exhausted people who kept choosing endurance.

When I entered the University of Khartoum in 2015, I thought I was entering a sanctuary. The conversations that shaped us happened beside roads, under trees, around tea stalls that surrounded campus from every direction. The women who ran them knew who was always late, who never had money, who argued too much, who quietly listened. They knew us better than the administration.

For a long time I thought we had to be hard to win. I thought we had to stop feeling to keep going. I was wrong. The only thing that ever saved us was the opposite. The tea. The sitting together after. The hand that was out before you asked. They can turn violence into money. They can turn gold into weapons. They cannot turn care into money. Care refuses to be bought. That is why they fear it.

In the republic of the unimportant — at the tea stalls, in the resistance committees, in the unions that kept meeting in borrowed rooms after being banned — we kept a different ledger. Not gold. Who was missing, who needed medicine, who hadn’t eaten. That ledger didn’t make anyone rich. It kept people alive.

At Gallal, Mahmoud orders a second tea without asking me. He knows I will want it. We have this habit from Khartoum — you order for the other person before he finishes, so he doesn’t have to say he wants more but has no money. He pushes sugar toward me. That small push is the whole essay. You notice who needs sugar and you push it without making a speech.

And finally — to the child walking into a school that hasn’t been built yet, with a notebook slipping against his arm. Inside, a poster on the wall is crooked. Someone taped it in a hurry and left one corner hanging. He will stop, shift the notebook to the other arm, and straighten it without thinking. He learned that from someone who sat next to him when he cried. That is ordinary. That is how a child inherits care.

title: Khartoum courts UN-backed relief to stave off truce pressure; Tasis govt heedful after health minister’s angry exit; Abyei strike tests Juba ties; Drones hit RSF, military’s seats of power; RSF pushes in Kurmuk, military wins Geisan ground
content:
Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter


here

.


From Khartoum and Nyala, to a gold mine in South Kordofan, a town in West Kordofan and a power station in White Nile, drones tore through Sudan this week, killing hundreds and destroying homes, livelihoods and critical infrastructure.


Both sides traded blame, and each pointed to neighbors it said let the drones through. Some strikes went unclaimed, but silence from the military over its attack on the disputed Abyei region didn’t stop Juba from summoning Sudan’s ambassador on the same day to warn of a “dangerous development” in a border territory already straining relations between the two countries. Khartoum weighed in days later, with a Foreign Ministry statement denying the military was involved.


The strike on the RSF-held Naam market in Abyei set fuel depots burning. The fires were still consuming the area as the death toll exceeded 150 and thousands were displaced, and residents took to the streets in protest, activists and Abyei administration sources said.


In the Security Council, in Geneva and among mediators on Sudan, the warnings this week over the drone war and the humanitarian toll sounded much as they have for months, and they still amount to little beyond adding pressure on the warring parties to stop the fighting.


But Khartoum won’t concede an end to

RSF territorial control

before a truce can take hold, and won’t see the paramilitary group at the table in any political process on the country’s future.


So instead of committing to a broader settlement, it is now trying to show it can deliver on humanitarian issues, betting that progress on aid deliveries and civilian protection will

blunt

 international criticism, former and current Sudanese officials and sources close to the Transitional Sovereignty Council told Mada Masr.


Hence the letters to Western capitals over the week and the talks with the United Nations on internationally monitored aid deliveries, which allow Khartoum to appear willing to engage without participating on terms it rejects, former officials said. Any plan, however, has to keep aid under the authority of state institutions, they added.


In western Sudan, the RSF’s parallel administration is trying to hold on to the very recognition Khartoum is trying to deny it, but its own infighting is getting in the way. Tasis’s Cabinet is trying to take oversight of medical aid away from a health minister who had protested for months over interference by the RSF and influential figures looking to monopolize medical supplies. He left for Nairobi in protest last week, and a government already reeling from recent defections is treading carefully, wary of another exit that would further damage its image as a viable administration before aid organizations.


In Blue Nile State, the push and pull on the battlefield goes on. The RSF and its ally, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North led by Abdel Aziz al-Hilu, tried to take two of the military’s bases in Kurmuk locality, part of the network protecting the state capital of Damazin, though accounts of how it ended conflict. The military, meanwhile, gained ground in neighboring Geisan locality, taking two areas that a former military officer said could help check the RSF’s new advances in Wad al-Mahi locality.


***


Military drone strike on Abyei market draws protest from Juba


Caption: Undersecretary of the South Sudanese Foreign Ministry Agnes Adlino Orifa Oswaha and Sudan’s ambassador to Juba, Essam Karar, discuss the attack on the Naam market in Abyei, October 19. Courtesy: The South Sudanese Foreign Ministry via Facebook.


A drone strike carried out by the military on the Naam market in northern Abyei — the disputed border territory between South Sudan and Sudan’s RSF-held West Kordofan — on Monday has stoked new diplomatic friction between Khartoum and Juba.


The death toll from the strike has risen to more than 150, as efforts to recover bodies were initially hampered by fires spreading from fuel depots hit in the attack, a South Sudanese source in the office of

Yohana Akol Ngor

, the caretaker information minister in the Abyei administration, told Mada Masr.

 Around 8,000 people have also been displaced, the source said.


Juba responded by

summoning

Sudan’s ambassador to Juba,

Essam Karar

, on the same day to protest the attack, a source at the South Sudanese Foreign Ministry told Mada Masr.

author: Ndivhuwo Mukwevho
title: Multi-million rand sports facility finally opens in Limpopo
content:
Finally, Waterval residents in Limpopo outside of Elim Hospital are now able to utilise their R55-million sports facility having waited for over a decade of delays. The Waterval facility is not the only one that has been neglected by Limpopo municipalities. Earlier this year,

Elitsha

reported on the R1.4-million upgrades to

Makwarela Stadium

 that never happened.


How it all started


The Waterval sports facility, which consists of a soccer field and a tennis court, was officially handed over to the Waterval community earlier this month. This came as welcome relief to local residents who had already lost hope that the facility would ever open. At one stage, it was left abandoned and turned into a drug den and a hiding place for criminals.


The facility is set to be utilised for various sporting codes by the local communities and schools. “At last, our children have got a ground where they can play their football with ease. Even though we had to wait for years for the facility to be completed, we are happy now that the ground is ours. To be honest, I am one of the people who had already lost hope that one day, the facility will ever be used for our benefit,” says Cedric Mulaudzi, a resident of Waterval.


Mulaudzi told

Elitsha

 that his 11-year-old son was not yet born when construction work began on the Waterval sports facility. “I am just happy that my son, who was not yet born when construction work started, will now have a place where he will be able to mature his football career,” says Mulaudzi.


The Waterval sports facility is the only decent, modern sports facility in the area and will be utilised by Mpheni, Shirly, Elim and other local communities.


Politically motivated?


“Why did it take too long for our government to complete this facility? This means that if it takes our government more than 10-years to complete just one stadium!” says Mulaudzi.


Nelson Mudzanani, who was born and raised in Waterval, also has questions about the timing of the project’s completion, while welcoming its completion. “For years, we have asked questions to the local municipality [Makhado] on why it was taking too long for them to complete the project and we never received any response. But now, we are due for elections in the coming weeks, and all of a sudden the stadium is finally completed. I just hope that the timing is not politically motivated,” says Mudzanani.


He believes that the sports facility will go a long way in empowering the local communities. “Those who want to exercise and those who want to play various sporting codes now have a decent place to do so. I just hope that the facility will be maintained accordingly,” he says.


During the handover of the Waterval sports facility, Makhado mayor, Dorcus Mboyi urged the local communities to utilise the facility properly and refrain from vandalising it. She also extended apologies for the delays they endured during the construction of the facility.

author: ROAPE
title: Life after Museveni
content:
I have argued before that moving forward, Uganda will need General Muhoozi Kainerugaba, son of current President Yoweri Museveni. Or a person like Gen. Kainerugaba. This is not necessarily about the man, Muhoozi Kainerugaba. More that the trajectory of Museveni’s politics needs a man of this texture.


My intention here is neither support nor endorsement. But acknowledging Muhoozi’s usefulness in the transitional phase which must happen soon – or that is already underway.  Of course, his autocratic display thus far, is difficult to ignore.  But we have to acknowledge that Gen. Kainerugaba is a very important actor in an ongoing transition.


As

the

 son of a sitting president, and current commander of the nation’s military, this is an unusual combination for anyone, and is therefore discussable on its merits. Especially with an octogenarian president, and a nervous country, surely this person – whoever they may be – is a key component.


I know, we are all running scared. Many comrades in the struggle for a good governance are still missing – Sam Mugumya. Many are rotting in jails and ‘safehouses’ across the country.  National Unity Platform (NUP)’s incarcerated supporters and leaders – Waiswa Mufumbiro, Eddie Mutwe, among others – are constantly threatened with public executions by the CDF himself, who is currently the president in waiting. We are all scared.


Exile has become an even more common word in our conversations. But I will say one more time, viewed comparatively, President Kainerugaba will never be as brutal as his father – even if he so badly wanted. But presently, the country needs him sober and rightly guided.


If we are looking towards a peaceful, gradual, no-deadline transition, Gen. Muhoozi features prominently – importantly.  This does not mean to suggest I’m anti-revolution, but instead aware, on the one hand, that most African countries do not have the critical mass for revolution, and on the other, that Africa remains a colonised continent with leaders being decided

elsewhere

. You should have read my disappointment when Mr Museveni refused to appoint him, Vice President.


Is Yoweri Museveni leaving?


It is no cynicism to say that opposition forces – mainstream opposition, civil society, activists – have struggled to challenge Gen. Museveni. In fact, as journalist Charles Onyango Obbo observed one time, most of us in Kampala on either side of the isle are resigned to the man’s death. Undoubtedly, Museveni – and his mostly Western backers – have proved too strong to beat. We have tried elections, and failed. Opposition leader, Dr Besigye led the country into peaceful protests and failed. We have tried the judicial route and failed.


Presently, a leading opposition candidate, Dr Kizza Besigye and his lawyer, and former Kampala City Lord Mayor, Eria Lukwago are fighting for their lives in an inhumane judicial system.  They are both in jail. Legal rebel and president of the Uganda Law Society, Isaac Ssemakadde, and leading human rights lawyer, Nicholas Opio were forced out of the country. Activist Male Mabirizi, a pioneering activist lawyer, is in jail.


Even when Museveni’s own comrades – Amama Mbabazi, Jaberi Bidandi Ssali, Miria Matembe, Eriya Kategaya, among others – nicely asked him not to stand again, and let them lead the transition, the man simply sidelined them.


In truth, besides our rhetorical belligerence, we have been defeated. Leading opposition figure, Bobi Wine is in exile, while the other key figure, Dr Kizza Besigye in jail. We on the outside are walking zombies, scared and talking in whispers. But in appreciating our blighted condition, we ought to find solace in the fact that we will have the chance to fight another day – maybe audition for a new opponent.


Indeed, it is here that I see Gen. Kainerugaba as the man of the moment. Not out of endorsement or affection, but Kainerugaba as the product of the contestations spelled out above. Indeed, Gen. Kainerugaba stands as ‘president-in-waiting’ as testimony of the success of his father’s politics – where all potential competitors in the race to replace him (inside and outside) have all been defeated, humiliated, exiled or thoroughly emasculated. Only one man is left standing.


To this end, I don’t see Gen. Kainerugaba withdrawing his preparation/candidacy for president, neither do I see Museveni seeking to fight a supposedly impatient son, say dropping him from the position of CDF.  Museveni has no other choice, but to …

author: Moussa Traoure
title: The Palace Guard Against the Trenches : What the Mutiny in Niamey Revealed
content:
The mutiny that broke out in

air base 101 in Niamey

 in the night of 29 August 2026 failed. The real question now is to understand why it took place. Those who took up arms against General Abdourahamane Tiani were young soldiers from the front lines, those who fought the ‘jihadists.’ For all of the Sahel, it’s a much more worrying sign than any plot from the army high command.


Until Saturday morning, fighting took place in the Nigerien capital near to Diori Hamani airport, the presidential palace, and the public television channel RTN.

Loyalists retook control only with the support of the Russian Africa Corps

.

The state television broadcast

 the live arrest of several tens of soldiers being arrested, most of them extremely young.


Three juntas, one promise


In Mali, in Burkina Faso, and in Niger, soldiers took power putting forward the same argument: civilian leaders had failed in front of the ‘jihadists,’ and the army would now do better. Assimi Goïta carried out two coups in Mali in 2020 and 2021. Ibrahim Traoré took control of Burkina Faso in September 2022 and overturned another putschist, Paul-Henri Damiba. Tiani deposed President Mohamed Bazoum in July 2023.


The French were asked to leave, and the Russians invited to come in. The three countries concerned founded the Alliance of Sahel States and

withdrew from ECOWAS in January 2025

. Each then solidified its grip on power through legislation. In Mali,

political parties were banned in 2025

, and the leadership was granted a

five-year renewable term in office

—without elections.

Until 2030, Tiani will remain president of the transition

. In Burkina Faso,

all political parties were dissolved in January 2026

, clearing the way for the regime to consolidate control.


The promised security, however, never materialised. This gap between promises and actions has fuelled anger—an anger that is now festering in the barracks.


Two armies in one


Niger effectively has two armies

: the Presidential Guard, and everyone else. Tiani commanded the Guard for twelve years; since the coup, it has received the best equipment and the most secure and comfortable postings. Meanwhile, regular units stationed in the southwest and along the Nier’s borders are losing personnel in the fight against the Islamic State in the Sahel and the al-Qaeda-linked JNIM.


According to observers, it is these soldiers who have mutinied. US researcher

Alex Thurston

 that most accounts align: regardless of infighting at the top, it is the anger of the rank-and-file that has driven the revolt.

Paul Melly, of Chatham House

, aptly summari the sentiment among young officers: three years ago, things seemed to be improving; today, the opposite is true.


When dealing with generals, a regime can either negotiate or simply swap out loyalists for other trusted figures. But for soldiers suffering from a lack of ammunition and reinforcements, a reshuffle within the high command changes nothing.


Niamey, Niger.


How the juntas protect themselves


The first pillar: the purges. In Mali, following a

reported coup attempt in August 2025

, two generals and more than fifty military personnel were arrested. At the end of December,

a decree mandated the forced retirement

 of several high-ranking officers, including the former intelligence chief. In Burkina Faso, after a plot was uncovered in January 2026, Damiba—identified by Ouagadougou as one of the organizers—

was extradited to Togo

. Tiani has taken a more cautious approach: on 11 September,

he replaced Chief of Staff Moussa Salaou Barmou with Mamane Sani Kiaou

. Former Defense Minister

Kalla Moutari has been arrested

, and former RFI journalist

Moussa Kaka

 has been shot. According to Thurston, this reaction suggests that

Tiani does not wish to appear fearful

.


The second pillar is the law. With political parties banned and terms of office extended, the opposition has no remaining legal path to power.


The third pillar is an external protector.

Between 200 and 300 fighters

 from the Russian African Corps are stationed in Niger, with their headquarters located south of Base 101. Russian Ambassador

Viktor Voropaev maintains that Niamey merely requested assistance

. According to Thurston,

the Algerian air force also provided support

 to the loyalists. For the first time, forces tasked with fighting jihadists have openly opened fire on soldiers from the very countries that employ them.

author: Omar Kalinge-Nnyago
title: Uganda: The Entrenchment of a Hereditary Military Oligarchy
content:
Uganda is approaching one of the most precarious political transitions in its post-independence history. The likely trajectory is not democratic consolidation but the slow institutionalization of a hereditary military oligarchy. Four developments are driving this shift: President Yoweri Museveni’s advanced age; the elevation of his son, Gen. Muhoozi Kainerugaba, to Chief of Defence Forces (CDF); the operationalization of the Patriotic League of Uganda (PLU) as a parallel mobilization vehicle; and the legal entrenchment of military authority over civilian institutions. Taken together, these amount to what might be called a “slow-motion coup” already under way.


The most probable outcome is best described as contested dynastic authoritarianism, a system in which elections continue to serve as instruments of international legitimacy, while substantive power is contested within the first family and the military elite rather than at the ballot box. The formal opposition faces structural decapitation through repression and co-optation. Yet two under-examined institutions – the Anglican and Catholic Churches, and segments of Uganda’s Muslim community – offer potential, if imperfect, nonviolent pathways for mediation or resistance over the coming decade, complicated by the risk of Muslim youth radicalization.


A conventional, extra-constitutional military coup remains possible even as the regime works to secure de facto military dominance through promotions, strategic retirements of senior officers, legislative amendment, and patronage. The PLU’s grassroots strategy is designed to insulate the succession from exactly this risk, cultivating broad loyalty and framing dynastic continuity as patriotic inevitability rather than rupture. The principal danger to the plan, accordingly, lies less in popular revolt than in intra-elite fracture or palace intrigue should the succession falter.


Anatomy of a slow-motion coup


The regime has moved beyond personalist autocracy toward a durable, self-perpetuating system built on four pillars: fusion of military command with the first family, political mobilization through the PLU, subordination of parliament, and kleptocratic control of the state’s resources.


Uganda’s slide toward dynastic rule no longer needs to be projected; it can be observed directly. In 2024, Museveni handed his son the office of Chief of Defence Forces, together with an unusual personal grant of authority to promote senior officers – a clear departure from the constitutional design of a professional military answerable to civilian rather than familial command. Muhoozi has used this platform expansively, maintaining an active, often combative social media presence, intervening openly in partisan disputes, and, in June 2026, ordering troops to shut down Nation Media Group’s operations after critical coverage of his conduct. He has also directly ordered the arrest of opposition lawyer Erias Lukwago and the deportation of Kenyan lawyer Martha Karua, both members of Dr Kizza Besigye’s defence team – a signal that the regime now treats defence counsel, and not only defendants, as targets. In his national address of 4 July 2026, President Museveni appeared to defend his son’s actions, placing blame on Besigye for allegedly delaying court proceedings.


The institutional scaffolding around Muhoozi has matured alongside his personal profile. The Patriotic League of Uganda, rebranded in 2024 from an informal network of birthday rallies and fan clubs known as the “Muhoozi Project”, now runs village-level structures, community clean-up campaigns, and youth roadshows, and openly courts the same rural base the National Resistance Movement (NRM) has cultivated for four decades. It functions less as a political party than as an insurance policy: it absorbs potential rivals into patronage, builds a loyalty network running parallel to the NRM’s own, and softens the ground for a hereditary handover by presenting it as continuity rather than rupture. Leadership changes, such as the appointment of Hon. Fadil Twaha as Secretary General, signal a deliberate effort to deepen outreach among Muslim communities that feel marginalized in the League’s rise.


The 12

th

 Parliament offered an early demonstration of the PLU’s reach. The League withdrew its earlier backing for then Speaker Anita Among and her deputy, Thomas Tayebwa, clearing the way for Jacob Oboth-Oboth’s election as Speaker – a small but telling exercise of veto power …

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Morocco’s First Woman Prime Minister and the Terms of Freedom
content:
Something changes when a woman occupies an office men have treated as their natural inheritance. Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri’s

appointment

 on 29 September 2026 makes that change visible in Morocco. For women whose competence is routinely scrutinised, the pleasure is neither naïve nor trivial.


But the woman forming a government and the woman labouring in the fields, raising children without pay and denied an equal share of her inheritance encounter power differently. Representation changes who governs; emancipation changes what all women have the power to do. That distinction shifts our attention from PM Mansouri’s gender to the politics of the centre-right

 Party of Authenticity and Modernity (PAM

)

, which she leads. Will its programme redistribute the resources and rights on which women’s freedom depends?


The history beneath the headline


Calling women’s leadership foreign to Morocco requires forgetting its history. Historian Osire Glacier

documents

 women’s authority long before the contemporary premiership. Kenza al Awrabiya, the Amazigh mother of Idris II, helped secure the Idrisid dynasty, founded in the late eighth century in what is now Morocco. Zaynab al Nafzawiyya influenced eleventh-century Almoravid politics around Aghmat, near Marrakech. Sayyida al Hurra governed Tétouan, a city in northern Morocco, during the sixteenth century. Khnata bint Bakkar intervened in eighteenth-century dynastic politics.


Across the region,

Dihya

 is remembered as an Amazigh queen who led resistance to the Arab conquest in the Aurès, in present-day Algeria, during the late seventh century. Tuareg oral tradition remembers

Tin Hinan

 as a queen and founding ancestress of noble lineages in the Ahaggar, in present-day southern Algeria.


These histories expose how male authority is made to appear natural. Fatima Mernissi’s

The Forgotten Queens of Islam


challenges that selective memory. Colonialism also reorganised authority: French Protectorate administrators

reshaped

 customary courts around imperial priorities. What survives as tradition can carry the history of political intervention. 


Religious interpretation can give exclusion another claim to permanence. Islamist and other conservative opponents invoke this

hadith

 against women’s political authority:


«لَنْ يُفْلِحَ قَوْمٌ وَلَّوْا أَمْرَهُمُ امْرَأَةً»


Usually translated as saying that a people governed by a woman will not prosper, it becomes a prohibition irrespective of her competence. Asma Lamrabet, a

Moroccan Islamic feminist thinker

, questions turning a

narration linked

 to Persia’s dynastic succession into a universal ban. She reads it against the Qur’anic Queen of Sheba, whose judgement demonstrates capable leadership. Her argument contests male authority’s claim to divine necessity.


PAM’s promises and its record


Women have long contested how authority is distributed within the family. Fatima Sadiqi

documents

the Union de l’Action Féminine’s 1992 million-signature campaign to reform the Moudawana, Morocco’s family code. The 2004 reform abolished wives’ duty of obedience but retained unequal inheritance and exceptions to the marriage age of eighteen. Proposals announced in December 2024 left fundamental equality demands unresolved. In October 2025, more than sixty civil society organisations and public figures

joined to call for comprehensive reform

. Rights in Morocco have advanced through organised demands, not the gender of an officeholder.


PAM, a centre-right party founded in 2008,

advocates

 social modernisation and positions itself against the Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD). It entered government in 2021 alongside the National Rally of Independents and conservative nationalist Istiqlal. Opposition to Islamist conservatism, however, does not itself entail reforming the laws and economic conditions that subordinate women.


PAM’s

2026 programme

author: WoMin
title: Press Release | Women’s Climate Assembly strengthens Pan African solidarity, women-led resistance and the struggle for a just future
content:
“

Empowering women is a radical way to transform the world!

” –

Ivorian activist


The fourth regional

Women’s Climate Assembly

 (WCA), held in Yaoundé, Cameroon, from 5–8 October 2026, concluded with a powerful reaffirmation of African women’s determination to defend their lands, territories, livelihoods and communities, and to demand climate justice and reparations.


Under the theme, “

Our lands, our voices: African women united for climate justice and reparations!

”, the Assembly convened over 75 women community leaders, activists, feminist organisations, civil society groups and allies from twelve countries including Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Guinea-Conakry, Liberia, Namibia, Niger, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Senegal and Zambia.


The gathering provided a vital space for women on the frontlines of the climate crisis, extractive industries, land dispossession and environmental destruction to share their experiences, strengthen relationships across borders and build collective strategies for change.


As the Assembly closed, one message rang clear: African women are not merely bearing the costs of the climate crisis. They are leading the struggle for solutions, defending their communities and shaping the future they want.


“

There’s an adage in my village that women cannot build a nation. The Women’s Climate Assembly has proved that women build nations. We counter this adage with the unity and solidarity of African women!”

 –

DRC activist-participant


Turning shared struggles into collective power


From communities confronting oil and gas expansion and destructive mining to women defending forests, seeds, water sources and ancestral lands, participants brought forward the lived realities of communities too often excluded from decisions about their territories and futures.


Through collective reflection, popular education and movement-building, women connected struggles that may take place in different countries but are rooted in common systems of exploitation, inequality and environmental destruction.


Designed by women activists and members of the WCA Steering Committee, the thematic teach-ins explored a range of political concepts, questions and practices, including:


The erosion of farmers’ seeds

: A challenge for building resilient and sustainable food systems. What solutions are there for preserving our seed heritage?  


Nature Commons

: The defence of the Congo Basin’s forests.


Counting the Costs of Mal/Bad Development and Demanding reparations

: The case of the African Development Bank campaign.


Fighting some of the false solutions to the climate crisis

: Gas extraction, enclosure of our forests and lands for carbon trading, green conservation and more.


Building democratic, accountable, ‘loving’ leadership

: Why are these principles so important to feminist leadership? What else do we feel is critical to leading as feminists?


Lessons on organising and movement building

: Growing National/sub-regional grassroots movements.


Building knowledge from what we know

: Building feminist popular knowledge as the basis for Building Women’s Power. How can we go about doing this locally in our communities and beyond that.


The WCA celebrated the knowledge, resistance and organising power of rural, Indigenous, peasant and working-class women. The

Each One, Teach One

 sessions embodied this spirit of knowledge-sharing, collective learning and liberation. On Day Two, participants exchanged practical skills, crafts and tools, sharing techniques for making baobab candies, producing eco-briquettes from cassava and creating seed bricks to cultivate and protect Indigenous seeds. Weaving, cloth-dyeing, beadwork and other practices also featured, affirming the value of knowledge held, practised and passed down through generations of women.


The gathering reaffirmed the importance of strengthening a Pan African ecofeminist movement that recognises the connections between the climate crisis, extractivism, gender injustice, food insecurity and the loss of community control over natural resources.


It also reinforced a fundamental principle: communities must have the power to determine their own futures, including the right to say NO to destructive development projects that threaten their lands, livelihoods and ways of life.


Climate justice means reparations, not empty promises
