author: Caleb Okereke
title: Matthew Blaise wants to be your friend and neighbor
content:
Matthew Blaise and I must have been in our mid teens when we first met. I don’t remember the exact year, but I remember that it was on Facebook. It did not take long for that online connection to become a real friendship, and it is one that has persisted despite life carrying us in different directions.   


When we sit down for this conversation in September, I am in Philadelphia and Matthew is in Brazil. He is preparing for

Friends and Neighbors

, a new art and literary festival in Lagos built around a deceptively simple question: What responsibility do we have to the people we call our friends and our neighbors?


It is a question that makes our own friendship an interesting place from which to begin. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 


Caleb:

 Something I find provocative about the title “Friends and Neighbors” is that you also seem to be making a statement about the ways queerness shows up in the ordinary. I’m thinking about this song, “Your driver could be LGBT, your friend could be LGBT, your neighbour could be LGBT.” Was that part of the conceptual framing?


Matthew:

 Actually, that’s another way to see it. When I thought of this concept, I thought of proximity within our community. A trip from Lagos to Europe is cheaper than a trip from Lagos to Abidjan, which is a neighboring country. For me, that’s a metaphor for what a lot of friendship within the African continent, especially around queerness, has been due to bad policy, homophobia and criminalization.


Queer people within Africa are not so familiar with themselves. And in that sense, we really haven’t constructed what queer Africanness is because we are still not so close to ourselves. But I find it interesting that you also see it from the point of everyday life, where people you come in contact with could be of this community or could possess these identities without you knowing.


Caleb:

 That’s what immediately came to my attention. Even when you say, “Hello, friends. Hello, neighbors,” you’re talking to all of us, right? It’s not “queer friends and neighbors.” The implicit read is that even if you’re straight, queer people are all around you. They’re your friends. They’re your neighbors. They might not tell you that they’re queer, but they’re there.


Matthew:

 From the perspective of bell hooks, societies should be built on love and friendship. This very important foundation of love has been taken away from queer people, or we’ve not been given that due to our queerness. Governmental policies and criminalization also make us live our lives in isolation. What it means to be friends right now is also very transactional, especially for queer people.


Caleb:

 One thing that has defined our friendship, at least for me, is honesty. There are things I can tell you that I can’t tell anybody else, obviously, so a sort of radical honesty. And as you were talking about transactional relationships, it made me think, what is the place of honesty in friendship, especially in a context where being honest about yourself can carry consequences?


Matthew:

 I think you don’t owe everyone that truth about yourself. For those who I truly trust, I owe them that responsibility of truth. And I do believe, for every friendship, there has to be that investment in honesty.


Caleb:

 But friendship in and of itself is a risk. I don’t think we realize that, but every friendship is a risk.


Matthew:

 Yeah, friendship sometimes, I mean, it’s not a constant state of feeling a certain way. It’s a roller coaster of emotions. It’s a journey. It’s an adventure. So you encounter a lot of things on the way.


You stretch your hand to someone and they actually bite your hand, then you know they are not really having that good intention towards you. So you can decide to stretch your hand again or push them away. But for me, I think it’s important that we’re able to stretch our hands and bring people together and do the work of educating them until we just know they’re irredeemable.


Caleb:

 Yeah…


Matthew:

 What responsibility do you think you owe me as your friend?


Caleb:

 You are now the one asking me questions. But no, I mean, I think you owe your friend loyalty. That’s one of the things that I’m non-negotiable on. I mean, there are many other things you owe your friend.


Matthew:

 You owe them honesty also?


Caleb:

 You owe them honesty. You also owe your friends grace. I give grace a lot. Maybe it’s not even grace. I’m also like, oh …

author: Saif Eddine Ghobr
title: Why does Tunisia become African only when Europe needs it to be?
content:
Tunisia is an African country that has spent much of its modern political imagination looking north. That sounds like a question of identity. In reality, it is a question of power — and more precisely, a practice of domination through classification.

For decades, Tunisia has imagined its economic future through the Mediterranean: European markets, French education, tourism, and European investment. Africa has often appeared somewhere beyond the Sahara, associated with instability, migration, and security.

Europe, however, possesses its own geography of Tunisia — one that shifts depending on what Europe needs from it. When Brussels discusses trade, investment, and political cooperation, Tunisia is a Mediterranean neighbor. When Europe discusses migration, border control, Libya, or the Sahel, Tunisia becomes something else: an African frontier state.

This is not a mere contradiction. This is a deliberate mechanism of geopolitical subordination through classification. Europe does not need Tunisia to be culturally European; it needs Tunisia to be strategically African when African space becomes relevant to European security.

The economic relationship makes this asymmetry impossible to ignore, revealing a genuine policy cage. The European Commission identifies the EU as Tunisia’s largest trading partner. In 2025, the EU accounted for 59.5% of Tunisia’s total trade. Some 73.2% of Tunisian exports went to the EU, while 49.6% of imports came from the European market. The EU is also Tunisia’s largest foreign investor, holding 85% of the country’s foreign direct investment stock.

These figures do not merely describe a successful trading relationship; they reveal an extraordinary concentration of Tunisia’s external economic relations in Europe. When three-quarters of a country’s exports depend on one economic space, that relationship ceases to be mere commerce and becomes an instrument of control, shaping industrial priorities, investment decisions, and the political imagination of what is economically possible.

Europe consequently becomes not simply Tunisia’s largest market, but its economic horizon — where economic dependence transforms into geographical dependence. Africa becomes secondary, not because it is irrelevant, but because Tunisia has spent decades learning to imagine prosperity through a northern market. As Kwame Nkrumah warned in 1965, the most insidious form of domination is control through financial and structural instruments, not direct conquest.

The contradiction becomes sharper when migration enters the picture, exposing the biopolitics of European border management. The EU’s relationship with Tunisia increasingly includes border management, migration control, and the fight against migrant smuggling. European support has included equipment, training, and operational assistance to Tunisian security and coast guard structures.

From Brussels’ perspective, this is cooperation. From a geopolitical standpoint, it is the externalization of Europe’s borders. Europe is not merely helping Tunisia secure its own territory; it is moving part of Europe’s migration-control architecture southward, closer to the routes through which migrants attempt to reach European territory. This is the essence of extraterritorial sovereignty as described by Giorgio Agamben in 2005: the European state exercises its power over human bodies beyond its borders.

This changes the meaning of Tunisia’s geography. Tunisia is no longer simply a neighbor across the Mediterranean; it becomes part of a European security perimeter without becoming part of Europe itself. Tunisia consequently occupies a peculiar geopolitical position: its economic relationship with Europe is framed as partnership, while its position on migration is treated as strategic infrastructure. The Mediterranean neighbor becomes the African frontier.

Yet another geography is beginning to emerge — one that challenges the idea of Tunisia as merely Europe’s southern security buffer. In June 2026, AfCFTA Secretary-General Wamkele Mene visited Tunisia. The visit concluded with an agreed action plan aimed at deepening Tunisia’s trade across Africa.

This matters because it offers Tunisia a role fundamentally different from that assigned to it by the European migration agenda. The African Continental Free Trade Area offers Tunisia the possibility of becoming an economic actor within Africa, rather than a buffer between Europe and Africa. The African Development Bank is …

author: Keelan Jacobs
title: Few details released as First Nations–First Ministers meeting approaches
content:
With the first dedicated

 First Nations–First Ministers Meeting (FN-FMM)

 set for Monday, a number of key issues are still being worked out with the Prime Minister’s Office, according to the Assembly of First Nations. 


On Friday, chiefs gathered in downtown Ottawa to discuss strategy and rehearse speeches ahead of the meeting. 


The gathering is scheduled for Oct. 26 on unceded Algonquin territory in Ottawa, preceded by a day of ceremony on Sunday. 


Prime Minister Mark Carney, provincial and territorial premiers and a limited First Nations delegation are expected to discuss rights, treaties, jurisdiction, economic partnerships, major projects and other shared priorities. 


The main table is reported to seat 28 people, with additional First Nations invitees outside that room.


In an interview with APTN News on Friday, AFN National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak said First Nations have waited a long time for a seat at this table.


“I’m sorry that it took 119 years to get to this point, and hopefully it doesn’t take another 119 years, that it’s not a one-and-done,” Woodhouse Nepinak said. “We are thankful for rights holders, Elders, and provincial delegations traveling from across the country. We’re also looking forward to Sunday’s ceremony.”


The government once banned First Nation ceremonies, she noted. She framed the moment against a longer history of First Nations standing with Canada through wars, the pandemic and recent unity votes.


“The trust is very fragile, and the relationship is very fragile,” she said. “This is another one of those times where we can really make things or break things.”


Asked about her highest priority coming from the meeting with Carney and the premiers, Woodhouse Nepinak returned to permanence.


“To make sure that this isn’t a one and done, because one meeting isn’t going to solve 119 years of FMM meetings, but even before that, since the creation of this country,” she said. 


She said First Nations are the original landowners “of every square inch of this country,” and have traditionally been partners in its creation without receiving the corresponding respect.


COO-Grand-Chief-Abram-Benedict in 2025. Photo by APTN.


Abram Benedict, chief of the Chiefs of Ontario, told APTN everything is scripted.  


“The agenda is still an evolving document,” he said. “Our regions will have an opportunity to make three-minute opening remarks and reflections.” 


“There are still some negotiations happening on who’s doing opening remarks overall for the entire forum,” he added. “There has been a request for additional time for the regions to speak. So right now we have three minutes per region. They’re going to try to push that up a little bit. Some of the logistical information has not all been solidified yet, and we’re doing the best as we receive that to share that with the leadership.”


Benedict said his region’s high-level ask is to advance the relationship under Section 35 of the Constitution, including the treaty relationship with Ontario and Canada, and to establish a trilateral process to support nations on program delivery and jurisdiction issues that will continue after Monday’s meeting.


Relations between First Nations and Ontario Premier Doug Ford have been strained since the passing of Bill 5 – the Protect Ontario by Unleashing our Economy Act, that gives the province sweeping powers to ignore laws to get infrastructure projects built. 


It’s expected that Carney’s proposed Building Canada Strong Act will get a lot of attention. Like Ontario’s building law – it will give the federal cabinet massive powers to push projects “of national interest” through the regulatory phase while ignoring laws that protect the environment. 


Recently, Carney added the proposed Pacific Link pipeline as a national interest project. It will carry Alberta bitumen to the B.C. coast. Carney said there was two months of “rigorous” consultation but chiefs along the pipeline route complained Canada came to the table with little information. 


Another issue that may be raised was contained in a draft AFN paper obtained by APTN. It proposes a First Nations National Benefits Sharing Framework and a First Nations-controlled sovereign wealth fund fed in part by contributions from projects of national interest, both leaders were measured.


Woodhouse Nepinak said there is no commitment yet.


“We don’t have a commitment on the sovereign wealth fund, and of course that’s just a concept… First Nations …

author: Daron Letts
title: Hudson Bay MLA raises alarm over proposed Port of Churchill expansion
content:
Newly

elected

 Hudson Bay MLA Jason Iqaluq hit the ground running during his first week representing his Sanikiluaq constiuents in the

fall session

 of the legislative assembly.


When it was his turn to question Premier John Main on Friday, Iqaluq raised an alarm over his community’s concerns about proposed upgrades to the Port of Churchill, located about 900 kilometres northwest in Manitoba.


“This project has the potential to have impacts on the Hudson Bay ecosystem and the waters surrounding Sanikiluaq,” Iqaluq said.


He was following up on correspondence shared with the government in May by his predecessor, Daniel Qavvik, who resigned from the legislature in June, spurring t

he Sept. 28 byelection in which Iqaluq was elected.


Iqaluq pressed the Premier for a response to the correspondence before the end of the fall session on Nov. 5.


Main assured Iqaluq the government would reply prior to that date.


The project, dubbed Port of Churchill Plus, was referred to the federal government’s new

Major Projects Office

 in September 2025,

 which means it has the ability to speed up the permitting process.


The project seeks to upgrade the Port of Churchill, Canada’s only deep-water Arctic port, and “expand trade corridors with an all-weather road, an upgraded rail line, a new energy corridor, and marine ice-breaking capacity,” according to the federal government’s website.


While Nunavut is not a direct proponent of the project, the territory is a stakeholder, Main said.


“It is an exciting time to look at the concept of strengthening transport links to benefit Nunavut residents,” Main said. “Nunavut needs to be connected to the rest of the country.”


However, Main said he agrees it’s important Nunavummiut’s environmental concerns be heard during the process.


Iqaluq followed up by asking if the Nunavut Impact Review Board would have an opportunity to assess the project.


Main said that would be clarified in the government’s written response later in the session.


“As it is a transboundary issue, it’s quite complex,” he said.


Iqalu

q said he was satisfied with Main’s response to his question, in an interview in his office following the session.


However, he does not share Main’s optimism for the project.


“If it scares off wildlife, it is definitely going to be a bad thing for our community,” Iqaluq said.

“We have to make sure that nothing is going to be disturbed.”

Many deaths have been linked to medical neglect, including four of five recent deaths at California’s Adelanto Processing Center, according to a 2026 report by the state attorney general. author: Sara Fayyazi
title: Making Women’s History Part of the Curriculum
content:
Two teachers from Sacred Heart Preparatory School in California, Kristen Kelly and Serene Williams, have proposed an Advanced Placement U.S. Women’s History course in response to the issue of students not learning about women’s history. The courses would allow studying women’s experiences and contributions in greater depth. Establishing this course would create a better understanding of American history as it includes the diverse experiences of women and would help students connect the historical struggles for equality to gender issues today.

Women have contributed to shaping the nation’s politics, economy, and social movements, yet their participation is often overlooked by traditional history classes. From fighting for the right to vote, challenging discrimination, and advocating for female autonomy, women have had a significant role in building the foundation of the United States today.

One of the main arguments for WAPUSH is that women’s experiences are not explored in the classroom. In the article Educational Activism: Creating an AP U.S. Women’s History Course, Serene Williams, Kristen Kelly, and Clara Robinson explain that topics such as women’s suffrage and reproductive rights receive limited attention in the current AP U.S. History curriculum. The women’s suffrage movement involved decades of organizing, political campaigning, and resistance. However, teachers may not introduce this topic to students or have enough time to examine its strategies and leaders in detail. A dedicated course would allow students to study these movements more thoroughly and understand how women helped shape American democracy.

Women’s history is much broader than the fight for voting rights. The proposed WAPUSH curriculum includes women’s labor, politics, religion, culture, war, and violence against women. It also examines how race, class, sexuality, religion, and other identities shaped women’s experiences. This approach is important because women throughout the years have never shared one universal experience. Indigenous women, Black women, Immigrant women, etc., have faced different opportunities and forms of discrimination. Studying these differences would help students develop a greater understanding of American history and that America was not built on just our founding fathers, but by women who paved the path for opportunity and development through blood, sweat, and tears.

An AP course would also help students recognize the connection between historical events and current issues. The debate over reproductive rights and other feminist struggles today cannot be fully understood without examining the laws and political movements that shaped access to contraceptives, abortion, and female economic support. Studying topics from the suffrage movement to the Equal Rights Amendment can help students understand the political equality that has developed through activism and engage in feminist discussion. Learning this history would give students the context needed to evaluate debates instead of viewing them as different events.

Establishing this course would show that women’s history is worthy of advanced academic study. The WAPUSH campaign began in 2022, and according to its website, the campaign gathered more than 4,000 petition signatures and received encouragement from College Board leadership as it worked toward launching this course. Its proposal has also received university support, while the campaign continues seeking letters from high schools willing to offer the course. This continued support brings women closer to bringing light to women’s history and giving women a space in school systems and curricula. This petition is one step closer every day to its goal to educate and inform people all across America of women’s contributions.

An AP U.S. Women’s History course would make education more comprehensive, inform students even more about the history of the U.S., and connect past struggles to present issues. Women have influenced American politics, economics, culture, and social movements, yet their experiences are not always given sufficient attention in existing courses. By offering students an opportunity to examine these experiences, the College Board could help create a more inclusive and accurate understanding of the nation’s past. Women’s history is not separate from American history but instead an essential part of it.

author: Santana Dreaver
title: ‘Gratifying and humbling’: First Nation leads ghost net cleanup from Interior ‘B.C.’ rivers
content:
Volunteers Lyza Adoplh, John Redan, Nick Froese and Roxx Ledoux work to haul abandoned fishing gear out of the Fraser and Thompson rivers. Photo by Santana Dreaver


This article has been co-published

with the Narwhal

 as part of their

2026 Indigenous journalism fellowship

.


After starting the day with a prayer and a safety demonstration, a group of volunteers gears up in water-resistant clothing and lifejackets, ready to hit the water.


The crew is preparing to scour a stretch of the Fraser and Thompson rivers, removing any fishing gear or waste left behind. Fishing nets left underneath the water are commonly known as ghost nets, which trap and kill fish. 


As the saying goes on a volunteer call out poster, “ghost nets create ghost fish.”


TLKemchEEN (Lytton First Nation) has led the river clean-up program in the area for the past 20 years, all in an effort to preserve salmon populations and aquatic life following harvest season.


Over two days in September, a group of 40 volunteers spent a total of 20 combined hours on the water.


From Lillooet to Lytton during the first day, and from Lytton to Yale during the second day, volunteers passed through white-water rapids and rugged terrain such as the famously turbulent passage of Hell’s Gate.


When the raft leader yells “hold on,” that’s exactly what participants do, reaching down for a rope attached to the raft, laughing and hollering, ripping through the Fraser Canyon rapids. 


The cold river water splashes everyone — waking up the crew as countless bald and golden eagles watch from above.


“I didn’t realize how impactful everything is along the shores. I guess I didn’t realize that some leave their garbage and nets out there,” volunteer Rebecca Riley, who is from the Stʼatʼimc Nation, said.


“Once I saw that with my own eyes, I wanted to jump in and be a part of it.”


A newspaper ad about the river clean-up project inspired Rebecca Riley to get involved. She has helped remove ghost nets since 2018. Photo: Supplied by Rebecca Riley


‘That fishery is a communal right’


It’s a sentiment shared by many volunteers on the boat, who eagerly approach the shoreline when a ghost net comes into sight. 


Whether the net will take one person to remove, or up to five to pull out of the water, is unknown until people get their hands wet. 


During the non-rapid portion of the cleanup, countless stories were told, Indigenous people exchanged words in their languages to compare similarities and differences and folks even had hot chocolate along the shore, courtesy of Kumsheen Rafting, which was contracted to support the program this year. 


During the first year of the program, 126 ghost nets were collected.


“This year we picked up six nets and some garbage, some years prior we’ve picked up zero. We have to remind our fishermen not to be lazy and take their gear home,” Kevin Duncan told the Narwhal.


Duncan is an elected councillor for TLKemchEEN in “B.C.’s” Southern Interior, part of the Nlaka’pamux Nation Tribal Council. He has been involved with the program since its inception. He attended both cleanup days this year with his son, Aaron.


Kevin Duncan, an elected councillor for TLKemchEEN, has been involved in Lytton’s ghost net clean-up initiative since it started 20 years ago. He always leads a prayer before they begin. Photo: Supplied by Rebecca Riley


For TLKemchEEN, stewarding their waters as they always have is crucial — especially as salmon numbers decline. Life along the Fraser and Thompson rivers is deeply connected to salmon. And TLKemchEEn is home to where the two rivers meet, in the country’s largest salmon-bearing watershed.


“For future generations, sometime down the road, I’m afraid all they’re going to be looking at is pictures of salmon in a book,” said Duncan. 


The nets recovered by the program are given to those in need, including single mothers, low-income families and Elders from the nation. 


“As a Nlaka’pamux or Stʼatʼimc member … that fishery is a communal right, it’s not an individual right. It’s looked after by your nation,” Duncan said.


“Most times, you just get to see portions of the river from the highway, but once you’re down on the water, floating for eight hours from Lillooet to Lytton, it gives you a better perspective on where people fish.” 


Now 20 years into the program, volunteer spots fill up months in advance. Photo by Santana Dreaver


Removing fishing gear from the cold and fast-moving river can be …

author: Mehk Chakraborty
title: Inside the resistance to Spain’s crackdown on migrants in Ceuta
content:
This article

Inside the resistance to Spain’s crackdown on migrants in Ceuta

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


On July 30, images streamed across TVs, social media feeds and newspapers of thousands of people approaching a fence along the beach, in boats and by foot. Migrants, including children and families, were attempting to cross into Ceuta, a Spanish enclave bordered by Morocco. Facing violent border guards and the threat of drowning, over 70,000 people made it to Ceuta, with hopes of eventually reaching the Spanish mainland. Officials in Ceuta

said

 that 100 people died in the crossing — either by drowning or being crushed — and sources on the ground believe the number was higher. 


“I lost my phone, my money, my ID card, everything I had,” one Moroccan teenager recalled. “At one point I got pulled to the bottom, so far down that my feet touched the sand. When I looked around me, I saw women and babies who had drowned.”


“There was no proper humanitarian response from the local authorities — whether it is basic hygiene, food or shelter,” said Ric Fernández, coordinator and spokesperson for humanitarian and migrant advocacy group No Name Kitchen, or NNK, about the first days after the mass crossing. “Instead, there was an institutional response of pressuring people to ‘voluntarily’ return to Morocco. … There was repression, violence against people on the move in every form — legal, administrative and physical, and the forced expulsion of people.”   


Facing intense pressure and violence from both the Spanish police and military, within 96 hours most people returned to Morocco. Estimates about how many migrants remain are in flux, but the Spanish government

said

 in late September that up to 10,000 people are still in Ceuta.


While the global mainstream media quickly moved on from this story, the situation in Ceuta has

remained tense

 over the last three months, with increased violent harassment by the police, evictions and collective expulsions. In recent weeks,

“voluntary returns” and evictions

 from makeshift camps on the beach have ramped up.


Embed from Getty Images


Irene Estébanez Gutiérrez, a family and community doctor in Madrid, spent two weeks in Ceuta as a volunteer. “An information campaign has been waged that portrays people on the move as invaders, violent and dangerous,” she said. The

media coverage

, she believes, has failed to adequately address “the resulting humanitarian crisis, the systematic violation of rights, the lack of protection for minors, and the systematic violence and discrimination to which people are being subjected to, particularly by the military.”


Those who remain include Moroccan men and women, alongside Sudanese, Syrians, Palestinians, Malians and Nigerians. According to NNK, a significant number are minors. They are still stranded; the majority of them have slept in the street or in makeshift tents since they crossed into Ceuta over two months ago. 


Kora, who uses a pseudonym as an activist to protect her identity, arrived in Ceuta to volunteer in early August and found the violence and the lack of access to basic necessities particularly angering. The authorities were “not letting them access the supermarkets to get food or water,” she said. “They turned off the publicly and freely accessible water [to shower or drink] on the beaches and beat them or scare them in the middle of the night … to purposefully making their lives more miserable.” 


Organizing solidarity, facing criminalization


This

violence

, however, did not prevent activists and migrants from developing forms of organizing and resistance. Hundreds of migrants

staged a protest

 on a popular beach in Ceuta in August to demand asylum. On Sept. 21, Migreurop, a Euro-African network of organizations, activists and researchers that monitors European migration policies, noted in a

joint statement

 with over 100 organizations: “We have witnessed forms of resistance in everyday survival practices.” They mentioned the sharing of information, food and medicine, as well as safety and protection practices.

distributing food

 at Trampolín Beach, the site of one makeshift camp. Other local charities like Luna Blanca, have been

providing

author: C4SS
title: C4SS Panelists on the Enduring Legacy of Don Lavoie
content:
The

Markets and Society conference

 this weekend (October 23-26) will feature many interesting panels on topics from public policy to self-governance to digital privacy to immigration and beyond. There will also be longtime C4SSers presenting.


On

Saturday from 9:00-10:30am

, Nathan Goodman is chairing the panel “The Enduring Legacy of Don Lavoie” featuring:


Cory Massimino – National Economic Planning: What is Right?


Don Lavoie argued in “National Economic Planning: What is Left?” that economic planning was inherently reactionary and thwarted genuinely left-wing aims like peace and liberation. Despite the prevailing conservative-libertarian fusionism of Lavoie’s day, his study of economics and history helped him see the transience of such an alliance: libertarianism was left-wing until the left became obsessed with economic planning and the right was always about militarism and hierarchy no matter how much libertarian rhetoric it adopted. Lavoie’s new (yet old) framing went under appreciated during his time and deserves careful reconsidering for anticipating the contemporary right’s increasing authoritarianism. This essay will build on Lavoie’s framing of economic planning as essentially right-wing, apply that framing to the contemporary American political situation, and argue such a framing is essential for any coherent conception of the political landscape going forward.


Jason Lee Byas – A Role For Lavoian Democracy


Don Lavoie argues for detaching our concept of democracy from the particular institution of voting, and instead seeing it as “openness,” or accessible means to shaping the world around you and its rules. An advantage of this approach is its complementarity with markets and property rights, which might otherwise be seen as in tension with democracy — thus partially reuniting liberalism’s “libertarian” and “democratic” commitments. Yet there is still a tension here. Philosophically, many libertarians may think that any social rules involving force should simply be set by natural rights, and so leaving these open to adjustment by anyone at all (let alone with open access to everyone) will be a problem. Practically, open access to reshaping the rules may spell uncertainty in problematic ways. I resolve these remaining tensions by suggesting a specific role for Lavoian Democracy. In short, many things are left radically indeterminate by any socially-practiced system of rights, and so too are many things left radically indeterminate by a commitment to natural rights. Questions of interpretation and resolution loom large, and the process of interpretation and resolution can either be hierarchical and authoritarian, or a product of ground-up contestation. There are principled liberal grounds — both moral and epistemic — for favoring the latter, and this is the role for Lavoian Democracy. I then offer a handful of institutions and practices that Lavoian Democracy might favor, including unions (of a certain form), adverse possession, and the common law.


Akiva Malamet – Beyond Recognition: Identity, Cultural Discovery, and the Limits of Social Planning


Scholars in liberal theory and political economy have long emphasized what Don Lavoie called the “knowledge problem”: social information is dispersed, local, emergent, and personal, and thus inaccessible to centralized or “high modernist” institutions. Lavoie and others showed that state economic planning fails because planners cannot access or generate this kind of knowledge and often undermine its creation. Liberal institutions, by contrast, enable people to align diverse plans and generate forms of knowledge no top-down authority could anticipate. I extend these insights to issues of identity, cultural development, and interpersonal life. Identity and cultural formation are bottom-up, organic processes reflecting the nuances of how people self-conceive, relate, and find meaning. State planning and institutional treatments of identity often obstruct pluralistic self-concepts and cultural discovery, flattening human diversity and complex individual lives into simple, legible categories. Ironically, formal recognition can perpetuate the injustices it was intended to remedy and reinforce intergroup conflict. State recognition of identity undermines the processes through which identity becomes meaningful, and conflicts with core liberal values of pluralism, self-authorship, and cooperation. Immigration restrictions present an analogous case: they …

author: Unknown
title: Introducing the NSPM-7 Defendants Union
content:
Earlier this month,

The Guardian


announced

 the existence of the

NSPM-7 Defendants Union

, a new experiment in movement defense. We reached out to the organizers for an overview of their project, which we present here.


Announcing the NSPM-7 Defendants Union


National Security Presidential Memorandum 7 (NSPM-7) is a government-wide strategy to investigate, disrupt, and prosecute what the Trump administration calls “left-wing political extremism.” They have already used it to justify publicly killing Minneapolis anti-ICE rapid responders Renee Good and Alex Pretti,

raiding the homes

 of University of Michigan students protesting the genocide of Palestinians, and

re-indicting

 Stop Cop City protesters.


But by the tens of thousands, newly politicized people are learning to fight: Minnesotan moms tracking BORTAC agents, students throwing back tear gas outside

Delaney Hall

, nurses making split-decisions to help people escape from ICE. Especially in the movement against Trump’s deportation agenda, thousands of people are taking brave actions for the first time.


NSPM-7 is intended to turn their lives upside down. We want to make them stronger.


For decades, social movements have developed strategies to withstand repression, learn, and propagate revolutionary politics. Those of us who have had our homes raided, organized collective defense,

resisted grand juries

, built

support committees

, devised

media strategies

, and stayed active through periods of repression have something valuable to offer the growing list of NSPM-7 defendants. That’s why we built the NSPM-7 Defendants Union.


We aim to make our social movements resilient. To do so, we need to make everyone aware of Trump’s strategy to crush dissent and mount a common defense against it while recentering the discussion about what Trump calls “antifa” on our own terms, so that we can speak proudly and publicly in defense of our politics and our resistance.


The Defendants Pledge


NSPM-7 treats Trump’s adversaries as if they all comprise a single united movement. We should use that to our advantage. We want a critical mass of new defendants across the country to adopt a shared framework to fight their cases. If everyone embraces bold, political publicity and commits to collective defense, we could amass leverage across hundreds of cases.


We want you to take this

pledge

 if you are a political defendant, if you have been contacted by the police or federal agents, if you are under surveillance, or if you believe that any of these things could happen in the foreseeable future. We take this pledge across movements, as a promise to each other.


I pledge:


To Go Public with My Case

: I will not be quiet. I want as large an audience as possible to know about my case.


To Benefit the Movement

: When I talk about my case, I will link it to the larger movement. I will use the platform of my case to spread the ideas and values of the movement, so that many more people can learn what I believe in and be inspired by those ideas as well.


To Share Lessons Learned

: I will talk openly within the movement and to the public about the repressive strategies I learn about in the course of my case, so that everyone can learn how the state is targeting activists.


To Take the Offense

: I will take an aggressive legal and media strategy to beat my case, call the state’s bluff, and politicize others.


To Pursue Collective Defense

: I will prioritize legal strategies leveraging collective defense so that we all beat the charges, together. I will encourage my lawyer to communicate with my co-defendants’ lawyers and other elements of the movement. When possible, I will utilize joint-defense agreements with my co-defendants.


Not to Denounce Others in the Movement

: I will not publicly denounce the tactical choices of anyone accused of actions I don’t personally agree with.


Not to Cooperate with Law Enforcement

: I will not cooperate with any investigatory or prosecutorial arm of the state. If I am pressured to do so, I will refuse. I will go public and tell the movement if law enforcement visits me.


Our goal is to make these ideas hegemonic. We want this pledge to reach far and wide. Print it out and read it with your friends. Paste it up at encampments. Go on the news and recite it. Distribute it at a No Kings march. Read it aloud at a court support event. Tag it across your city. Hang it by your front door. Get creative.

author: By Sean Summers, Unicorn Riot
title: Line 5 Opponents Confront Wis. Gov. Evers: ‘Drink the Future Water of Lake Superior’
content:
Milwaukee, WI — As Governor Tony Evers took the stage during the annual Wisconsin Association for Justice dinner, an audience member rose to lead a toast for the state’s leader.


But rather than honoring Evers’ accomplishments, the patron issued a challenge. Thrusting a glass of thick black fluid into the air, Tom Hoy asked Evers to drink the liquid which served as a representation of Lake Superior’s waters which protesters say will be contaminated by oil and other hazardous waste from Enbridge’s Line 5 pipeline if the state, and Evers specifically, doesn’t revoke the company’s construction permits.


“I have a glass of water with crude oil,” Hoy announced, holding aloft a cup filled with liquid resembling oil-laden water. “Will you drink the future waters of Lake Superior, sir?”


Hoy, an activist with the group

Climate Defiance

, continued to challenge Evers to have a drink as attendees, security personnel and police shoved them out of the audience and toward the door.


Protesters attended the dinner calling on Evers to reject the pipeline not on vague objections to the project but under specific conditions spelled out in the state’s agreement with the company.


See all of Unicorn Riot’s Line 5 Coverage


Under the Line 5 reroute

permit issued

 in 2024 to Enbridge by the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources, or DNR, the state has the right to terminate the project for good cause, including if the project is not completed according to the conditions of the permit.


Activists, and increasingly the state itself, say that Enbridge’s work has fallen outside the scope of the original permit and violated numerous state regulations.


On October 13, the Wisconsin DNR issued a

Notice of Violation

 to Enbridge for what it calls a “persistent pattern of non-compliance” stretching back to at least March of this year.


The violations listed in the notice include unpermitted construction, unpermitted activity in wetlands and other waterways, and violations of air quality laws, among others.


Language in the permit says that no work outside the originally approved plan the company submitted is allowed, but in September the company

began construction on an unpermitted reroute

 for the pipeline in response to a rupture this summer.


And on August 25, the company was responsible for what’s been called the state’s

largest oil spill

 in more than 50 years when an unoccupied truck rolled into a section of Line 5 at a work site. The

line ruptured

, leading to 31,000 barrels, or 1.3 million gallons, of natural gas spilling just east of the Bad River Reservation in Iron county.


Related:

Enbridge Line 5 Spills Natural Gas Liquids in Northern Wisconsin


In light of the violations and pattern of not complying with state rules, opponents are calling on Evers, the state’s top executive, to exercise his power to revoke the permit.


“If he has a conscience, he needs to act now on the power he has right now to cancel the Line 5 permits,” Hoy, the oil-toasting protester, said in a recorded statement shortly after the disruption happened.


Immediately after Hoy was ejected, another Climate Defiance activist approached the stage calling on Evers to reject the Line 5 permits. They were quickly confronted by an attendee, but resisted removal while demanding the governor consider his legacy and stop work on the pipeline.


The action is the latest in an ongoing battle against the Canadian oil company’s reconstruction of the Line 5 pipeline. For years, organizers have opposed the project on the grounds that it violates Native sovereignty and poses a dire threat to the region’s fresh water, all while accelerating climate change by propping up fossil fuel infrastructure.

title: The Student Revolt in France Spreads : Moving Forward with Rage and Solidarity
content:
October 17 marked one of the fiercest days of mass protest in recent French history. Scenes of ferocious resistance unfolded throughout the day, not only in Paris but in


Bordeaux

,


Dijon

,

Marseille

,

Nancy

, and dozens of other cities across the country. Some observers have described the day’s events as

more explosive

 than the

Yellow Vest movement

 of 2018-19—and the rebellion shows no sign of slowing.


How did we get here? Courageous high school students

have been protesting for weeks

 against abominable conditions in schools, the rise of the extreme right, and the bleak prospects they face in a world dominated by technocrats and tech barons. Alongside growing anti-government protests from

Albania

,

Italy

,

Spain

, and beyond in recent days, the French student rebellions may herald the emergence of a new wave of global struggle.


In this article, our correspondent from Paris explains the context behind the youth rebellion, tracks the movement’s growth over the two weeks leading up to October 17 and the government’s failed attempts to repress or to pacify it, and clarifies the stakes moving forward.


Stay tuned for a full report on the uprising of October 17 and the ongoing rebellions across France and beyond.


Thousands gather to protest police violence and support the students in revolt (Nantes, October 6, 2026)


This update on the student unrest in France picks up where we ended

our previous report

, on the eve of the national call to take the streets on October 6, 2026.


The stakes were high on this crucial day of action. It was critical to show massive solidarity with the high school students fighting like hell against the empty future looming on their horizon. The day presented an ideal opportunity to expand the scope of the current movement by joining forces to resist the authoritarian state power that has been growing stronger every day.


The following article provides further context and analysis to understand the current situation in France, along with reports on what went down in the streets over these last rebellious weeks.


Background: The

Banlieues

 and the Enemy Within


When governments or powerful institutions feel threatened, they often strive to reaffirm their authority by inventing scapegoats to hold responsible for all supposed misfortunes. By invoking the menace of an “enemy within,” politicians can shift blame for systemic problems that have resulted from their own actions onto a specific category of individuals. In France, the most common targets are the residents of the

banlieues

, the impoverished suburbs on the outskirts of Paris and other cities.


At the beginning of the student blockades, the movement remained limited to a handful of high schools in these Parisian suburbs. In response, President Emmanuel Macron and his ministers decided to react quickly and do everything in their power to silence this emerging wave of youth protest. Due to the location of the first blockades, authorities believed that they could act more freely and repress the unrest with impunity, since these specific territories have been targeted for generations by all government administrations across political lines.


The condition of the

banlieues

, which remain populated by descendants of the French Empire’s colonized subjects, reflects France’s ongoing role as a

neocolonial power

 that continues to exploit African territories. Consider the disastrous

oil project

 in Uganda orchestrated by the France-based multinational company TotalEnergies, or the

corruption case

 involving the French far-right business tycoon Vincent Bolloré and his bribery and money laundering schemes across West African ports.


French governments and corporations have no scruples about extracting enormous wealth from African countries. This neocolonial pillaging fuels France’s position as the

seventh richest country

 in the world today, according to the IMF. Yet despite these astronomical profits, the nation refuses to address the problems facing its post-colonial population and their descendants within its national territory.


At the twilight of France’s colonial empire, decades of occupation and racist violence had created political and economic instability across northern and western Africa. As a result, waves of migrants began leaving their countries to come to France for work in the 1950s. Upon arriving, they continued to face systemic colonial racism, relegated to the economic margins …

title: ‘Grey’s Anatomy’ Kicked Off Season 23 With a Sapphic Smooch
content:
Grey’s Anatomy came back with a bang. (Well, a smooch. But we’ll get there.) Amelia spent the entire episode getting the cold shoulder from Toni because, as I’m sure you remember, we left them last season with Toni showing up at Amelia’s door to profess her love for her, only to realize a naked Cass was already in Amelia’s apartment.

When we return for season 23(!), Toni is giving Amelia the cold shoulder all day. Amelia desperately wants to talk to her, but Toni isn’t hearing her out. They clash over work decisions, and Amelia starts to get frustrated. And at this point I was afraid the show was ending their storyline. I thought it was going to be a dramatic fight and then back to no wlw relationships on the show. I was thankfully wrong!

Eventually, the day leads Amelia to Toni’s front door, where she apologizes again for sleeping with Cass, and explains it was an emotional reaction to being so sure Toni was about get back together with her ex. She regrets it if it means she would lose Toni. She says she’s truly, madly, deeply in love with Toni and that if Toni is done, she’ll move on, but if not, she really doesn’t want to let what they have died. Toni considers her for a moment but then breaks; she’s still in love with Amelia, and she’s not done. The two kiss about it, and while I doubt their road ahead will be paved with roses and rainbows (especially because Toni’s ex is still in the picture, and goodness knows if/when Cass will return to drop bombs) but I’m glad we at least aren’t done with their story yet. I look forward to seeing what Season 23 will bring for our resident gays; here’s hoping none of them disappear into the parking lot of no return.

author: Admin101
title: Sanctuary as a Verb: Experiences and Directions from Transversal Organizing for Immigrant Defense
content:
Black Rose/Rosa Negra Anarchist Federation (BRRN) is excited to announce the publication of

Sanctuary as a Verb: Experiences and Directions from Transversal Organizing for Immigrant Defense

.


Drawing on organizing experiences of Black Rose/Rosa Negra members across the United States, this pamphlet explores how workers, neighbors, and communities are building collective resistance to ICE and defending their immigrant coworkers, classmates, and loved ones. By connecting struggles across workplaces, schools, and neighborhoods, the

transversal organizing

 approach we prioritize builds solidarity across different sectors of society to confront the interconnected structures of domination that shape our lives.


You can find a downloadable PDF version of the pamphlet at the end of this text.


Two Years of Trump II: Immigrants in the Crosshairs, Resistance Under Attack


Upon returning to office, Donald Trump wasted little time fulfilling his white supremacist campaign pledge of “Mass Deportations Now.” Via a flurry of executive orders and congressional acts his administration reinstated the reviled “family separation” policy; directed virtually unlimited resources to stop a fictitious “invasion” of the country’s borders; and sought to end birthright citizenship. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents blitzed Los Angeles in June 2025 with spectacular raids, followed shortly by similar operations in dozens of cities across the country including New York City; Chicago, IL; New Orleans, LA; and Durham, NC. This “shock and awe” strategy culminated in Operation Metro Surge, a months-long invasion of the Minnesota Twin Cities that deported over 2,000 residents. 


Meanwhile, support for the deportation machine plummeted as collective action against it swelled. Everyday people covered their cars, lawns, and lips with the slogan “Abolish ICE;” as of July 2026, nearly 50% of US adults support such a measure. Both May Days since Trump’s second inauguration centered immigrant defense in their celebrations. Rapid-response networks that keep watch for ICE, document kidnappings, and sometimes disrupt them spread wildly. Know-your-rights training flourished at worksites and community centers. Millions of Red Cards–wallet-sized cards outlining the holder’s constitutional protections around interactions with ICE and other police–were distributed at schools, churches, restaurants, and municipal buildings. Children and their parents caged in concentration camps went on hunger strike as constituents bombarded politicians’ hotlines and town halls demanding humanitarian treatment and release outside their walls.


Popular responses in St. Paul and Minneapolis demonstrate the possibilities of mass resistance. Like the Los Angeles Tenant Union’s community defense centers that countered ICE’s Southern California invasion, organizers reactivated dormant neighborhood networks from the 2020 uprising and began building new ones when word spread that Commander-at-Large Greg Bovino was bringing his paramilitary forces to town. Once Operation Metro Surge launched, everyday Minnesotans refined sophisticated systems to track, delay, and disrupt arrests. ICE agents retaliated by killing rapid-responder Renée Good and shooting Julio C. Sosa-Celis, a Venezuelan immigrant targeted for deportation. Instead of cowering from the naked clampdown, neighborhood networks coordinated with unions, churches, and other civil societal organizations to shut down their cities on January 23rd. In its wake, Trump ousted Bovino and immigration enforcement plummeted.


But July 2026 saw record high immigrant detentions since Trump’s return to office with little public opposition. What explains it? ICE’s tactical shifts undoubtedly played a role. Bovino replacement and “Border Czar” Tom Homan traded provocative street operations with quiet detainers at jails and prisons and “targeted operations” at sites protected from activist impediment like airports. Escalating repression has also raised the costs of resistance. ICE’s bevy of brutality has included intimidation, beatings, and shootings, culminating in murdering Good and rapid-responder Alex Pretti. Federal grand juries fish from the shadows for information about our movements, stoking fears of informants that slow our organizing. From the Prairieland defendants to the Minnesota 15 and more, indictments and convictions on flimsy charges could make prosecuting dissidents even easier. Evidentiary discovery in the …

author: Caio de Freitas
title: PF acha nota de Willer Tomaz citando indiciado no caso Abin Paralela e “180 mil dólares”
content:
Uma anotação salva no aplicativo de notas usado pelo advogado Willer Tomaz de Souza, amigo do candidato a presidente Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), chamou a atenção dos investigadores da Polícia Federal (PF).

A nota continha um valor de “180 mil dólares” (R$ 908 mil, na cotação atual) atrelado às palavras “Corregedoria”, “Agosto/21” e ao nome Paulo Maurício Fortunato.


Naquele mesmo mês, Paulo Fortunato havia deixado o comando do Departamento de Operações de Inteligência (DOINT) da Agência Brasileira de Inteligência (Abin) do governo de Jair Bolsonaro, em um período de atividade da chamada “Abin Paralela”, como ficou conhecido o grupo que fazia uso, principalmente, do DOINT para comandar buscas contra adversários políticos, e até mesmo aliados, de Jair Bolsonaro (PL) por meio do

software

 israelense de espionagem First Mile – o que a PF classificou como “organização criminosa”.


Ao resumir as acusações contra Paulo Fortunato, o

relatório final da PF

 no caso “Abin Paralela” aponta que “o DOINT, sob sua direção [Fortunato], era a unidade central para a execução de buscas no sistema First Mile”, com “uso da estrutura para fins políticos e a perseguição de servidores”. A PF apontou que Fortunato teria sido “a autoridade demandante e o principal gestor da aquisição do sistema First Mile” em 26 de dezembro de 2018, nos últimos dias de governo Michel Temer (MDB) – imputação negada pela defesa de Fortunato, segundo apurado pela

Agência Pública

.


Para os investigadores, o ex-diretor da Abin “omitiu-se dolosamente no seu dever de implementar controles efetivos sobre o uso do First Mile e evitar a execução de ações clandestinas no DOINT. Sua omissão foi crucial para a continuidade das atividades clandestinas” e que “havia conhecimento, desde a origem, da ‘real natureza’ e das ‘características intrusivas’ da ferramenta

, que permitiam a localização de dispositivos móveis sem autorização judicial por meio de interceptação de sinais, explorando vulnerabilidades do sistema de telefonia nacional”.


Segundo a PF, o DOINT “era o principal demandante e utilizador da ferramenta para monitorar alvos de interesse da ORCRIM [organização criminosa], incluindo políticos, jornalistas, advogados e servidores públicos, muitas vezes sem amparo em investigações formais ou finalidades institucionais legítimas”. Como já se sabe hoje,

um dos alvos

 foi a então repórter da

Agência Pública

 Alice Maciel.


Em 2025, Fortunato foi indiciado pela PF por seu suposto envolvimento com a Abin Paralela, pelos crimes de organização criminosa, realizar interceptação de comunicações sem autorização judicial ou com objetivos não autorizados em lei, peculato, prevaricação de forma continuada e violação de sigilo funcional. Ele foi desligado oficialmente do governo somente

em 9 de janeiro deste ano

, com a conclusão do processo administrativo disciplinar contra ele por parte da Controladoria-Geral da União (CGU). 


Jornalismo investigativo é antídoto contra a desinformação. Ajude a garantir informação acessível e gratuita para mais pessoas. Faça um Pix para

contato@apublica.org

 ou doe em

apoie.apublica.org

.


O que dizem Paulo Fortunato e Willer Tomaz


O advogado responsável pela defesa do ex-diretor da Abin, Oscar Luís de Morais, disse à

Pública

 que a decisão da CGU foi “protocolar”, pois referia-se a um processo de exoneração de cargo em comissão na Abin. “O próprio senhor Paulo Maurício Fortunato pediu seu afastamento do órgão após a operação da Polícia Federal em outubro de 2023, e à época ele já estava aposentado, após 38 anos de serviço público sem qualquer registro de punição disciplinar durante sua carreira”, disse, acrescentando que ele é inocente no caso Abin Paralela e que seus atos à frente do DOINT se respaldam em um parecer técnico elaborado pelo próprio órgão de inteligência à época.

author: CMI Argentina
title: Europa: una generación parece decir basta
content:
Una oleada de protestas generalizadas recorre el viejo continente teniendo como trasfondo una situación económica europea cuyas perspectivas son de un bajo crecimiento, a lo que hay que agregarle la persistencia de las guerras y sus consecuencias económico-sociales. ¿Será el inicio de un nuevo ciclo de la luchas de clases en la región?


Protestas en París. Foto: Martin Barzilai


Como otras veces en la historia la situación despuntó en Francia, hace casi un mes atrás, protagonizada por el movimiento estudiantil, fue evolucionando y creciendo frente a la falta de respuestas del gobierno y la radicalización de la represión, casi en simultáneo las protestas se extendieron a Bélgica, Portugal, España Italia, Albania, tomando cuerpo en unas 28 ciudades europeas, llegando hasta la India.


Las protestas fueron reprimidas por los cuerpos represivos de los estados, lo que derivó en enfrentamientos, incendio de autos y edificios, miles de manifestantes que desbordaban calles y avenidas y cientos de heridos y detenidos. Ni corto ni perezoso el presidente Donald Trump culpó a la inmigración y afirmó que Europa debía “cerrar sus fronteras”, mientras que el premier israelí Benjamín Netanyahu señaló que Francia sucumbió a “la invasión del islam extremista”. Sin embargo varios analistas internacionales concluyeron que los inmigrantes no han tenido un papel destacado en estas manifestaciones. Mientras que el presidente de Francia, Emmanuel Macron, impuso el toque de queda en varias ciudades y la Presidenta del Consejo de Ministros de Italia, Georgia Meloni, convocó al ejército y amenazó con aumentar las penalidades.

Reminiscencias del ‘68


En cierto sentido la simultaneidad de estas protestas semeja a la deriva de los movimientos de 1968 que, nacidos en Checoeslovaquia y Polonia pasaron rápidamente a Italia y llegaron a Francia, en lo que se conoció como el Mayo Francés, aunque su influencia traspasó las fronteras de esos Estados. En aquellos años del siglo pasado Europa era todavía una potencia mundial, con un buen nivel de vida de sus ciudadanos producto del Estado del Bienestar y la idea generalizada de que era posible un futuro mejor. La rebelión tenía que ver con la democratización de las aulas, con cuestionamientos a la sociedad de consumo, contra el imperialismo y el estalinismo, contra el propio sistema del capital. Fue el mayor desafío al sistema desde la Revolución de 1917.


Una Europa en Crisis


La actual oleada de protestas generalizadas se desenvuelve en una Europa en crisis, tanto política como económica, que arrastra una extensa etapa de bajo crecimiento. El capítulo europeo del reciente informe del FMI “Perspectivas Económicas Mundiales” (Bangkok, Tailandia octubre 2026), proyecta un crecimiento de apenas 1.1% del PBI este año y 1.2 el próximo para toda la eurozona, mientras que la región muestras fuertes vulnerabilidades fiscales y una deuda pública regional cercana al 90% del PBI. Es esa desaceleración que llevó a una mayor desigualdad social, también entre países, mientras que la inflación (3.6% en septiembre pasado) impulsada por los mayores costos de la energía se tradujo en descontento generalizado por la carestía de la vida y la falta de acceso a derechos básicos, como la vivienda.


El protagonista principal es la juventud estudiantil, pero no solo por ella, también sectores de la clase obrera y fracciones de clase atravesadas por la crisis. Miradas de conjunto los manifestantes se expresan por el derecho a la vivienda, contra las políticas de austeridad que desfinancian los servicios públicos (especialmente salud y educación), contra la inflación (que impulsa la carestía de la vida) y los bajos salarios, por el aumento del gasto militar y por los temores a que toda Europa se involucre en la guerra. Con algunas excepciones, la oleada se caracteriza por no tener líderes definidos ni presencia de partidos u organizaciones políticas (las redes sociales volvieron a jugar un papel decisivo), también por la violencia desatada por las fuerzas represivas y la reacción de los manifestantes. Lo que ha puesto en discusión en todas partes (también en nuestro país) la legitimidad de la violencia de masas frente a la …

author: anred
title: Francia: ante nuevas protestas, Macron prohibe manifestaciones no sindicales, amenaza con el Ejército y limitar internet
content:
Protestas en Marsella, Francia. 17 de octubre de 2026. | THIBAUD MORITZ – AFP


Ante una nueva jornada de protestas convocadas por los Chalecos Amarillos, organizaciones estudiantiles y sectores sindicales para este sábado 24 de octubre, el gobierno de Emmanuel Macron anunció que prepara un operativo represivo reforzado, con la movilización de 70.000 integrantes de las fuerzas de seguridad en todo el país, la participación de militares de la operación antiterrorista Sentinelle y el apoyo de unidades especiales de la Policía y la Gendarmería. También anunció la prohibición de manifestaciones que no estén convocadas por organizaciones sindicales y que no respeten un recorrido previamente informado, y acusó a «grupos de la ultraizquierda» de intentar «hacer caer la República». En tanto, su

 ministro del Interior,

Laurent Nuñez

, propuso evaluar la suspensión temporal de redes sociales como TikTok y Snapchat para frenar la organización popular y la difusión en tiempo real de los movimientos policiales. Mientras, las protestas recrudecen en medio de una crisis socio-económica por las dificultades económicas de los hogares populares, el encarecimiento de la vida, los precios de la energía, los recortes presupuestarios en educación, salud y políticas sociales, y el deterioro de los servicios públicos.

Por ANRed.


El gobierno de

Emmanuel Macron

 anunció que prepara un

operativo represivo reforzado para este sábado 24 de octubre

, ante una

nueva jornada de movilizaciones convocadas por los Chalecos Amarillos, organizaciones estudiantiles y sectores sindicales

. En este marco, el ministro del Interior,

Laurent Nuñez

, anunció que

el gobierno francés desplegará 70.000 integrantes de las fuerzas de seguridad en todo el país, que incluirán militares de la operación antiterrorista Sentinelle, unidades especiales y vehículos blindados

.


La principal novedad del operativo es la participación de efectivos militares para «tareas de apoyo y protección de edificios públicos», con el objetivo de complementar las tareas represivas de policías y gendarmes en el control de las movilizaciones. El gobierno de Macron también anunció la

intervención de unidades especiales como el RAID, la Brigada de Investigación e Intervención (BRI) y el Grupo de Intervención de la Gendarmería Nacional (GIGN)

. En esa línea, Nuñez amenazó con una

respuesta «extremadamente firme»

 ante posibles saqueos, ataques a edificios públicos y enfrentamientos con las fuerzas de seguridad.


Foto: @EuropaPress


En paralelo,

Macron anunció la prohibición de las manifestaciones que no estén organizadas por sindicatos, por considerarlas «carentes de legitimidad» y afirmó que la recomendación general es que no haya manifestaciones durante los próximos días.

 A pesar de ello, en París,

el recorrido propuesto por los Chalecos Amarillos fue rechazado, mientras que se autorizó una marcha sindical con un itinerario alternativo

.

Mientras que en otras ciudades, como Lyon y Marsella, se prohibieron las movilizaciones previstas para el sábado

.


Las restricciones se producen en un contexto de creciente conflictividad social:

las protestas del 17 de octubre reunieron a Chalecos Amarillos, estudiantes, trabajadores y otros sectores que reclaman mejoras salariales, medidas frente al encarecimiento de la vida y el freno a los recortes presupuestarios y al deterioro de los servicios públicos.

 Durante la jornada también hubo saqueos, ataques a comercios y edificios públicos y se registraron alrededor de 2.700 detenciones.


Foto: ABDULMONAM EASSA/AFP


En este marco, a las 

protestas estudiantiles iniciadas en septiembre contra la falta de docentes, el deterioro de las escuelas y las dificultades presupuestarias del sistema educativo

, se suma también el movimiento de los

Chalecos Amarillos

, que irrumpió en Francia en 2018 contra el aumento de los combustibles y la pérdida de poder adquisitivo, y ahora vuelve a recuperar protagonismo en una nueva coyuntura de malestar socio- económico generalizado, mientras

buscan ampliar la movilización a trabajadores, jubilados, docentes y otros sectores afectados por el aumento del costo de vida

.


Con este escenario,

Macron acusó a «grupos de la ultraizquierda» de impulsar acciones destinadas a «hacer caer la República» y reclamó «la mayor firmeza» a las fuerzas represivas estatales contra las protestas

author: Anikibawal
title: Lof Juan Currin de Temuco enfrenta una nueva orden de desalojo del único predio en reivindicación que queda de su territorio ancestral.
content:
Durante el mes de junio del año 2026, dos integrantes del Lof Juan Currin fueron denunciados ante el Juzgado de Garantía de Temuco por el empresario Pablo Jacobi Bauman por los delitos de Usurpación u ocupación violenta de inmueble, en el único predio que queda de su territorio ancestral, el cual figura en su Titulo de Merced. Los dos lamgen que se encuentran procesados en la causa son Leonardo Catrileo Chiguaihuan y Oscar Chiguaihuan Chiguaihuan, quien cumple el rol de Lonkopalife en su comunidad. Durante el mes de octubre, el lof y en particular, los lamgen Oscar y Leonardo han sido notificados con una orden de desalojo.


Este no es el primer proceso judicial que interpone el empresario en contra de la comunidad, durante el año 2001, Pablo Jacobi anuncio una querella por destrucción de propiedad privada, ante la negativa del Lof Juan Currin a la instalación de un cerco dentro del terreno que pretendía instalar el empresario para materializar un proyecto inmobiliario en el predio. Durante esos años, Mariquina Trecamán, dirigenta de la comunidad declaro que el empresario Jacobi tendría una visión parcial de la historia del conflicto, ya que este se remonta al año 1950, cuando Alfonso Taito Schneider llegó al lugar como arrendatario, donde instaló una fábrica de ladrillos, en palabras de Mariquina Trecamán «Este señor fue designado como tutor de un menor de la comunidad, quien al fallecer ambos padres quedó al desamparo. Valiéndose de esta situación, no sólo se apoderó del terreno del menor, sino que se apropió de casi todo el terreno de la comunidad Juan Currín utilizando distintas maniobras en tribunales» (fuente: https://mapuche.info/archivo/news02/austral010528.html).


El Lof Juan Currin lleva décadas resistiendo en este predio ante la usurpación y despojo de casi la totalidad de su territorio ancestral, arrinconados entre edificios y proyectos inmobiliarios han logrado mantener y preservar sus practiiicas sociales, políticas, culturales y espirituales, espacios ceremoniales como un un Rewe y Paliwe, ademas en el lugar se emplazan viviendas pertenecientes a las familias de la comunidad.


 A continuación, compartimos una declaración del lamgen Oscar Chiguaihuan Chiguaihuan, Lonkopalife de la comunidad:


«Bueno, yo soy Óscar Chiguaihuan. Hace tiempo atrás recibí una denuncia aquí en mi territorio, pertenezco a la comunidad Juan Currín. Hubo una denuncia hace tiempo atrás por usurpación violenta, según yo… le usurpé el territorio a Pablo Jacobi, me acusa de haber puesto un rewe, el rewe era de mi abuela y tiene más de 30 años,… me imagino yo que tiene, yo tengo 35 años… yo me crié ahí, siempre había un rewe ahí y el winka me echa la culpa a mí que yo puse un rewe. No es lógico lo que dice.

Esta comunidad es muy antigua, tengo documentos donde se registra la comunidad, el lof, el título de Merced tiene muchos años, documentos de 1922 hacia estos años, hay documentos de que la comunidad está asentada aquí en este territorio y sin embargo hoy día me acusan a mí de yo usurpar territorio donde yo he sido toda la vida de aquí.


Y pasa que después de la denuncia, hoy día llega otra mala noticia, de que el Winka y sus abogados pidieron una audiencia de urgencia en Fiscalía, no sé cómo se harán esos temas y llegaron un acuerdo de desalojar aquí a la comunidad, digamos, despojarnos de donde tenemos el Rewe, que es un lugar ancestral para nosotros lo tomamos como donde hacemos nuestras ceremonias, jugamos al palín, tenemos nuestra salida hacia digamos hacia la hacia la calle, mi familia circula por aquí todos los días y nos quieren encerrar prácticamente, nos aislarían, no tendríamos salida, nada. No entiendo lo que quieren hacer los Winka, pero nosotros queremos evitarlo realmente porque no sería lógico que nos dejen encerrados, sin salida, ni siquiera caminando.


Entonces pasa que salió la audiencia que pueden desalojarnos y nosotros estamos en contra y queremos apoyo, necesitamos que la gente haga visible todavía como el winka usurpa la tierra, se empeñan en despojarnos de nuestra forma de ser, se niegan a reconocer los que nosotros todavía hacemos, nuestro guillatü, nuestro palines, hacemos ceremonia, celebramos Wetripantü, entonces nos van a despojar de todo eso si logran su acometido los winka. Nosotros como comunidad, digamos, como familia siempre hemos sido afectados, siempre hemos tenido que estar luchando. Yo tengo 35 años, pero hay registro de lucha de mi comunidad mucho más de la edad que tengo yo, hay mucha …

author: Darío Aranda
title: Miguel Mirra: "Cuando la comunidad participa en contar su historia, la recupera para la lucha"
content:
Por Ivana Carino


Desde mediados de la década del 80 Miguel Mirra trabaja una filmografía que recupera lo que suele quedar por fuera del plano de las narrativas industriales: las luchas de los pueblos originarios, los conflictos territoriales y las resistencias socioambientales, entre otros temas. Director de cine, guionista y docente, se formó en historia y antropología antes de pasar por la escuela de cine de Avellaneda.


Nacido en Lanús en 1950, en el seno de una familia de clase trabajadora, Mirra relata su recorrido con calidez, humor y un particular gusto por las anécdotas. Entiende

la cámara como una herramienta de lucha

: no solo para registrar y visibilizar los conflictos, sino también para

construir memoria, poner en circulación experiencias y hacer cine junto a quienes protagonizan esas historias

. Desde

La máscara de la conquista

 (1985)

, hasta sus trabajos más recientes, hay una preocupación que atraviesa su recorrido: que el documental acompañe las resistencias y permita que quienes las protagonizan se reconozcan también en las imágenes.


Foto: Télam


Entre el documental y la ficción


“Llegué al documental porque no sabía hacer otra cosa”, bromea Mirra. En la escuela de cine de Avellaneda había dos vertientes, documental y ficción, y él probó las dos. Su primera realización con equipo completo fue una ficción de época ambientada en la mal llamada "Conquista de América",

La máscara de la conquista

, rodada en 16 milímetros en 1985, con escenas filmadas en Mar del Plata y Córdoba. “Para una escuela era un lujo”, recuerda.


Fue durante ese rodaje cuando comenzó a explorar el cruce entre ambos lenguajes. Había escenas que no sabía cómo resolver y decidió filmarlas como documental: “Les planteé a los actores que siguieran más o menos el guion y las filmamos en el aquí y ahora, donde había sucedido aquello”. El resultado funcionó mejor de lo que esperaba. “Me di cuenta que había quedado bueno”, recuerda. Allí comenzó a descubrir las posibilidades del documental.


Ese descubrimiento tomó forma con

Hombres de barro

, rodada entre 1986 y 1987, y estrenada en 1988. Mirra la define como “el puntapié” de sus trabajos como documentalista. Fue, dice, una experiencia extraordinaria. El equipo, de cinco personas, filmaba en las Sierras de Zenta, en el límite entre Jujuy y Salta, cuando se cruzó con una camioneta en la que uno de sus ocupantes llevaba una cámara. “Nos preguntamos ¿quiénes son estos?”, recuerda. Era Miguel Pereira, que estaba filmando

La deuda interna

 (1988).


A partir de entonces, Mirra fue y vino entre el documental y la ficción. En

Crónica de un extraño

 (1998)

 retomó la historia de Eulogio Frites, abogado kolla y referente del derecho indígena en América, a quien había entrevistado para

Hombres de barro

. Frites le había contado que su familia lo había entregado a la familia administradora de un ingenio, donde pudo estudiar y recibirse de abogado. A partir de esa historia, Mirra construyó un relato de ficción sobre un padre que viaja a Buenos Aires en busca de su hijo, un joven que se había alejado de su comunidad para probar suerte como boxeador. “Hay parte del documental anterior y otras son ficción”, explica.


Pero no todas las historias admiten ese cruce. En sus documentales biográficos sobre Adolfo Pérez Esquivel,

Otro mundo es posible

 (2010);

Darío Santillán,


la dignidad rebelde

 (2012); y

Norita, Nora Cortiñas

 (2013), la ficción no tuvo lugar. En el caso de Santillán, es categórico: “Ahí no correspondía meter ficción. Trabajamos con la gente que lo conoció”.


La exploración de esas formas híbridas continuó con

Fuego en Casabindo

 (2022). Mirra llegó a la historia a partir del descubrimiento de una ópera sobre la rebelión kolla de 1874 en la puna jujeña, cuando unos 2.000 kollas se enfrentaron primero al ejército provincial y luego al nacional, en la

Batalla de Quera

. La investigación lo llevó a escribir un guion que pone en diálogo la ópera con los acontecimientos históricos y construye un personaje ficcional que funciona como nexo entre ambos planos.


La película debía exhibirse en Casabindo, pero antes fue presentada en San Salvador de Jujuy. Mirra recuerda que, cuando estaba por entrar a la sala, vio llegar una columna de personas: eran kollas que iban a verla. Al finalizar la proyección le regalaron un pequeño toro de porcelana. “Es uno de los recuerdos más lindos que tengo de ese momento”, cuenta.

title: Zapatistische Vorbereitungen für das umarmende Treffen mit den Familien Sucherinnen. Teil II. »Plan D«.
content:
»Die Delegation der Reise für das Leben – Kapitel Mexiko beim Ausüben der bekannten Spielvariante »Gemeinschaftlicher Fußball« oder »Massiver Fußball«. Kein Ball erlitt dabei einen Schaden … die Spieler*innen … nun, Ihr seht es im Video.«

Musik: Cuatro Pesos de Propina: »La Verdadera – Die Wahre« und »El Maleficio – Der Fluch«. Aufnahmen, Bearbeitung, Produktion: Terci@s Compas Zapatistas.

Zapatistische Vorbereitungen für das umarmende Treffen mit den Familien Sucherinnen.

Schwestern, Brüder, Schwestern-Brüder* der Familien Sucherinnen.

Compañeras, Compañeros und Compañeroas.

Comunidad originaria Otomí der Casa de los Pueblos Samir Flores Soberanes.

Wir informieren Euch darüber, dass der sogenannte Plan C gescheitert ist. Wir kommen jetzt nicht, wie wir gesagt haben, mit 1.509, nein, wir kommen nun mit 1.530. Hoffen wir, ein Plan E wird nicht notwendig sein, aber mensch weiß ja nie – nachher kommen welche mit dem Trick an: »Wir sind ja nur zum Abschiednehmen hier« – und steigen dann in die Busse: »Tja, nun seht mal zu«.

Wir haben uns als gesamte Delegation versammelt, um uns gut vorzubereiten und Euch ein gutes Wort der Ermutigung und Unterstützung zu bringen.

Viele* von uns können nicht gut castilla [spanisch]. Unsere Muttersprachen sind Maya-Sprachen. Somit müssen wir auch die vorbereiten, die übersetzen werden – und korrigieren, so weit wir können – damit unser Wort nicht falsch und verdreht herauskommt.

Wir sind froh, weil wir Euch zuhören, mit Euch sprechen, Euch umarmen werden können. Somit praktizieren wir. Lediglich die Umarmungen praktizieren wir nicht [vorher], denn wie Ihr wisst, nachher gibt es auf einmal eine*n Clevere*n, der*die befiehlt, das heißt, profitieren will.

Manchmal spielen wir zusammengeballt Fußball, falls dort [in Mexiko-Stadt] ein Spiel organisiert werden sollte.

Innerhalb der Delegation sind wir:

709 Männer, 622 Frauen und 2 Otroas-AnderE*.

24 des Comando Popcorn: 10 Jungen und 14 Mädchen.

110 der Comunidad Jugendliche Gemeinsam: 66 Männer und 43 Frauen. [Gesamtzahl?]

27 der Koordinierungsequipe: 7 Frauen und 20 Männer.

39 der Miliz [zapatistische zivile Selbstverteidigungsstruktur]: 16 Milicianos und 23 Milicianas.

Bis heute, 18. Oktober 2026, sind es insgesamt, ungefähr, 1.530 Delegierte* sowie verflixte Rasselbande aus Mädchen und Jungen. Somit seht zu.

Für den Moment ist das alles, Compañeras, Compañeroas und Compañeros, Schwestern-Brüder*, Brüder und Schwestern.

Falls es eine Änderung gibt (wir beten, es gibt keine), sagen wir Euch Bescheid. Wir werden Euch weitere Videos schicken, wie wir uns am Vorbereiten sind.

Wir senden Euch unsere gemeinschaftliche Umarmung, darauf hoffend, sie Euch bald persönlich zu geben.

Aus den Bergen des Südosten Mexikos.

Subcomandante Insurgente Moisés. Hauptkoordinator der Reise für das Leben – Kapitel Mexiko.
