author: La Zarzamora
title: DESPEDIR A JUAN…
content:
Esta mañana nuestro compañero Juan Aliste Vega ha partido de su cuerpo, cuerpo que el poder mantuvo en encierro los últimos 16 años, cuerpo que practicó el conflicto y lo materializó en acciones armadas, que acompañó su vida en el álgido recorrido de ser él. Fue en el hospital penitenciario de Santiago, donde en compañia y calma, se fugó definitivamente.

Aún no podemos confirmar donde ni como será su despedida, ló que sí sabemos es que serán muchas, en muchos territorios, en las calles, en los puentes, en las jaulas, en avenidas y carreteras.

Juan Aliste es y será reivindicado, pese a los esfuerzos incansables de la prensa del enemigo y de sus múltiples intentos de desprestigiarlo, nosotrxs sus compañerxs sabemos que en este momento estamos despidiendo a un guerrero de gran envergadura. Pese a sus miserables conjunciones de palabras, el mundo sabe quien es Juan y en todos los territorios se levantará fuego en su memoria.

Que desesperanza deben sentir los poderosos, al saber que amamos pese a estar en guerra, que nuestra historia es escrita por nosotrxs, pese a sus asquerosos relatos oficiales, tan indignos como ellos mismos.

Hoy es un día de nuestra propia historia, hoy parte el guerrero combatiente que se alzó en armas contra la dictadura y la pestilente democracia de burgueses y traidores, el que no se dejó abatir, el que atacó y acertó, el que siguió compartiendo conocimientos y enseñanzas pese al encierro, el que enviaba notas y saludos, el que hacía llegar sus palabras a actividades y espacios.

Cada vez es más difícil despedir, esto no es una noticia, ni tampoco un comunicado, es nuestro adiós a un hermano…

A nosotrxs ahora nos quedará volver a mirarnos, tensionar el encierro de nuestrxs compañerxs, cuestionarnos y autocriticarnos, dejar de hacernos tolerantes al encarcelamiento, dejar de normalizar la sociedad carcelaria y hacer. Arduo camino nos dejas.

Juan que tu fuga sea eterna querido compañero.

Ternura y ataque frontal por ti y por todxs nuestrxs muertxs.

author: Rafael Custódio
title: ‘Judicialização freestyle’ de Kassio mira Exército do Lula e ajuda Flávio, diz professor
content:
A dois dias do

segundo turno

, o Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) atuou para impedir que fosse derrubado o principal canal de comunicação da campanha digital de reeleição do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) — o Exército do Lula.

O ministro Floriano de Azevedo Marques ordenou nesta sexta-feira, 23 de outubro, que Kassio Nunes Marques, que comanda a Corte, se abstenha de suspender por via administrativa o canal de WhatsApp, criado e administrado pelo deputado federal André Janones (Rede).


Floriano escreveu que a presidência do TSE não tem competência para tirar do ar canais de pessoas físicas e viu o risco de abuso de poder. A resposta veio após um pedido do presidente da Corte, na última quinta-feira, 22 de outubro, para que a Meta – dona do Instagram, Facebook e WhatsApp –, o Google e o X (antigo Twitter) entregassem um relatório sobre a atuação do canal Exército do Lula, que reúne quase 10 milhões de pessoas. O prazo vence no início da noite desta sexta-feira, 23 de outubro. 


A decisão de Nunes Marques foi avaliada como “desastrosa” pelo professor Afonso Albuquerque, do curso de Estudos de Mídia da Universidade Federal Fluminense (UFF).

“[O TSE] atribui a uma empresa privada estrangeira o poder de produzir diagnóstico capaz de orientar a vida pública no Brasil”

, criticou. 


Professor Afonso Albuquerque, do curso de Estudos de Mídia da Universidade Federal Fluminense (UFF)


O docente também descreveu como “judicialização freestyle” a forma como o principal órgão eleitoral do país tem atuado, por estabelecer um desequilíbrio na forma como analisa os movimentos das duas campanhas eleitorais e por favorecer a campanha de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL). 


O canal de Janones entrou na mira de Nunes Marques após o fim do primeiro turno, depois que a campanha do candidato Flávio

pediu

 a suspensão do grupo por suposta disseminação de desinformação – fato que não foi constatado por peritos do próprio TSE. A equipe do candidato do PL também foi responsável pelo pedido ao ministro para que as plataformas fornecessem um relatório completo sobre a atuação do Exército do Lula, que estaria promovendo ações coordenadas. 


Às 10h12 desta sexta-feira, 23 de outubro, Janones avisou aos seguidores do canal de que eles estavam prestes a perder o lugar que os reunia. No Exército do Lula, o parlamentar mineiro disse que a página “deverá sair do ar ainda hoje” e que seria perto do horário do último debate entre presidenciáveis, que será realizado nesta noite na TV Globo, e que o pedido teria vindo do TSE. 


Com o anúncio de uma suposta restrição, os integrantes do grupo começaram a se mobilizar nas redes sociais, por conta própria, e disparar hashtags que apontavam para uma possível censura administrada por Nunes Marques. 


Uma minuta de resolução – que proibiria canais com mais de 200 mil seguidores nas 48 horas anteriores à votação – chegou a circular entre os ministros, mas foi abandonada por falta de maioria. 


A reportagem procurou o TSE que “não determinou a retirada de nenhum canal de WhatsApp do ar. Os prazos dos processos de propaganda são sempre curtos. Ilações a partir desses despachos que pedem informação em tempo curto são absolutamente indevidos.” 


A nota acrescentou ainda que “na manhã de hoje, os ministros da propaganda do TSE se reuniram  com as plataformas Meta, X, Google, TikTok e Kwai. Em pauta, as providências para o atendimento da legislação eleitoral. O ministro Kassio Nunes Marques, pediu reforço de pessoal e atuação isonômica por parte das plataformas a fim de garantir o cumprimento do plano de conformidade assinado por todas as empresas.”


A

Agência Pública

 entrevistou o professor Afonso Albuquerque, leia as principais respostas aqui.

 ou doe em

apoie.apublica.org

.


Como você avalia a decisão do ministro Nunes Marques em pedir um relatório para a Meta sobre o Exército do Lula e uma possível derrubada do canal ainda hoje?


Eu avalio como desastrosa. Porque atribui a uma empresa privada estrangeira o poder de produzir diagnóstico capaz de orientar a vida pública no Brasil.

Isso é não apenas privatização da Justiça, porque você atribui poder público a um agente privado, mas também um ataque à soberania nacional, porque você atribui a um agente estrangeiro a capacidade de formar decisões que impactam na vida política …

author: CMI Argentina
title: Súper El Niño: la barbarie capitalista recalienta el planeta y amenaza con multiplicar el hambre
content:
El calentamiento global agrava los riesgos de un fenómeno climático extremo. UNICEF advierte que 25,8 millones de niños de América Latina y el Caribe están expuestos a sequías e inundaciones. Detrás de la emergencia climática, una economía organizada para garantizar las ganancias y no las necesidades humanas.


Por Adrián Flores para Red Eco Alternativo


El mundo se encamina hacia un episodio de El Niño potencialmente histórico. El 10 de septiembre, la Administración Nacional Oceánica y Atmosférica de Estados Unidos (NOAA) estimó en más del 90% la probabilidad de un fenómeno muy fuerte durante el otoño y el invierno boreales de 2026-2027. Sus efectos podrían extender las sequías, las inundaciones y las pérdidas agrícolas en distintas regiones del planeta. 

Fuente:

NOAA


El problema no es solamente climático: es profundamente social. El calentamiento global, provocado principalmente por las emisiones derivadas de la actividad humana, agrava los riesgos sobre los que actúa El Niño. Pero sus consecuencias no golpean a todos por igual. Mientras los grandes capitales cuentan con recursos para proteger sus negocios, millones de trabajadores, campesinos y comunidades vulnerables quedan expuestos a la pérdida de sus viviendas, sus cosechas y sus fuentes de ingresos.


Las cifras son alarmantes. Según UNICEF, 25,8 millones de niños de América Latina y el Caribe —uno de cada siete— viven en zonas expuestas a sequías e inundaciones asociadas con El Niño. El organismo advirtió sobre los riesgos para la alimentación, el acceso al agua potable, la salud y la educación. Además, de los 53,8 millones de dólares solicitados para prepararse y responder a emergencias en la región durante 2026, el 55% seguía sin financiación al cierre de junio. 

Fuente:

UNICEF,

 28 de septiembre de 2026. 


La amenaza se extiende al hambre mundial. El Programa Mundial de Alimentos estima que El Niño podría empujar a otros 49 millones de personas hacia la inseguridad alimentaria aguda, elevando de 225 a 274 millones el total de personas afectadas en los países analizados. La pérdida de cosechas, el encarecimiento de los alimentos y los elevados costos de producción pueden convertir una alteración climática en una catástrofe alimentaria.

Fuente:

PMA


Pero el hambre no es una consecuencia inevitable de la naturaleza. Es también el resultado de un sistema que convierte los alimentos en mercancías, subordina la producción a la rentabilidad y condena a millones de personas a no poder comprar aquello que necesitan para vivir. El capitalismo destruye ecosistemas, impulsa la explotación intensiva de los recursos naturales y traslada sus costos a las mayorías populares.


Frente a esta barbarie, no alcanza con declaraciones ambientales ni con medidas de emergencia insuficientes. Se necesitan inversiones públicas, prevención, protección de los pequeños productores y garantías de acceso al agua, la vivienda y la alimentación. Eso exige enfrentar los intereses económicos que subordinan la vida a la ganancia.


El súper El Niño expone una contradicción central de nuestra época: la humanidad posee los conocimientos y la capacidad productiva para garantizar una vida digna, pero el capitalismo convierte esa posibilidad en privilegio. La lucha contra la catástrofe climática es inseparable de la lucha de clases y de la reorganización socialista de la economía al servicio de las necesidades humanas.


Fuente:

author: Unknown
title: Olive groves of locals seized in Afrin
content:
According to local sources, the Rajo Economic Office seized an olive grove belonging to an 80-year-old woman named Fidan Bilal.


On October 22, the Rajo Economic Office reportedly disregarded the law by bringing workers to Fidan Bilal’s grove and having them harvest the olives for its own benefit.


In the Bilbil district, the Bilbil Economic Office seized resident Ahmed Mamo’s olive grove in the village of Qestel and harvested 28 sacks of olives.


The Bilbil Economic Office stated that the regional director had ordered the seizure of Ahmed Mamo’s grove and prohibited him from harvesting his own olives.


Ahmed Mamo still has 140 olive trees that have yet to be harvested.

author: Brian Hioe
title: KMT Passes National Health Insurance Policy To Benefit Seniors, At Risk Of Fiscal Sustainability
content:
MINISTER OF HEALTH and Welfare Shih Chung-liang has criticized new legislation that would require the government to fully cover National Health Insurance (NHI) premiums for people aged 65 and older whose total consolidated income has an income tax rate of less than 20 percent. Such individuals would no longer have to pay premiums. Specifically, Shih has criticized the proposal as putting the burden for the NHI on working-age taxpayers, seeing as medical services are used disproportionately by the young and elderly, when Taiwan already has among the world’s lowest health insurance premiums.

The proposal has been criticized in the past as favoring elderly taxpayers and exempting them from having to pay health insurance premiums. In this way, apart from putting the burden of covering NHI premiums on working-age people, it has been criticized as benefiting wealthy elderly individuals.

Those who pay 20% in income tax are those who make above 1,330,000 NT per year. Those who make below 590,000 NT per year pay a 5% income tax premium. The KMT later amended the idea to only exempt seniors who pay under 5% in income tax. But the Ministry of Health and Welfare then warned that the proposal would lead to a loss of 54 billion NT for the NHI each year.

Taiwan’s universal health insurance system enjoys bipartisan support. Nevertheless, the KMT would be aiming to please a core support demographic for the party, that of elderly privileged individuals. This may be a demographic that the KMT increasingly leans into for support, even at the expense of young people, when several years ago, the party had fewer than 10,000 members under 40. Indeed, one notes that the KMT has consistently called for cash hand-outs for the elderly, whether this is carried out at the national level or municipal level, even when the same money might be spent more meaningfully on social services.

It proves ironic for the KMT to take measures that make the NHI less financially sustainable. Both this year and last year, the KMT has undertaken drastic financial cuts to the national budget, presumably in the hopes that the public would blame the DPP for any downturn in social services. It is to be seen whether there is public backlash over the issue, however, or if the issue is too in the weeds. One notes that the public has failed to have any strong reaction over moves by the KMT aimed at diverting money away from the central government and to local governments it supports will lead to the end of rental subsidies for 750,000 individuals, for example.
sourceTags: National Health Insurance system in Taiwan

author: groundxero
title: Bonus Is Not Charity: Tea Workers in Dooars Demand Unpaid Dues, Justice and Accountability
content:
Six Merico-Sammelan managers are in custody, but the group’s directors and employers remain unarrested. As workers continue to wait for bonus and other outstanding dues, PBCMS demands arrest of owners, recovery of payments, Rs 5,000 relief for workers denied bonus, and protection of abandoned garden assets.


 


20 October 2026 | Groundxero Desk


 


Even after workers took to the streets, blocked highways and forced the authorities to act, thousands of tea garden workers in the Dooars in North Bengal are still waiting for the bonus they were promised before Durga Puja. In a particularly brazen display of political appropriation, the distribution of bonus money in some gardens has been turned into a BJP publicity event, presenting workers’ bonus payment as a favour bestowed by political leaders.


 


Meanwhile, six Merico-Sammelan managers have been arrested and two other managers are reportedly absconding, following cases filed by the Paschim Banga Cha Majdur Samiti (PBCMS), but the directors and employers evade accountability and remain untouched. The arrest of managers has failed to resolve the crisis confronting thousands of workers across tea estates. Five of the arrested managers were due to appear before the Alipurduar court on Tuesday, 20 October, after spending four days in police custody. The question now is whether the police and administration will pursue the cases against the garden owners allegedly responsible for the non-payment of workers’ dues, or whether the action will stop with the managers.


 


The latest developments follow weeks of protests over the failure to pay the promised 20% annual bonus by the government’s 5 October deadline. As documented in Groundxero’s earlier

report

,

“No Bonus, Unpaid Wages, Missing PF Dues: Thousands of Tea Workers Take to the Streets in North Bengal”

 (16 October), the dispute is part of a wider crisis involving unpaid wages, outstanding leave allowances, provident fund contributions allegedly not deposited since June 2023, and gratuity dues owed to retired workers.


Tea workers block highway over withhold bonus


The management’s repeated assurances have not translated into payment. Workers have had to organise demonstrations, march to police stations and block highways to demand money earned through their labour. The arrests mark a development in the struggle, but they do not settle the outstanding dues or establish accountability across the ownership and management of the gardens.


 


PBCMS has demanded that the authorities pursue all cases filed by the union and the Labour Department, recover workers’ outstanding payments and ensure accountability through due process. The union has also called for effective action to secure the arrest of the remaining accused.


 


Bonus is a workers’ right, not BJP’s charity


 


The struggle has also exposed how a workers’ entitlement can be appropriated for political publicity.


 


On 17 October, a 10% bonus (half of the promised of 20%) was distributed in Dumchipara, Hantapara, Gairganda, Tulsipara and Birpara gardens. Workers at Bagrakote, Kilcott and Nageisuree were still waiting for bonus payment.


 


At Samsing tea garden, the distribution of bonus became a ruling party spectacle, with three BJP ministers, two MLAs and an MP present. The MP was seen counting and handing out money amid prominently displayed BJP flags.


BJP leaders distributing bonus to workers


The political message was unmistakable: a payment due to workers was being projected as a favour delivered by the ruling party. But bonus is not charity, nor is it a favour from ministers or MPs or MLAs. It is an entitlement arising from workers’ labour, and its payment should not depend on political patronage or turned into publicity event of a political party.


 


The irony is especially sharp because the BJP government, like the previous Trinamool Congress government, had announced a 20% bonus and set a deadline of October 4-5 for payment. Yet the failure to enforce that deadline has left workers to take to streets to protests to secure their own earnings. The government has failed to effectively enforce its own assurance and take action against employers who deliberately refused to pay the workers their dues.


 


Fresh promises, more unanswered questions


 


Puna Bhengra, BJP MLA from Metelli, has announced that a new owner would pay a 20% bonus in Nageisuree, Kilcott, Bamandanga-Tundu and Samsing. This was followed by assurances of …

author: Roy Barbosa
title: Long-time labor activist Bob Reyes walks free after eight years of imprisonment.
content:
with reports from Kline Vergara, Jessica Obciana, and Shaine Peñaranda

“Anak, sana paglabas mo, huwag mong kalimutan ang mga taong tumulong sa iyo at saka ang pamilya mo. Maging mabait ka, anak, sa paglabas mo. Tulong-tulong pa rin tayo sa mga kaibigan mo,” said 73-year-old Virginia Reyes, mother of long-time labor activist Juan Alexander ‘Bob’ Reyes.

On October 20, the Quezon City Regional Trial Court acquitted Bob Reyes in an illegal possession of explosives case, the 14th and final case which kept him behind bars in Camp Bagong Diwa for more than eight years.

Bob attended the promulgation virtually, allowing Virginia to see her son’s face as he learned of the acquittal. Virginia further recalled how difficult it was for their family during the first days of his arrest

“Noong nahuli siya, palagi akong dumadalaw. Hirap na hirap ako. Yung pambaon ko sa kanya kasi wala naman akong trabaho. Kaya malaki ang pagpapasalamat ko sa mga tumulong para sa anak ko,” she said.

Bob was arrested by five operatives of the Criminal Investigation and Detection Group (CIDG) in Barangay San Antonio, Quezon City in 2018.

Other cases filed against Bob included arson and murder in Agusan del Norte and Surigao del Sur, stemming from allegations implicating him in armed encounters between the New People’s Army and the military. In 2019, he was also acquitted of illegal possession of firearms in the same court in Quezon City.

During the promulgation, the court found that the prosecution failed to establish the existence of the alleged evidence against him.

“The inventory of seized items did not include a blasting cap and a sachet allegedly containing a substance from a detonating cord, although these were later mentioned in the information filed against him,” it added.

Bob is the convenor of Defend Job Philippines and coordinator of Sandigan ng Manggagawa sa Quezon City (SMQC), championing labor rights and welfare.

Prior to his arrest, Bob had been subjected to harassment, threats, and red-tagging following his work as a labor activist.

In 2015, he and three other unionists from COURAGE filed for writs of amparo and habeas data before the Court of Appeals but were ultimately disregarded. They were later arrested and charged with similar offenses of illegal possession of firearms and explosives.

“Hindi maaalis ang katotohanang walong taon ng buhay ni Bob ang ipinagkait sa kanya upang makasama ang pamilya at ang mga manggagawang inoorganisa niya. Hindi rin natatapos sa pag-acquit ang pagpapanawagan ng hustisya mula sa ilegal na pag-aresto hanggang sa samu’t saring delays sa kanyang proseso ng paglilitis,” Sandigan ng Manggagawa sa Quezon City wrote in a statement.

Under the Marcos Jr. administration, Kilusang Mayo Uno National Capital Region spokesperson Chito Guevarra shared how union-busting and red-tagging remain dangerous for labor activists being accused of links to the NPA.

For Chito and other labor groups, Bob’s acquittal underscored the justice system being weaponized against activists, workers, and human rights defenders.

“Tumagal siya ng walong taon at mayroon pang mga bilanggong pulitikal na magpahanggang ngayon ay sinampahan din ng gawa-gawang kaso. Kaya hindi rito nagtatapos ang panawagan para sa pagpapalaya sa ating mga bilanggong pulitikal,” he said.

author: rti_admin
title: The IITs: Tragic Failures That Beget More Tragedies
content:
From a social perspective, the IITs are tragic failures that beget more tragedies.

But you already know the IITs are the pinnacle of Indian aspirations, achievements, accolades, blah-di-blah, right? How about we celebrate by taking a closer look at the graduates, the faculty, and the institution?

The institutional charter, briefly. The IITs were conceived in 1946 to support the country’s industrial development and help meet the nation’s technological challenges. Parliament’s 1961 Act declares them institutions of national importance. It charges them with instruction and research, and with the advancement of learning and dissemination of knowledge. The same Act says every institute shall be open to persons of either sex and of whatever race, creed, caste or class, in admitting or appointing students and teachers alike. [1] Later laws reserve seats for SC, ST and OBC students, PhD seats included, and, since 2019, teaching posts at every rank.

Start with the product. As any IIT alum would confirm, a majority of IIT graduates wouldn’t be able to properly describe what ‘engineering’ is. Poorly educated and narrowly conditioned to chase status from a young age, most of them used to end up in finance or as middle management in US IT firms, but have lately diversified into mercenary ouroboros via IIT coaching and YouTube influencing. The institute’s own numbers: in IIT Bombay’s placement report for 2023–24, 29% of offers were in engineering and technology. The rest went to IT, consulting, finance, analytics and “other”. [2]

The defence is usually the famous founders. Let’s do the math. Seats went from about 2k a year in the 80s to about 20k now, so total grads ~400k. Unicorn founders ~117, high value startup founders maybe four thousand if you’re generous. So, 0.03% and 1%. [3, 4] Like unicorns, these founders are statistical anomalies. Sensible folks within the system will themselves readily acknowledge that their success is mostly despite it rather than because of it. And given the stated mission, funnelling billions in public subsidy into private equity accumulation for a minuscule minority is cause for shame rather than something to tom-tom about.

This is the deal then. Ruin your childhood to join an exclusive band of svayambhu achievers. Concoct jagatguru-brand gig economy “innovations” for exploiting cheap labor. Garland each other for contributions to the economic miracle of jobless growth and extractive digital feudalism. Parade your arrogant indifference or offer defensive apologies for the mockery of a social contract, dressed up in a lazy pragmatism argument about success.

By the way, who’s even there to teach them? Across all 23 IITs, 4,804 of 12,498 sanctioned teaching posts stood vacant in January 2026, or 38.4%. [5] It was 38.3% in December 2022. [6] In the nine IITs that disclosed the breakdown, about 60% of the empty posts were reserved ones. [5] Cryogenic sthiratva.

Sour grapes? I was there, eating them for four lost years. So chill. First week in the hostel, the rank was a common icebreaker question you asked people along with where they were from and in what department. Some hesitant answers made me stop asking. Only the rare, confident stud would openly declare he was SC, came through the preparatory course etc. The term in use was ‘schaddu’, and people would murmur in the early semesters, but soon some of them were ahead on GPA, and the murmurs lost voice. Years later, a friend who got a PhD mentioned feeling conflicted using reservations since their father was also a PhD and they went to good schools. Not long ago, an alum stated that even though they got in via reservation, everything after was earned by merit. I couldn’t make out if this was being defensive or proud. I don’t remember hearing of any campus suicides, and only learned about them from ‘The Death of Merit’ documentary. [7]

A decade after graduation and on another continent, the sourness still stung, in an interview by another pitiable alum. I was struggling for purpose and careening across career lanes. Unusual for an IIT grad, and he got suspicious… maybe I was a ‘category candidate’? So he asked for my rank, and then I asked for his, and then he said that’s not relevant, and then I agreed, and the interview went downhill. So, no chill.

Then the people who run the place. Do the IITs still hire blatantly sexist dogs as professors? It used to be de rigueur in several departments. A lot of the students were of a similar breed …

author: Dulce Amor Rodriguez
title: Social media ban may exclude children instead of protecting them, advocates warn
content:
Child rights advocates have warned that a proposed social media ban could restrict children’s access to information, education, expression, and participation without addressing the perpetrators and platforms responsible for online abuse.


The warning followed the Senate’s approval of Senate Bill No. 2424, or the proposed Safe Media Access and Responsible Technology for Kids in Digital Spaces (SMART KIDS) Act, on third and final reading on October 8.


The Senate approved the measure by a vote of 16-1, with no abstentions, advancing a proposal sponsored by Sen. Robinhood Padilla that would restrict minors’ access to digital services classified as high-risk.


Salinlahi Alliance for Children’s Concerns argued that the government must protect children from online exploitation, grooming, bullying, and other forms of digital harm without treating their access to digital spaces as the problem.


“Banning children from social media does not make the internet safe. It impedes children’s right to participation while the perpetrators remain,” said Teacher Elle Buntag, Salinlahi secretary general.


The group warned that restricting children’s access would not, by itself, establish whether platforms would respond more effectively to abuse or whether authorities would investigate and prosecute offenders more consistently.


Instead, Salinlahi called on the government to strengthen investigations into online sexual abuse and exploitation, require platforms to detect and remove abusive content, improve reporting and rescue mechanisms, and provide survivors with psychosocial and legal support.


“If the government’s answer to online abuse is simply to remove children from the platform, then we are asking children to bear the burden of a problem created by perpetrators and enabled by weak systems,” Buntag said.


The group maintained that children have rights to information, expression, education, participation, and connection in digital spaces, and urged the government to protect these rights while making online environments safer.


“The state must not confuse restricting children’s access with protecting children. Protection means making the digital spaces they inhabit safe and holding those who exploit them accountable,” Salinlahi said.


Different approaches


The debate over the Senate measure centers partly on whether an under-18 restriction offers a proportionate response to online harm or whether lawmakers should adopt age-specific safeguards.


Sen. Risa Hontiveros, the sole senator who voted against the measure, argued for a more targeted approach that would allow older adolescents to use social media with adequate safety measures.


Hontiveros had proposed restricting access for children under 13 while allowing those aged 13 to 18 to use social media if platforms provided adequate safeguards.


The Child Rights Network Philippines’ explainer questioned the basis for setting the minimum age at 18, and urged lawmakers to examine the evidence behind a blanket restriction before limiting children’s digital rights.


Sen. Win Gatchalian, a co-author and co-sponsor of the Senate measure, argued that aligning the age threshold with the legal definition of a child under existing laws would make enforcement more consistent and easier for authorities, according to the network’s explainer.


Padilla, meanwhile, said lawmakers could amend the measure after assessing its effects, and cited other countries’ experiences with restrictions and subsequent policy reviews, the explainer said.


The Child Rights Network challenged the idea that ease of enforcement should determine the age threshold, arguing that lawmakers must also consider the measure’s effects on children’s rights and daily lives.


The debate therefore goes beyond whether authorities can enforce an age restriction and asks whether the restriction would protect children effectively without imposing unnecessary limits on their participation.


Beyond entertainment


Child rights advocates said children use social media for more than entertainment, including research, learning, creative work, communication, and maintaining relationships.


The Child Rights Network noted that children also use digital platforms to connect with friends and peers and to communicate with parents working overseas.

author: chuang
title: “Every War Is a World War”: Interview with a Member of Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine
content:
The following is an interview with friends from Taiwan who have formed the umbrella coalition Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine (TWAFP). The interview includes an overview of the rifts in the Taiwanese left, and the frustration of TWAFP organizers carving out their place amid divisions between pro-unification and independence, or pro- and anti-American positions, in the contentious and highly polarized politics on the island.


The organizer recounts their efforts to confront Taiwan’s growing ties with Israel and direct support for the genocide in Palestine. They speak with sadness that, even as Taiwan is now the fourth-largest supplier of arms to Israel, surpassing mainland China, most Taiwanese care little for the distant genocide and the struggle in Palestine seems far away. And yet, TWAFP has led successful demonstrations, pulled together a broad coalition of disparate groups in support of Palestine, and conducted research to expose Taiwan’s complicity in the ongoing genocide.


Be sure to read their

report


from 2025, outlining specific pathways of material component support for Israel, including radar, armor, and an array of military hardware.


See also a recent

piece

 submitted to us, outlining Taiwan’s deepening ties with Israel under the DPP government.


–

Chuang


Q: To begin, let’s just set the stage. Over the last few years, the Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine (TWAFP) has helped to organize the largest mobilizations against the genocide in Palestine seen in Taiwan. Can you tell us a little about how TWAFP formed and maybe review some of the protests it has organized?


A:

Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine (TWAFP)

 was founded in April of 2024. Prior to this, Taiwan had already seen several groups doing Palestine advocacy work arise spontaneously, including Palestine Action Front, Taiwan Palestine Solidarity Network, and Parallel Government. As its name suggests, TWAFP is an “Alliance” that brings together groups that were already involved in initiatives related to Palestine. In addition to the three groups already mentioned, the alliance also includes a migrant worker organization, the

Taiwan International Workers’ Association (TIWA)

; the human rights organization, Taiwan Association for Human Rights; the cultural collective, Taiwan Rave & Punk Solidarity Front for Palestine; the gender issues group, Queer Margins; and the Christian group, Taiwan Olive Branch Peace Collective. From 2024 to today, we have organized one petitioning campaign, issued two open letters, held one candlelight vigil, hosted one book club meeting, staged five protest actions, held three press conferences, and organized three marches. In the future, we plan to engage in a number of other activities, many of which may be smaller in scale.


Q: TWAFP also did some very interesting research on material links between Taiwan and Israel. We can link to the report here, but can you briefly go over the main findings, and maybe go over any new information that you’ve found since that report was released? For example, have there been more details since then?

      


A: In September of 2025, we released our report,

Taiwanese Companies’ Complicity in Israel’s Ongoing Genocide

, which identified specific manufacturers assisting Israel in the production of military weapons, including via the production of components. For example: Gloria Material Technology Corp (GMTC) supplies superalloys and high-grade steel produced through electroslag remelting, while ADLINK Technology supplies embedded computing systems and industrial-grade computers. In another case, Transcom marketed its vertically integrated capabilities—spanning chip design to module production—to enter the Israeli defense supply chain and is now a key, long-term supplier of components for the EL/M-2084 multi-mission radar, which is a core element of the Israeli “Iron Dome” air defense system designed by Israeli defense company Elta.

title: IFJ passes motion in support of press freedom and against censorship in Turkey
content:
At its online meeting on 19 and 20 October 2026, the Executive Committee of the International Federation of Journalists (IFJ) unanimously passed a motion expressing solidarity with journalists, trade unions, and professional organisations in Turkey in their fight against censorship, intimidation and the criminalisation of journalism. The European Federation of Journalists (EFJ) also supported the motion.


Considering:


The increasing repression of independent journalism in Turkey, including the detention and prosecution of journalists, restrictions on media outlets, the appointment of government-appointed trustees to media organisations and the blocking of journalists’ social media accounts;


The fundamental right of journalists to report freely, investigate matters of public interest and hold those in power accountable, without intimidation, censorship or criminal prosecution for their legitimate professional activities;


The joint call by Turkish journalists’ professional organisations for nationwide demonstrations on 24 October 2026, marking the first anniversary of the appointment of a trustee to TELE 1;


Resolves:


First:

 To express its full solidarity with journalists, their trade unions and professional organisations in Turkey in their struggle against censorship, intimidation and the criminalisation of journalism.


Second:

 To strongly condemn all forms of repression targeting independent media and to demand the release of journalists detained solely for carrying out their professional duties.


Third: 

To support the nationwide mobilisation organised by Turkish journalists’ organisations on 24 October 2026 and their legitimate demands for press freedom, editorial independence and the public’s right to information.


Fourth:

 To urge the Turkish authorities to respect their international obligations concerning freedom of expression and press freedom, and to put an end to judicial harassment, arbitrary restrictions and political interference in the media.


The IFJ Executive Committee reaffirms that journalism is not a crime, press freedom is not negotiable, and the public’s right to know must never be denied.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Despite Budget Passage, Defense Items Remain Frozen on Legislative Agenda
content:
QUESTIONS ABOUT defense procurement have been raised, with less than two months in the fiscal year, and the legislature’s Foreign Affairs and National Defense Committee not having scheduled any review of over 150 requests to unfreeze funding.

The KMT finally relented on budgetary spending–including defense spending–in August, this being more than 351 days after the budget was submitted by the Executive Yuan for review. Though defense spending was passed, this was in the form of part of the Executive Yuan’s regular budget, rather than as a special operational expense.

The conditions of passage also froze funds or subject them to yearly approval by the legislature. Among what was cut was 10% of funding for the Taiwan Tactical Mission Network and the Team Awareness Kit, while the KMT also slashed additional funding for programs it does not like, such as funding for Taiwan’s domestic submarine fleet after the initial submarine, the Hai Kun. That drone funding is subject to additional approval by the legislature makes it difficult for industry to have assurances of continued funding if this is subject to change every year. Apart from the Taiwan Tactical Mission Network and the Team Awareness Kit, which provide for situational awareness, the military has also submitted requests to unfreeze maintenance and replenishment parts for its M1A2T Abrams tanks.

Nevertheless, the Foreign Affairs and National Defense Committee has not scheduled any discussion of unfreezing such funding. Instead, the committee has scheduled discussing the relocation of the Songshan Airport, something proposed by Taipei mayor Chiang Wan-an, as well as allegations of misuse of funds against former Overseas Community Affairs Council Minister Hsu Chia-ching, a scandal that the KMT has used to attack the DPP. Indeed, it could be expected that KMT committee co-chair Hsu Chiao-hsin would act to block any discussion of unfreezing such funds, Hsu having downplayed Chinese threats directed at Taiwan in the past.

In the meantime, earlier this week, the Coast Guard stated that it had driven away 16 Chinese vessels. Such vessels reportedly included fishing vessels, research vessels, and Chinese Coast Guard vessels that engaged in coordinated operations.

Maritime authorities have reported an uptick in Chinese maritime activity in waters east, south, and southwest of Taiwan, as well as around Pratas Island. Experts have suggested that such an increase in Chinese maritime activity in these waters further points to the need for Taiwan to strengthen maritime cooperation with other regional powers, such as Japan and the Philippines. China is probably aiming not only to project power and to probe Taiwan’s defenses, but to enhance and practice cooperation between various elements of its fleet that would need to cooperate in the event of military action against Taiwan. Still, even at a time of such rising threats, it can be expected that the KMT has little interest in Taiwan’s defense.

author: Ben Radford
title: US must end its cruel blockade of Cuba
content:
Every year since 1992, the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) has overwhelmingly voted to end the United States government’s cruel and illegal economic blockade of Cuba. One-hundred-and-sixty-five countries voted last year for the resolution on the “Necessity of ending the economic, commercial and financial embargo imposed by the United States of America against Cuba”, with just six against.

This year’s vote, on October 28, takes place as escalating US economic warfare against Cuba is causing a devastating humanitarian crisis. The blockade’s impacts have been characterised as a “silent genocide”, severely restricting Cubans’ access to food, medicine, equipment and fuel, and impacting every aspect of daily life.

The Cuban government submitted its annual report to the UNGA in September, detailing last year’s impacts of the US blockade. Between March last year and February this year, the blockade inflicted more than US$8 billion worth of damages.

The economic cost of just four days of the blockade amounts to the cost of all fuel imports needed to meet Cuba’s demand.

On top of existing strangulation mechanisms, the US government imposed an energy blockade on Cuba in January, claiming that the country posed an “unusual and extraordinary threat” to US national security.

The US announced tariffs on goods from countries that, directly or indirectly, sold or provided oil to Cuba. Following the US’s January 3 attacks on Venezuela, it also blocked all Venezuelan oil shipments to the country.

The energy blockade is the reason for widespread blackouts, as well disruptions to water supply, waste collection and transport.

The fuel shortages are severely impacting hospital operations, including treatments that require a steady energy supply, such as haemodialysis. There are harrowing reports of surgeons having to perform operations by mobile phone lights, due to the blackouts.

The US blockade has affected Cubans’ access to vital treatment and medicine. One example is Cuba’s cancer survival rates, which, while still higher than many low- and middle-income countries, have dropped from 85% to 65%.

Cuba’s infant mortality has risen from 4 out of 1000 live births in 2018 to 9.9 last year — a 148% rise.

Cuban authorities say that the current transport crisis is more acute than during the “Special Period” in the 1990s following the collapse of the Soviet Union, which plunged Cuba into a prolonged economic crisis. Fuel shortages have affected refrigerated transport, preventing more than 30,000 children from receiving vaccines.

In May, the US imposed a regime of secondary sanctions against governments and companies that invest in or trade with Cuba.

For example, the US Office of Foreign Assets Control has imposed fines on US companies for handling cargo shipments bound for Cuba and providing services for people living in the country.

Over the past year, 34 international banking institutions suspended or declined to conduct operations with Cuba, citing risks of secondary sanctions.

Several airlines have ceased operations in Cuba and many international hotel chains also abandoned management agreements for hotels, citing the risks posed by the secondary sanctions regime. These sanctions — along with other US measures — have contributed to the collapse in Cuba’s tourism industry.

“The application of these measures has produced a sophisticated mechanism of asphyxiation directed at the Cuban population, exceeding by far the levels of pressure historically imposed over decades,” the annual report said.

It also notes that the blockade has caused US$3.9 trillion worth of damages since it was imposed. However, it said the impacts go far beyond economic losses, causing suffering, illness and death.

The US blockade of Cuba violates not just international law, but any semblance of humanity.

The US government has made its intention of achieving “regime change” in Cuba by the end of the year very clear; it is openly considering the possibility of military attacks. This has been the US’s policy since Cubans overthrew the US-backed Fulgencio Batista military dictatorship in 1959 and set about implementing a planned economy based on meeting people’s needs.

Since then, the US has undertaken or sponsored terrorist attacks, a military invasion and an economic blockade against the Cuban people, with the explicit aim of bringing about “hunger, desperation and overthrow of government”, as revealed by a 1960 US memorandum.

author: Nick Everett
title: Palestine supporters guilty once again, declares Murdoch press
content:
Within hours of Indi MP Helen Haines’ alleged attacker Brendan Nugent being named by police, the Murdoch media stable and a coterie of Zionists were weaponising the attack to smear the Palestine solidarity movement.

Whether it’s the shooting of fifteen people on Bondi Beach, explosives found in caravans, the looting of shops in Paris or a shocking attack on a politician with a LandCruiser, Palestine supporters cop the blame. 

“‘Plant person’ and ‘pro-Gaza’ radical Brendan Nugent arrested over Helen Haines attack,” 

announced

 a headline in the 

Australian

 on 21 October. 

Nugent’s real crime was not causing grievous bodily harm to a popular, independent MP, but rather being “an environmental activist who has regularly slammed Australia’s political leaders on social media, accusing them of ‘giving Israel impunity to kill thousands of children’.”

Nugent’s social media posts denouncing politicians’ complicity in Israel’s Gaza war crimes “have become increasingly toxic,” claimed reporter Damon Johnston. The evidence? Calling Prime Minister Albanese and Foreign Minister Penny Wong “a couple of US lap dogs”.

A front-page op-ed in the same issue of the 

Australian

 declared the attack on Haynes is a “message to the Left” to “stop minimising extremist threats.” 

Australian Jewish News

 predictably followed suit, 

posting

 on X the same day: “Anti-Israel extremist allegedly attacks and seriously wounds Australian member of parliament.” 

Australian actress and TV presenter Rachel Griffiths joined the bandwagon, 

posting

 on her Instagram account that this attack “is what globalise the intifada looks like”.

None of this makes any sense if you were to take a cursory look at Haines website: she has been one of the most trenchant opponents of Israel’s genocide over the past three years in a House dominated by Israel apologists.

On 18 March 2024, five months into the genocide, just six MPs in the House of Representatives voted in favour of allowing a debate on a motion calling for a ceasefire between Israel and Hamas. Haines was one of them, alongside independent Andrew Wilkie and four Greens parliamentarians. Half the members absented themselves from the chamber while 63 voted against allowing debate.

Two months later, Haines 

told

 the House that there must be “consequences” for Israel’s actions and the time for restraint had passed. Last month Haines reiterated her call for the Australian government to impose sanctions on Israel, 

stating

: 

“It’s been more than two years since the International Court of Justice confirmed that Israel’s occupation of Palestine is illegal under international law. The government has acknowledged Israel’s actions are extinguishing the possibility of a two-state solution. The Prime Minister has just confirmed this. Twelve countries have announced sanctions in the hopes of saving the two-state solution.”

Haines asked, Defence Minister Richard Marles, “what will it take for Australia to join our allies [in imposing sanctions on Israel]?” Unsurprisingly, Marles obfuscated, stating “We will continue to look at further targeted measures, working collaboratively with our allies and partners around the world in respect of this issue.”

We don’t know what was in Nugent’s head at the time of his alleged attack on Haines. We do know from a statement by his lawyer that Nugent had poor mental health and a neurological illness and that he had never been in custody before. But facts are not important when right wing media pundits have a score to settle with a movement for justice that refuses to be silenced. 

And where is Labor in all of this? 

We need to “turn the temperature down” says prime minister Anthony Albanese. The same PM who, in the wake of the Bondi massacre, turned the temperature up by establishing a royal commission to provide a high-profile public platform for defenders of Israel’s crimes to slander and vilify Palestine solidarity protests.

The attack on Haines is a terrible tragedy, and the conditions under which someone decides to carry out such an atrocity warrant investigation and reflection. Using such a tragedy to pursue a political campaign in support of Israel, without concern for facts or evidence, is, on the other hand, nothing short of obscene, and indicates the degree to which bludgeoning progressives trumps truth in the editorial offices of the right-wing press.

author: Luca Tavan
title: Europe’s youth and workers in revolt
content:
The metaphor of a tinderbox is one of the most overused in politics. But how else could you describe the situation in Europe today, where every small spark of resistance seems to be catching and turning into a powerful blaze? 

Things kicked off in France in late September, when students in the working-class suburb of Créteil in the South-east of Paris blockaded their school in protest against poor conditions. This has since grown into the deepest challenge French President Emmanuel Macron has faced in his ten years in power. On October 17, students were joined by workers in a national mobilisation of 800,000. Strikes, demonstrations, blockades and riots have all played a role in this movement. It’s not just the radical left comparing this situation to the legendary student and worker uprising of May 1968.

In Spain, anger at the eviction of María del Carmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman whose rent was raised 230 percent when her apartment was acquired by an investment firm, has generated a massive movement for housing justice. The streets have forced the centre-left Sanchez government to call early elections, and typically hesitant union leaders to schedule a general strike for November 11. 

Protests have rocked Albania since May, in response to an environmentally catastrophic luxury resort development tied to the Trump family. On October 13, youth inspired by the French protests brought their own demands over education and wages into the mix, turning the movement into a national uprising. Government buildings have been invaded and burnt, and the call for the downfall of Edi Rama’s government is widespread. It is the country’s largest revolt since the fall of Stalinist regime in the early 1990s.  

In Italy, mass protests pledging to “fare come in Francia” (to do as in France) last weekend turned into standoffs against the police. In Milan, 250 people were detained, more than 80 percent of whom were minors. Belgium, Portugal, and Ireland have seen mass protests and strikes taking aim at austerity and intolerable working conditions. 

This marks the biggest wave of protests on the continent in at least a generation. Anyone who wants to see capitalism one day toppled and replaced with a system really fit for human beings should take great hope from these events. 

There’s no telling how long these struggles will continue, whether they will lose momentum, or if massive state repression will succeed in intimidating many off the streets. But this convergence of different struggles provides a glimpse of the possibility of rebuilding class-based politics after a decade characterised by despair and far right ascendancy. 

The roots of the revolt 

While these different movements are profoundly shaped by their specific national contexts, they have common roots in decades of battered living standards and attacks on workers. An entire generation suffered the consequences of the 2008 economic crisis - wages were slashed, young people were left without the prospect of ever finding a job, and social services were gutted to bail out the banks. 

Italy provides perhaps the sharpest example of the consequences of this class war waged by the rich: according to data from Italy's Parliamentary Budget Office, private sector workers have seen their real wages fall by 6.6 percent between 1990 and 2026. 

In countries experiencing economic recovery, young people are learning that they bear the costs of boom as well as bust. New jobs created are insecure, and wage increases are offset by soaring housing costs. 

This long, bitter experience has brought questions of social class back to the fore and changed the character of struggle. A comparison of the current occupation of Madrid’s Puerta del Sol with the last one is instructive. 2011’s 

Indignados

movement shared many characteristics with the protests of today, fuelled by anger at low wages, evictions and the callousness of the political class. It was an inspiring and important moment for the left. But the politics of the movement were organically populist, seeking to build a cross-class alliance of Spanish ‘citizens’ against the political caste they blamed for the country’s ruin. The most popular slogans reflected this - like “real democracy now!” and “they don’t represent us”. 

This sentiment was also expressed in a hostility to the organised left and workers’ movement within the occupation - seen by many participants as just another facet of the “politics” they felt alienated from …

author: Pip Hinman
title: NSW Labor to introduce law overriding High Court coal mine ruling
content:
The NSW Labor government will introduce a law to allow MACH Energy to expand output at its contested Mount Pleasant coal mine in the Upper Hunter region of NSW, in response to a High Court ruling that invalidated the expansion approval.

The High Court ruled on October 7 that the NSW Independent Planning Commission (IPC) failed to consider how pollution from its coal would affect the region. It also emphasised that the IPC must consider Scope 3 — downstream emissions from coal burned elsewhere, including overseas — as part of its approval process.

Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group (DAMSHEG) first challenged the IPC’s approval in 2023 in the NSW Land and Environment Court. Following a protracted legal battle, DAMSHEG had its case upheld in the High Court.

Premier Chris Minns told the ABC on October 19 that he was moving to protect jobs that would be “on the line”. He said the new law would “guarantee” 400 direct jobs until 2032 — the deadline for the temporary extension MACH Energy sought and was given, even though the High Court was considering MACH Energy’s case against DAMSHEG.

The mining corporation wants a licence to mine thermal coal until 2048 — something Minns and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese support.

However, the 22-year extension of the coal mine would include no guarantee of 400 jobs. DAMSHEG’s Tony Lonergan said the mine relies on contractors who can be laid off at any time.

Wendy Wales, also from DAMSHEG, said she wants fossil fuel workers to be able to transition to alternative employment. “We have never wanted anyone in the Hunter to lose their livelihood.”

“A law written for one company, days after the High Court ruled against that company, is an inappropriate use of the NSW legislative process,” she said. “The laws should reflect a balance where the overall welfare of citizens and environment is paramount and industry serves the needs of all citizens.”

The NSW Minerals Council welcomed Labor’s move. Chief executive Stephen Galilee said: “The Mount Pleasant mine has endured four years of activist legal challenges, creating uncertainty for hundreds of mine workers, their families and local supplier businesses.”

Greens MLC Sue Higginson said NSW Labor is being “fed lies about the job numbers at Mount Pleasant” and “selling the integrity of the NSW planning and legal systems down the river”.

She said MACH Energy had threatened to sack 400 workers at Mount Pleasant mine unless Labor introduced this law. It has been revealed that new job advertisements were posted by MACH Energy shortly after Minns announced the special law allowing expanded coal mining.

“MACH Energy’s own documents show that the increased coal mining that will be allowed by Minns’ special laws would only create around 100 jobs, completely undermining its threat to fire 400 workers if they didn’t get their way,” Higginson said.

“This is state capture — a form of modern day corruption ... where billion dollar corporations are writing laws that benefit them, in defiance of the law as laid down by the High Court of Australia.”

Retired Supreme Court judge Anthony Whealy has called for an independent review of the Minns government’s decision to draft laws to circumvent the High Court ruling.

Whealy told the ABC on October 20 that the government’s decision is “reprehensible” because it “obliterates” the legal process.

“The idea that a substantial mining venture can approach the government and say, ‘Look, let’s go behind the court processes and sort this out between ourselves’ is a very dangerous precedent, and that’s exactly what appears to have happened here,” Whealy said.

“They’ve effectively ignored what I would call respect for the rule of law by overriding it.”

The Greens are supporting his call for an independent review.

Higginson said Labor has “decided to step over the independent planning process ... the High Court of Australia and they are trashing the rule of law”.

The ABC also reported on October 20 that MACH Energy is being investigated over allegations it breached its coal production limits, as it scaled up construction during the High Court appeal process.

Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group

author: Dougal McNeill
title: Striking for Palestine in Aotearoa
content:
Thousands of workers at universities and polytechnics (TAFEs) across Aotearoa (New Zealand) went on strike Wednesday 21 October, rallying against poor pay offers and the increasing precarity of employment in tertiary education. This was exciting enough on its own terms. The last time we went on strike, in 2022, it was the first in decades, and felt like something new. Now tertiary workers join teachers, public servants, health workers and others who have taken action over the last two years.

Our right-wing coalition government has attacked many of our rights but, in the fightback against their assault on everything from Te Tiriti o Waitangi (the country’s founding treaty with Indigenous groups) to pay equity, we’ve seen that the long drought around industrial action in these islands has been broken by welcome and nourishing rain.

Each bargaining campaign has different priorities and, at Te Herenga Waka in Wellington, my university, one part of our campaign stands out. We went on strike for Palestine. University Workers for Palestine, a campaign group bringing together staff across the country, emerged from the anti-genocide protests since 2023 to make concrete demands of institutions here. One focus is university superannuation schemes and their investments, including in weapons companies and others connected to Israel’s ongoing war against the Palestinians. A core part of our demands, then, is for the superannuation scheme to divest from the genocide.

We are striking for the “Three Ps”: pay, precarity and Palestine. The last of those got the loudest cheers at the strike rally yesterday, and there were signs from “Librarians for Palestine” to staff committing “from the river to the sea” that Palestine will be free. Unionised workers here have shown that our action for everyday pay and conditions can be linked to a wider vision of justice and liberation.

It’s a small start, but an exciting one, and another sign that the protest moment of 2023 has, over the years, become a long-term movement for Palestinian freedom.

author: Kerry Smith
title: Hunter Jobs Alliance says new law on coal transition gives hope
content:
The Future Jobs and Investment Authority (FJIA) Bill 2025 passed both NSW houses on October 20.

According to the Hunter Jobs Alliance (HJA), it is a major achievement and testimony to the many organisations and individuals that have campaigned over five years to secure a better future for workers, communities and the environment across NSW’s four coal regions.

HJA started with publishing Building for the Future: A ‘Hunter Valley Authority’ to secure our region’s prosperity in June 2021, which made the case for a “dedicated regional authority to support workers, diversify our economy and secure the Hunter’s future beyond coal”.

Since then, it has worked to get NSW Labor to commit to establishing a Transition Authority in its policy platform before the March election next year.

It is seeking 10 amendments to strengthen the law, particularly workforce transition planning obligations for coal companies.

HJA singled out the Australian Manufacturing Workers’ Union for “critical political and strategic support in advancing the proposal”, as well as Hunter Renewal, which championed this reform long before HJA’s involvement.

It said the new law establishes a dedicated public authority, and funds to support economic diversification, attract new industries and create jobs across NSW’s four coal regions.

“Importantly, it will also require coal mine owners to develop workforce transition plans to support workers affected by mine closures. This represents a significant shift from the current system, where coal companies have had limited enforceable responsibilities to prepare workers and communities for closure.”

HJA said its next job is to ensure the regulations are “developed and finalised before the caretaker period” in the lead-up to the March election next year.

“These must establish meaningful minimum standards for workforce transition plans, including paid retraining, paid training leave, career and financial advice, and assistance securing new employment.”

HJA is also seeking at least $150 million each year for the Future Jobs and Investment Fund, up from the current $22.5 million a year. “Securing this as a budget commitment ahead of the March 2027 election will be a key focus.”

HJA said its member organisations and everyone who has contributed to this campaign “demonstrates what can be accomplished when unions, environmental organisations, community groups, business and industry work together towards a shared vision for the future of the Hunter and NSW’s other coal regions”.

Future Jobs and Investment Fund

author: Robert Narai
title: Hungary 1956: a workers’ revolution against Stalinism
content:
Seventy years ago, Hungarian workers and students rose up against a brutal dictatorship that justified itself in the language of Marxism. In its place, they built workers’ councils: organs of working-class democracy, giving future generations a chance to discover the essence of revolutionary Marxism.

My grandfather, Vendel Koroknai, often played Beethoven’s Egmont Overture on his record player and spoke fondly of its role in the 1956 revolution. The overture tells the story of Lamoral, count of Egmont, who defied Spanish tyranny under the duke of Alba. His execution sparked a broader rebellion that led to Dutch independence. For the Hungarians who heard it, the parallels were striking: the Russians as the oppressive occupiers, themselves as the Dutch seeking self-determination.

They heard it because on the evening of 23 October 1956, workers and students defeated the hated AVH, the secret police of the dictatorship that had ruled Hungary for the previous eight years, in fierce street fighting and gun battles, and took control of Magyar Radio in central Budapest. They turned it into a hub for broadcasting news, appeals, morale-boosting content and, importantly, political arguments about the way forward for their revolution. Between announcements, they played the overture over and over to lift people’s spirits and give them the resolve to fight a much better-armed enemy in the form of Russian tanks. It became the unofficial anthem of the revolution. My grandfather, who at the time was a farm labourer on the outskirts of Debrecen (Hungary’s second-largest city) and a delegate and militia leader in one of the workers’ councils, recalled: “It wasn’t just filler. It was a prophecy, articulating the hopes, dreams and aspirations of a people fighting for their liberation.”

Whether they knew it or not, Hungarian workers and students were also creating a radical alternative to both Stalinist and Western barbarism. At the height of the Cold War, they broke the so-called communist regime’s repressive arms—the secret police were dispersed, the police defected or stood aside, the army disintegrated—even as parts of its executive and bureaucratic machinery kept functioning. Into the space that opened up, they built workers’ councils, elected and recallable, running factories, farms, whole cities and towns. My grandfather was one of those workers, and it was his first taste of any political freedoms.

Stalinists who defend the bureaucratic monstrosities of the Soviet Union have always called this a counter-revolution, the work of fascists and Western agents, and used that claim to justify sending in the tanks. (The term “tankie” is derived from this argument.) The Hungarian far right, Viktor Orbán chief among them, calls it something else: a rehearsal for 1989 and the fall of the “communist” system, proto-capitalists fighting to restore private property and the free market. Neither is true. Hungarian workers were not fighting for capitalism, Stalinist or Western. The councils they built were organs of workers’ power and the basis for a democratic society run by the working class: genuine socialism and communism. This was a workers’ revolution, and the people who made it included men like my grandfather, who had lost his family’s farm to the regime that now called him a fascist.

As the American Trotskyist Hal Draper wrote at the time: “Hungary opens a new era with the first revolution against the Stalinist system.” Hungarian workers and students proved the working class could still make revolutions. They proved the so-called communist regimes were counterrevolutionary. And they cracked, for the first time on this scale, the grip Stalinism held over communist parties across the world.


PART ONE: THE OCTOBER UPRISING

Background

The Red Army occupied Hungary at the end of World War Two. With the tacit approval of the West, a Russian-backed dictatorship was installed under Mátyás Rákosi, who called himself “Stalin’s best Hungarian disciple”. Like the other Eastern European regimes established at this time, Hungary called itself a “workers’ state”. It was anything but. Workers like my grandfather had to perform backbreaking labour to meet production targets set by bureaucrats. They had no say in what was produced or how, or in any broader political decision. They were paid pitiful wages that could hardly buy bread and milk.

author: Sue Bolton
title: Sue Bolton: ‘Put working-class communities first’
content:
Sue Bolton, a fourth-term Socialist Alliance councillor at the Merri-bek City Council, is running for Broadmeadows in the Victorian elections.

This article is based on a speech she gave to the launch of SA’s campaign. The party is fielding candidates in Broadmeadows and Pascoe Vale in Naarm/Melbourne, and in four seats covering Djilang/Geelong. It is also standing in the Northern Metropolitan and Western Region for the Legislative Council.

Socialist Alliance’s campaign slogan “Fighting for people, not the billionaires” encapsulates our view that fundamental change won’t come from elected representatives.

Our approach is to work with communities getting organised so that they can become really strong. We need members of parliament who will champion a politics that defends working-class communities against the billionaires.

The only way to guarantee that working-class communities’ rights are safeguarded is by electing socialists who are also committed community activists.

The campaign to stop the redevelopment of the toxic site in Fawkner in 2017 is a case in point. When this development came through Merri-bek City Council, I objected and together with the community we fought hard against it. It would have sailed through because the Environmental Protection Authority had already approved it.

Right now the far right — and the mainstream right — are trying to take back social and political rights that took fights to win.

The Victorian Labor Party, following the One Nation (ON) playbook, is attacking migrants. It has stopped talking about renewable energy and the need to transition away from fossil fuels. Even if ON doesn’t get an MP, its policy announcements are pushing the major parties to the right — a core part of the billionaires’ divide-and-rule plan.

Billionaire mining magnate Gina Rinehart is writing Pauline Hanson’s policies. She has other billionaire supporters, but they prefer to remain in the shadows.

If migration was to be stopped tomorrow, there would still be a housing crisis. This is because state and federal policies allow developers and speculators to game the system. The destruction of public housing is another part of the housing problem.

What is the billionaire’s agenda? Pay zero or little tax and privatise, or cut, public services — not the fat cats but the people providing the services.

Even repairing potholes on roads and motorways has become political, after a man tragically died after hitting a pothole on his motorbike. VicRoads used to do those repairs. Since it has been handed to the private sector, the roads have deteriorated.

Labor’s privatisation agenda of critical public assets includes the Port of Melbourne, part of VicRoads and the Land Titles office. It includes demolishing 44 high-rise public housing towers, shafting people out of their communities and affordable homes.

The disintegration of the community health sector is part of this. The introduction of the national disability insurance scheme (NDIS) forced the community health centres to move to a user-pays model.

But communities have also shown that they will resist. Because of the community revolt, Labor’s plan to axe GPs and other services at various CoHealth sites, including Collingwood and Fitzroy, have been saved — for the moment.

While Premier Ben Carroll has sought to distance himself from Jacinta Allan and Dan Andrews, he supports the public housing demolition. Labor should be pledging to renovate and keep the public housing towers, and replace the dwellings that have been demolished.

The billionaire class wants to stop workers gaining pay rises which keep up with inflation. It wants to remove regulations so private businesses, like the mega data centre AI industry, or developers eyeing off the toxic site in Fawkner, can do whatever they like.

It is possible after the next election that the Treaty process in Victoria could be ripped up. The Coalition has promised to do that and ON would like to. Sections of Labor are nervous about the kind of rights First Nations people would have with a Treaty or treaties.

For First Nations people, the process is about more than symbolism; it is a way of improving their lives, including access to culture and practice to build stronger communities. This is important. We need to ensure that the rights of First Nations people are enhanced. Only then will we have improved rights for everybody.

author: Unknown
title: Merinos işçisinden sosyal medya yasağına tepki: Köle değil, işçiyiz!
content:
Biz Merinos’ta gecesini gündüzüne katıp alın teri döken işçiyiz. Fabrikada zaten hakkımızı ararken binbir türlü zorluk yaşıyoruz, şimdi bir de elimizdeki telefonu, kişisel sosyal medya hesaplarımızı kontrol altına almak istiyorlar. Biz patronun niyetini çok iyi biliyoruz. Amaç içeride yaşadığımız haksızlıkları, ağır çalışma koşullarını veya bir iş kazasını dışarıya duyurmamızı engellemek istiyor. Yarın bir gün haksızlığa ses çıkardığımızda, bizi tazminatsız işten atmak için şimdiden kılıf hazırlıyor. Hatta işten ayrılsak bile arkasından konuşmayalım diye gözdağı veriyorlar. Bu kağıdı imzalatmalarında, iş yerindeki ağır çalışma koşullarının sosyal medyada paylaşılmasının ve bundan dolayı da yeni işçi alımlarında işçi bulmakta zorlanmalarının etkisi de var.

Bu taahhütnameyle bizi tamamen susturmak istiyorlar. ‘Hakaret, iftira, yanıltıcı bilgi’ diyerek tazminatsız işten atılmanın altyapısını oluşturuyorlar. Düşük zam karşısında yapacağımız grevlerin önünü kesmek istiyorlar. Haksızlıklar karşısında basına, sendikaya ya da sosyal medyaya açıklama yapmamızı engellemek istiyorlar. ‘İşten ayrıldıktan sonra da benim kölemsin’ anlamına geliyor. Yani biri işten ayrılsa bile, Merinos hakkında tek kelime edemeyecek. Haksız şekilde işten atılsa hakkını arayamayacak. Hak arayan, taahhütnamedeki kurallara uymayan işçiler de tazminatsız işten atılmakla, şirkete tazminat ödemekle tehdit ediliyor.

Ama bu belgenin hukuki bir geçerliliği yok, biliyoruz. Tamamen bizi korkutmak için yapılan bir uygulama. Biz köle değiliz, işçiyiz. Anayasal hakkımız olan ifade özgürlüğümüzün ve hak arama hürriyetimizin elimizden alınmasını kabul etmiyoruz. Sendikamızın ve basının bu sansür dayatmasına karşı sesimizi duymasını ve yanımızda durmasını istiyoruz.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Joakim
title: Syndicalism With Extra Everything: How to Cut Through the Legal Thicket
content:
Article from Znetwork. Translated from the Swedish magazine Brand. The English version has been extended and modified for a wider audience. The Swedish article, in turn, is based on a more extensive education material. More articles in English here.

Illustration above by Stefan Ehn.

When workers organize and fight for their interests, they often encounter a complex legal framework – not least rules restricting strikes, blockades and other forms of industrial action. “As lawyers, we can help by getting the legal tangle out of the way, so that workers can focus on organizing.” This is how Rasmus Hästbacka, a lawyer at the Swedish union SAC, puts it. In today’s brutal labor markets, he advocates syndicalism with “Extra Everything”.

Even though workers are usually referred to in labor law as the weaker party, they are far from helpless. When workers come together in unions, they create the capacity to organize industrial action and win collective bargaining. When this happens on a broad front, unions become the vehicle through which the working class moves toward a brighter future.

Not even those workers who may appear the most vulnerable – migrant workers – are helpless. On the contrary, once the organizing gets going, they can become both an engine and a spearhead of class struggle.

In recent years, a small trade union in Sweden – the syndicalist union SAC, particularly its Stockholm Local – has distinguished itself by defending migrant workers against all kinds of crooks. A rambunctious Russian-speaking union shakes up Sweden’s labor movement, writes the freelance journalist Volodya Vagner. In Jacobin Magazine, he urges Swedish unions to wake up to new forms of exploitation and points to syndicalist examples of direct action.

But then labor law enters the drama offering help on the way as well as pitfalls and roadblocks. In 2019, the Swedish parliament introduced an anti-strike law. The law was pushed through by the Social Democratic government with support from top leaders of the three big union confederations – LO, TCO and Saco. The law entails certain amendments to the Swedish Co-Determination Act (abbreviated MBL). This has turned MBL into a legal thicket, a miserable mess.

At this point, the MBL framework may be difficult to grasp, but workers shouldn’t give up – for then employers have already won. Despite the anti-strike law, Swedish unions still have the right to launch so-called wage-extraction blockades to recover unpaid wages and take solidarity action in support of other workers. And this is just for starters – so join me for a closer analysis!

I will begin by discussing so-called soft pressure as a prelude to industrial action.

These are methods that don’t count as industrial action (in legal terms) and therefore aren’t covered by prohibitions against industrial action. This includes various forms of moral and psychological pressure, ranging from employees speaking with one voice to management at staff meetings to launching petitions and excluding bosses from workers’ social gatherings.

Soft pressure shouldn’t be underestimated. When employers aren’t receptive to arguments and facts, soft pressure can sometimes work wonders – simply because it creates a very uncomfortable situation for bosses.

Soft pressure also functions as a kind of union strength training. When a group of co-workers have successfully carried out soft pressure, they are soon ready for industrial action. Perhaps slowdowns, maybe an overtime blockade, perhaps even a strike. Once management has experienced industrial action, soft pressure too tends to become a sharper weapon. Management then knows that soft pressure may be followed by something even more uncomfortable. At that point, it might very well be deemed best to meet the staff’s demands.

Now, let’s proceed to industrial action and the legal framework in Sweden.

To get a clear picture of the MBL framework, we need to distinguish three types of situations. I start from the assumption that a syndicalist union wants to know if it has the right to take industrial action.

In the first type of situation, the syndicalist union is bound by a collective agreement (a union contract, as it’s called in the U.S.). This entails an almost total ban on industrial action (under Section 41 of MBL). In other words, a no-strike clause automatically follows every collective agreement. This contrasts with U.S. labor law, which allows union contracts without such clauses.

In the second …
