author: winter oak
title: Calling on our ancestors!
content:
by Paul Cudenec, who reads the article

here


After I published my articles on the Druids and ancient Celtic culture this summer, Franklin O’Kanu wrote on his

Unorthodoxy

 blog about the parallels to his own ancestral culture.


He

said

: “What’s interesting about all of this is how two cultures, across the world, Nigerian and Celtic, have the same spiritual view of the world”. [1]


And he

commented

 on one of my posts: “From the Yoruba and Igbo perspective, what the Celts experience in one continent is what the practitioners of Ifa experienced in another continent: the same honor of the Divine”. [2]


I have now discovered similar echoes from a reverse direction, as it were, through reading

Of Water and the Spirit: Ritual, Magic, and Initiation in the Life of an African Shaman

 by Malidoma Patrice Somé (1956–2021).


Somé belonged to the Dagara, a million-strong people spread across the artificially-created nation-states of Ghana, the Ivory Coast and Burkina Faso – he came from the latter, which was still called French Upper Volta when he was born.


The environment and particular customs of this African people are, of course, very different from those of the ancient Celts – roasted monkey would not have been on the menu at a Beltane feast in Ireland!


But there are similarities as well. In the essay series I

cite

 Jean Markale’s account of how at their celebratory events the Celts drank copious amounts of alcoholic drinks, producing “drunkenness, in other words the trance thanks to which one can go beyond apparent reality and see the supernatural”. [3]


He adds: “For Greek and Roman writers, Celts already had a reputation for being passionate lovers of fermented drinks. Drunkenness is an oft-occurring theme in the epics, especially in Irish accounts.


“Gods and heroes compete in their unquenchable thirst for alcohol, in the form of beer, wine or mead. A religious festival never went by without a serious drinking session”. [4]


In

his

 book, Somé writes: “Millet beer has always been a part of major rituals. Our rituals are long, and one gets thirsty”. [5]


He explains that his tribe was said to have been taught how to make beer by the Kontomboli, mysterious otherwordly beings who introduced a woman to their astonishing brew: “When she drank it, she was delighted. She felt merry and wanted to sing”. [6]


I was also intrigued to learn that the Dagara use a twenty-based counting system, so that eighty-three would be expressed as “four times twenty plus three”. [7]


In France the same number is

quatre-vingt-trois

, “four twenties and three”, after the old Celtic system, and we used to have the same concept in English with a score, meaning twenty, using which eight-three is “four score and three”.


A more important connection between ancient European and African societies has been the effects of colonisation.


From an African perspective it must be strange to hear a white man claim to be the victim of colonialism, but such is the case.


Following the destruction of our indigenous culture by the Roman empire and its religious wing, we were then

colonised

 by the empire of usury and commerce and used as fodder for its insatiable industrial Leviathan. [8]


With our true identities further smothered, our vital energy was hijacked to allow that same empire to enslave and exploit other peoples across the world, including the Dagara.


Somé writes: “My own elders had experienced French colonialism and the culture of the West as a force that used violence as a means to eradicate traditional lifeways.


“They had seen their own youth stolen from them as they vainly struggled against the incursions of these intruders.


“During these years, in which my people were trying to make sense of a people whose every action seemed to go against the natural order of things, creating chaos, death, and destruction, the sense of unified community that sustained their tribal life was profoundly destabilized. These foreigners seemed to have no respect for life, tradition, or the land itself…


“In spite of the best efforts of all my people, the whites kept on coming; kept on doing whatever they pleased; and kept on taking more and more of our land, our beliefs and our lives”. [9]


“It is a sad thing to realize how much my people have lost and how much yet of our reality is to be buried in the pit of oblivion”. [10]


Although Upper Volta officially became independent in 1960 (it became Burkina Faso in 1984), this …

author: Yohannes Woldemariam
title: The New Scramble for Africa
content:
Something important is happening across the Red Sea and the Horn of Africa. Wars that appear local are drawing in actors from increasingly far away. Ports built for commerce acquire military uses. Gold mined in conflict zones travels through international financial centers. Drones purchased abroad alter wars. Governments negotiate with foreign powers while those same powers cultivate armed groups or parallel authorities elsewhere.


Sudan, Libya, Ethiopia, Eritrea, Somalia, Somaliland and Yemen are usually discussed as separate crises. Look more closely and the connections become difficult to ignore. A

 

United Nations investigation

 found that forces aligned with Khalifa Haftar helped move Colombian fighters through Libya to support Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces. Sudanese gold travels toward the Gulf, while


Chatham House has documented

 the importance of the UAE to the regional gold economy. In western Ethiopia, a

 

Reuters investigation

 found a large training camp for fighters intended for the RSF, with reliable sources saying the UAE financed the facility and provided trainers and logistical support. 


These are not isolated developments. They point toward a changing system of power around the Red Sea.


What is emerging is not another Berlin Conference. Foreign governments are not openly dividing Africa into colonies, and African governments are not passive spectators. They bargain, invite investment, seek weapons and sometimes use outside powers against domestic or regional rivals. But something more than ordinary diplomacy is taking place.


One striking change is the growing importance of powers once treated as secondary actors in African geopolitics. The United Arab Emirates, Turkey and Israel do not possess the worldwide reach of the old European empires. Yet wealth, military technology, commercial networks and strategic geography allow these middle powers to exercise influence far beyond their borders.


They are also flexible about how that influence is exercised. A government can be the useful partner in one country, a paramilitary organization in another, a parallel authority somewhere else, and a commercial company across several of them. The relationship need not be ideological, and the partner need not even be a state. Strategic usefulness can be enough.


The UAE provides perhaps the clearest example. In Sudan, it has been supporting the RSF.


In Libya, it became an important external supporter of Khalifa Haftar’s eastern forces.


Reuters has documented

 earlier UN findings that the UAE helped Haftar’s forces build their air power, while Turkey supplied drones and air defenses to the government in Tripoli.


The Sudan and Libya stories have since begun to merge. The


UN Panel of Experts on Libya

 found that Colombian fighters transited through Haftar-controlled territory to support the RSF and described Libya as an operational, logistical and tactical base.


Gold reveals the economic side of the same system.


Chatham House

 describes gold as a major driver of Sudan’s conflict. Between 2012 and 2022, according to

 figures examined by Chatham House

, the UAE imported 2,569 tonnes of African gold that African countries themselves did not record as exports, worth approximately $115 billion.


The connection between gold and armed power is not abstract. The


U.S. Treasury

 sanctioned UAE-based companies connected to the RSF network. It said AZ Gold purchased Sudanese gold apparently for the benefit of the RSF and transported it to Dubai.


Money, weapons and military support can therefore move toward African conflicts while gold and other resources move outward. The old colonial economy required foreign administrators. The contemporary system does not necessarily need them. Governments, armed groups, mining companies, traders, port operators and financial intermediaries can perform different parts of the process.


A recent


Financial Times investigation

 traced a much wider Emirati expansion involving ports, mining, agriculture and infrastructure across Africa. A port can be a commercial asset, logistics hub, source of political leverage and, under different circumstances, military platform.


It is here that the idea of a new scramble for Africa becomes useful.


The old scramble sought possession of territory. The emerging one can operate at a distance. An outside power does not necessarily need to govern the mine, occupy the port or administer the population. It needs …

author: Publicación Abierta
title: La Matriz Ideológica de la Dominación Occidental y el nuevo cerco a los pueblos rebeldes de Nuestra Améfrica Ladina
content:
A 534 años de la Resistencia Indígena Planetaria, en homenaje al maestro Saúl Rivas Rivas: guerra cognitiva, tecno feudalismo y soberanía algorítmica cimarrona frente al cerco electoral, espiritual y epistémico del imperio.


Por Argenis José Delgado Vegas

| @ArgJoDel | 10 de octubre de 2026


Nuestra Améfrica Ladina despierta. En el marco de una resistencia que lleva más de cinco siglos frente a la colonización y la neocolonización, los pueblos de México, Cuba, Haití, Brasil, Colombia, Nicaragua, Bolivia, Venezuela, Ecuador y Argentina —con mayoría de población indígena y afrodescendiente— han impulsado en las últimas décadas procesos de liberación y descolonización estatal. Unos se han aproximado al zapatismo, panafricanismo, socialismo, comunismo, comunitarismo… No importa la etiqueta: importa que se atreven a caminar fuera del guión que Occidente les tenía reservado. Y cuando los pueblos rebeldes se mueven, el imperio afila sus armas. No solo las militares. Las armas más letales son las ideológicas.


La densidad afroindígena de Colombia, Brasil y Venezuela: el corazón demográfico de la rebelión


En Nuestra Améfrica Ladina hay tres países donde la matriz colonial muestra su rostro más descarnado porque allí se concentra una de las mayores densidades de población afrodescendiente e indígena del continente. Brasil, con más de la mitad de su población autoidentificada como negra o parda y cerca de 1,7 millones de indígenas; Colombia, con millones de afrocolombianos, raizales y palenqueros y más de un centenar de pueblos originarios; y Venezuela, con una presencia afrodescendiente que atraviesa la región norte costera frente al Caribe, los llanos y los Andes, el Sur y con 2,8 % de población indígena reconocida. No son datos menores: son la prueba viviente de que la colonialidad no terminó. Son también el sujeto histórico que el imperio teme, porque su memoria colectiva guarda el cimarronaje, el Cumbe, el resguardo, el conuco, el territorio y la espiritualidad como formas de libertad.


Esa densidad afroindígena explica por qué estos países son blanco prioritario de la Matriz Ideológica de la Dominación Occidental. En Brasil, el bolsonarismo no solo disputa el Estado: disputa el relato sobre la esclavitud, los quilombos y los pueblos indígenas. La bancada evangélica ultraconservadora, el agronegocio y la minería ilegal avanzan sobre tierras indígenas y quilombolas mientras se boicotea Durban y se criminaliza el racismo estructural. En Colombia, el giro a la derecha de Abelardo de la Espriella se monta sobre el miedo, el extractivismo y la guerra cognitiva contra el Acuerdo de Paz, justo en el país con mayor población afrodescendiente del mundo después de Brasil y con pueblos indígenas que han sido víctimas del conflicto armado. En Venezuela, el cerco financiero, el secuestro del presidente legítimo Nicolás Maduro y su esposa la diputada Cilia Flores, la ofensiva contra los cultos populares apuntan al corazón afroindígena del proyecto bolivariano.


 Estos tres países son, además, la demostración de que las Causas Comunes de la Humanidad no son abstracciones: la causa indígena, la causa de la diáspora africana, la causa del planeta, la de la mujer, la del trabajo y la intergeneracional se intersectan en la Amazonía, el Pacífico colombiano, el Cerrado brasileño, Barlovento y la Guayana venezolanaa ( incluye el Esequibo). Allí la colonialidad de los datos se vuelve concreta: los algoritmos de Silicon Valley clasifican, vigilan y expropian los saberes de pueblos que han cuidado la vida durante milenios. Por eso la soberanía algorítmica cimarrona no es un lujo teórico: es la continuación digital del palenque y del resguardo. Sin ella, la gran población afro e indígena de Colombia, Brasil y Venezuela seguirá siendo materia prima de la guerra cognitiva, del tecno feudalismo y del viejo Dios blanco que no tolera la pluriversalidad.


Marco Teórico:

«Saúl Rivas Rivas lo advirtió con claridad: existe una Matriz Ideológica de la Dominación Occidental, un entramado histórico, cultural, social y espiritual cuyo fin es ‘dar continuidad a toda una opresión capitalista occidental’. Esa matriz no es un invento reciente. Es la misma que construyó un ‘Dios blanco y europeo’ frente a un ‘Diablo negro, indio o árabe’, justificando la dominación como un acto de perfeccionamiento racial.»


Ramón Grosfoguel desmonta el mecanismo con precisión quirúrgica. El “universalismo abstracto” es aquel que, “desde un particularismo hegemónico …

author: Yasmine Benabderrahmane
title: Is "khawa khawa" a North African myth?
content:
In the haze of

el ghorba

 — the strangeness and alienation of living abroad — I gravitate toward the Maghrebi diaspora. For a moment, we relax our tongues from the unnatural twists of Arabic dialects foreign to us and speak in the Maghrebi

darija

s. Desperate to latch onto whatever whispers of home exist elsewhere, we claim that we are

khawa khawa

.

Among the Algerians, Moroccans, and Tunisians,

khawa khawa

 is an official nod to an unofficial alliance, loosely translating to

brotherhood

. It is an ode to our shared cultures and history in the face of North African identity discourses.

But what began as a salve for colonialism was lost in the monotonous chants for brotherhood.

Before the 19th century, North African states were “undefined” to European cartographers and authorities alike. Hence, like the concept of the Middle East and the Sahel, the Maghreb was prone to imperial invention. Unsurprisingly, this coincided with the Scramble for Africa — when the insatiable greed of European colonial powers took interest in dividing the African continent among themselves.

Encompassing other colonial legacies, the borders born out of the Scramble engineered the ethnic rivalries that persist in Africa today. Through the newly devised borders and the infamous “divide and conquer” regimes, the Maghreb was branded as distinct.

Despite the existing racial diversity of the region, the French colonial regimes rebranded the Maghreb as a biracial society: Amazigh or Arab. While the Amazigh identity was mislabeled in proximity to the whiteness of Europe, the Arab identity became an accusation of settler colonialism. North Africa became a geographic body for the Francophonie world, distanced from its neighboring regions’ cultures, politics, and society.

In 1962, Algeria — the last of France’s Maghrebi colonies — declared independence. In the years that followed, the Maghrebi people looked inwards and toward rebuilding the identity of North Africa. Thus,

khawa khawa

 was born and reinforced by the diaspora that fled their homes in the wake of political instability. It became a card dealt in moments of desperation to bond to something, or someone, that vaguely resembled home.

Khawa khawa

, and the brotherhood that blossomed with it, became the means to redress an identity obscured by European colonialism.

True

khawa khawa

 culture demands communal harmony void of ego. But when politics becomes inevitably entangled in the national identity of communities, the culture of Maghrebi brotherhood falls flat.

Shortly after 1962, newly independent Algeria and Morocco fell into border disputes. The following decades spiraled into attempted land grabs, fits of cultural monopolies, and accusations of expansionist ambitions. In response, the people cried out

khawa khawa; our governments do not define our brotherhood

!

But too often, the politics override the social bonds of Algerians and Moroccans (and occasionally, Tunisians). With the rise of the internet, discourse shifted, and social media became a useful mirror for the abstractions of the Maghrebi identity.

Most recently, the

khawa khawa

 culture was dramatically pronounced dead on social media platforms, following the 2025 African Cup of Nations (AFCON). Almost overnight, the football tournament became a litmus test for Algerian-Moroccan relations and spiraled into a warped perception of North African relations. A futile online back-and-forth that began as shared banter turned into personal attacks and political scrutiny.

The post-AFCON

guerre

 between Algerians and Moroccans — which coincided with the recent

UN support

 for Moroccan plans over the Western Sahara, disapproved by the Algerian government — is a recurring phenomenon of how Maghrebi culture wages war parallel to the political tensions of its respective countries. Despite the adamant denial, online Maghrebi communities fall into the habit of using our governments to verify the authenticity of

khawa khawa

.

The problem rests in the fact that both communities — Algerian and Moroccan — fall into the habit of claiming the minority of hateful comments as the consensus among the entirety of both nations. We see assertions made that we cannot prove, except that they are too insulting and their wounds far too inflicting to recover from. It has become a pattern of malice between both nations that resurfaces regardless of how loudly

khawa khawa

 is chanted.

Perhaps the fault is also in the fragility …

author: Tahrir Hamdi
title: Palestine Resists: From Fanon and Kanafani to Armed Struggle and Return
content:
How does one resist dispossession and displacement, ongoing genocide, culturicide, scholasticide and epistemicide, and all forms of erasure of a people’s past, present and future? The answer: Resist by all available means—armed resistance, cultural resistance, and economic resistance; this is a legal right recognized under international law, but before that, it is morally legitimate, justified, and necessary. Israel is a brutal settler colony that was made possible by two main strategies: the expulsion of the Palestinian people from their indigenous land (historic Palestine) and ongoing genocide that is now 78 years old.

Armed resistance, as theorized by anti-colonial theorists such as Frantz Fanon, Aimé Césaire, Amílcar Cabral, Ghassan Kanafani, and Edward Said, is an essential part of the anti-colonial struggle for the liberation of colonized minds and lands. In his book The Wretched of the Earth (1963), Frantz Fanon, a psychiatrist by training, forcefully argued for anti-colonial armed resistance, stating precisely because colonization is such a violent and dehumanizing process, “decolonization is always a violent phenomenon” (35). For Fanon, colonization always dehumanizes the colonized; therefore, the colonized must use violence against the colonizer to allow for the rehumanization of the colonized because revolutionary violence is meant to end the oppression, colonization and dehumanization of the colonized population (94).

The revolutionary thinker Amilcar Cabral argued in his speech titled “The Weapon of Theory, (1966)”: “the only effective way of definitively fulfilling the aspirations of the peoples, that is to say of attaining national liberation, is by armed struggle.” In his essay titled “National Liberation and Culture,” Cabral argues that the colonizer seeks to physically destroy a significant proportion of the dominated or colonized population; accordingly, the colonizer, in addition to resorting to mass killing and genocide, will always target the culture of the colonized. It is precisely for this reason that the preservation and continuation of people’s culture and their knowledge systems are essential to national liberation. Thus, cultural resistance and armed resistance go hand in hand.

The revolutionary Palestinian theorist and activist (who also wrote intellectual and theoretical pieces for the Arab Nationalist Movement and the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine), Ghassan Kanafani, like Fanon and Cabral, emphasized the absolute importance of cultural and armed resistance. Kanafani argued for a vibrant culture of resistance that would enable the armed struggle for liberation. This is why Kanafani wrote stories of Palestinian resistance. In a novella titled Returning to Haifa, Kanafani makes it clear, through his character Said, that any genuine return to Palestine required a successful armed struggle, a war. Kanafani also emphasized the absolute importance of the unity of armed resistance organizations. In his essay titled “Towards a Constructive Dialogue on Palestinian National Unity,” Kanafani writes: “Any setback to any active fida’i organization, whether militarily or fundamentally, cannot be limited to that organization, but rather is immediately reflected on all other organizations” (262). Kanafani was well aware that divisions do not just weaken one Palestinian organization, but the Palestinian struggle for liberation as a whole.

Echoing Kanafani’s and other anti-colonial theorists’ position on armed struggle, the Palestinian American intellectual Edward Said told Tim Sebastian on the BBC’s “Hardtalk” program in 2002 that he is “for any kind of violence that would resist occupation and apartheid […] occupation and apartheid have to be resisted by whatever means bring about their end.” Thus, Zionist settler colonialism must be resisted “by whatever means bring[s] about [its] end” or in the words of Fanon, by the “use of all means, and that of force first and foremost” (61). As Said was nearing the end of his life, he wrote about the absolute refusal to surrender, which he theorized in his book published posthumously, titled On Late Style (2006). The inevitable link between armed resistance and the culture of resistance is of great importance—it is this link that guarantees the continuation of resistance to oppression and brutal Zionist settler colonialism.

There has always been Palestinian resistance to colonization, which in the early 20th century began with popular …

author: Joseph Lee
title: Long after the Maui fires, toxic metals linger in residents’ bodies
content:
In August of 2023, a series of wildfires broke out across Maui, killing more than 100 people, destroying thousands of homes, and causing billions in damage. Noelani Ahia, who is Kanaka Maoli and co-founder of Maui Medic Healers Hui, helped mobilize nearly 600 volunteers in Lāhainā, including doctors, nurses, and therapists. 


Three years later, the housing and health crises remain acute. Maui Medic Healers Hui runs a free clinic, but Ahia wishes it had 10 more to address the community’s needs. “The fire may be out, but the catastrophe is not over by any stretch of the imagination,” she said. 


The devastation extended well beyond the lives lost and buildings destroyed. Research published last year by researchers with the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa’s Maui Wildfire Exposure Study, or MauiWES, found that

more than 1 in 5 residents

 had reduced lung function.


Now, new research from the same project has

found elevated levels of toxic metals

 in the island’s residents months after the fires, with higher exposure associated with impaired lung function. The findings offer further evidence that

the health consequences of catastrophic wildfires

 can persist long after the flames are extinguished and the smoke clears.


“What we consider and sometimes look at as a one-time event isn’t really one-time anymore,” Alika Maunakea, who is Kanaka Maoli and co-director of MauiWES, told Grist. 


Researchers don’t yet know how much of the contamination came from the fires and how much was already present in the environment. That distinction matters as wildfires increasingly race through towns like Lāhainā and cities like Los Angeles, where burning

homes, cars and infrastructure can leave contaminants

 that

people encounter for months

 or years afterward.


Community members hold hands in a prayer circle at a “Lāhainā Strong” gathering in October 2023.


Mario Tama / Getty Images


“We have traditionally thought about wildfire exposure primarily through the lens of smoke,” Maunakea said in a press release. “But when an entire community burns, we are dealing with a much more complicated exposure environment.” Researchers must also understand what contaminants were already present, what the fire may have released, and what entered residents’ bodies, he said.


The research, which studied 1,400 adults across Maui six to 18 months after the fires, measured 24 metals in urine samples. It found that participants had higher concentrations of several metals than people in a nationwide health survey conducted before the fires. That included 2.2 times as much arsenic, 2.3 times as much barium, and 3.8 times as much manganese. Antimony, which is used in flame retardant materials and has been previously

linked to lung irritation, stomach pain, and other symptoms

, was found at levels nearly 40 times higher.


Because the researchers lack comparable data from before the fires, they could not determine how much of the metal exposure resulted from the disaster. Maunakea told Grist answering that question is the next step for the project, which has received a $3.6 million grant from the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences. That work will include investigating whether and to what degree past agricultural and industrial activity contributed to the contamination.


“It’s important to realize that these are all part of settler colonialism,” Ahia said. “So what we’re looking at is confounding factors that are to the detriment of the health of our local people.”


Read Next


Two years after a wildfire took everything, Maui homeowners are facing a new threat: Foreclosure


Anita Hofschneider


Decades of plantation agriculture altered water systems, introduced herbicides, and displaced native plants, leaving a legacy on the islands that is still felt today. Disasters like fires and storms can compound those ongoing environmental problems. 


“If we begin the story when the fire starts, we miss the decisions that shaped the landscape and the community’s ability to respond,” said Katie Kamelamela, who is Kanaka Maoli and an assistant professor at Arizona State University based in Hawaiʻi. “Micro climate change acts on places already shaped by histories of land ownership, water diversion, development, and unequal access to resources.”


Kamelamela said true recovery must look beyond the fire. “I want recovery to be measured by whether people can remain in their communities, care for ʻāina, and pass on their knowledge and …

author: ROAPE
title: Fanon’s continuing presence and revolutionary Sudan
content:
Each generation must out of relative obscurity discover its mission, fulfil it, or betray it.


– Frantz Fanon,

The Wretched of the Earth

, 1968


I do not come with timeless truths … Every human problem must be considered from the standpoint of time.


– Frantz Fanon,

Black Skin, White Masks

, 2008


 


Introduction


Fanon was very aware of his time. And yet one hundred years after his birth, he remains strangely present, as if we are repeating the same history, the long durée of the unfinished anticolonial revolutions (see Gibson 2021). Published in 1961, Fanon’s last book,

The Wretched of the Earth

, is a product of his experience and reflections on Africa’s anticolonial struggle, including its first crisis in the Congo in 1961. Written as an intervention and addressing the readers as comrades, Fanon introduces the colonised challenge to the colonial world not as a rational confrontation of points of view, ‘but the untidy affirmation of an original idea propounded as an absolute’ (Fanon 1968, 41). Aware that colonialism carved up the continent into colonial fiefdoms, Fanon recognised that while the social struggle takes on a national form, it would inevitably degenerate into the regional, ethnic and racial lines often promulgated by colonial rule

if

 it did not put into practice a ‘minimum humanist’ programme (Fanon 1968, 163).


Challenging the imperial countries who speak of humanism but kill human beings wherever they find them, Fanon ends the book returning to the question of rehumanising the world, ‘For Europe, for ourselves, and for humanity, comrades, we must turn over a new leaf, we must work out new concepts, and try to set afoot a new [hu]man’ (Fanon 1968, 316). This was his idea of African liberation. Yet, on the hundredth anniversary of Fanon’s birth, not only has Africa become proportionately poorer and more unequal over the past 30 years but the post-independence ‘wa-Benz’, the newly embourgeoisified African ruling elites or simply ‘new whites’ (Nzongola-Ntalaja 2012, 40) – the ‘little greedy caste … with the mind of a huckster, only too glad to accept the dividends that the former colonial power hands out to it’ (Fanon 1968, 175) – keep reappearing.


While often dismissed as an advocate of violence rather than a thinker of African liberation, what is often elided in discussions of Fanon’s thought is the connection between the necessity of violence against settler colonies and Fanon’s criticisms of the military and the need for demilitarisation. This article focuses on what an engagement with Fanon’s thought could offer Sudanese revolutionaries. Understanding such an engagement dialectically, Fanon emphasised the importance of subjectivity in the ‘situation’ (and what Fanon also called the ‘lie of the situation’ (see Fanon 2018, 525)), which takes on a specific perspective because the Sudanese revolution involved millions of people in a non-violent revolution against military rule. It is this movement for life and liberation that must not be forgotten in the face of the reality of a counter-revolutionary military civil war that has led to daily human catastrophe for the Sudanese people.


While the Sudanese revolution began as a rejection of military rule, regional and world powers, including the United Nations (UN), have played a significant role in supporting the so-called civilian partnership of the Transitional Military Council, established in 2019, and have continued to support the armed forces following the 2021 military coup. The repeated failure of ‘international diplomacy’, notes Muzan Alneel (2023a), ‘is mainly due to the counter-revolutionary doctrine that animates its participants’.

1


The first section of this article discusses Fanon’s idea of demilitarisation and decolonisation. The second section, on the Sudanese revolution, discusses the importance, and legacies, of the resistance committees, while the final section returns to Fanon’s idea of revolutionary humanism in the praxis of anticolonial organisations.


National military or African solidarity through a corps of volunteers?


Fanon’s idea of an African legion was proposed in his speech delivered in December 1958 at the First All-African People’s Conference in Accra, Ghana. In an article in the Algerian National Liberation Front’s

El Moudjahid

, Fanon explained that the principle adopted in Accra was a ‘concrete response of the African peoples to the will to colonial domination of the Europeans to create a corps …

author: Soreti Kadir
title: Finfinnee is the Third Space
content:
At the end of 2010, I took a trip to Ethiopia to visit my family. At the time, my parents worked in Bole, the commercial centre of Addis Ababa. Being only 16, my movements were more or less regulated by my parents, which meant that I would travel with them into the city each day, after which it was the extent of my curiosity and creativity (and pocket money) that determined what I did until evening, when I would head back to our house on the outskirts of the city. Slowly, interactions with the staff at a nearby cafe, just a few hundred meters from the building where my family worked, became routine. 


Over the two months that I was in Ethiopia, with much of this time spent in Addis Ababa, we spent most of our lunch breaks together, hanging out on the steps of the cafe, sharing stories to pass the time. One day, the conversation of our relationship to ‘Ethiopia’, as a national identity, came up. It’s important to note that I was raised in the Oromo diaspora, a community that, in the years my mother and I migrated to Australia, was made up mostly of political refugees who fled the country after the adoption of the “Transitional Period Charter of Ethiopia” and the official establishment of a transitional government. 


This eventually led to the Tigrayan People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) monopolizing power within the Ethiopian People’s Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF), a process that resulted in the isolation of those seeking political power within the EPRDF through the ballot. Given the size and economic importance of the Oromia region, it was the Oromo Liberation Front (OLF), amongst others, that became a key target of political violence, creating political communities in exile exactly like the one that I grew up in.


I inherited a different definition of Ethiopia, coloured by memories and experiences of violence and displacement that informed my relationship to the state as a place of unbelonging for those who shared my identity. The day that the conversation with these two new friends wandered into political territory, we all engaged passionately, striving to reflect the extent of both our personal experiences and hopes for our country. They found my reflections to be overly nostalgic and antagonistic towards the country’s future.  Unconcerned for the good of the future. I found their insistence that we shared a national identity to be inaccurate and offensive. We agreed on little, and I found it exhilarating. 


That evening, I was restlessly anticipating the opportunity to tell my mother about what I thought was the most exciting experience of my trip to date. In recounting the story, I almost gave my mother a heart attack. Angry, afraid, and in shock, my mother warned me sternly against ever engaging in such conversation in public again. She asked me many questions about who these men were, how I knew them, and if we’d ever had such conversations before. What I was blind to, and what was the daily lived experience of my parents, was that Addis Ababa, primarily but not exclusively, was a heavily surveilled city, the State looking for the people doing exactly what I found myself doing that day – discussing the political reality of our country. Thereafter, I was careful, out of curiosity more than fear (being 16 with a high risk tolerance will do that), and refrained from fully-fledged conversations, opting for quiet enquiry when the opportunity presented itself. Although our conversation never veered down the road of politics again, I continued to visit my friends every day and remember rushing to say a heartfelt goodbye on the day I was due to fly back to Australia. 


For this piece, I will centre the discussion on Ethiopia’s capital, Addis Ababa, as opposed to extending the conversation to other parts of the country which exist with their own nuances and political realities, requiring more space for analysis than I have here. I share the introductory anecdote to forward the idea that, in Ethiopia, to nurture spaces of connection, community-building, and care, we must first invest in collective repair of the damage wrought by decades of state surveillance that has defined the range and breadth of relational life the city space can hold, and from the legacy of what can only be defined as settler colonialism. ‘Where’, figuratively and literally, can this process of repair take place? I argue that it must take place in Finfinnee, geographically the same location as Addis Ababa, but sociologically and …

author: Publicación Abierta
title: 12 de octubre: la conquista remata ahora la vida
content:
12 DE OCTUBRE: LA CONQUISTA REMATA AHORA LA VIDA


Por Rafael Bautista S.


La colonización ahora se propone


aniquilar al mundo entero, pues si no todos somos iguales,


la rebelión de las víctimas es el pecado


que hay que escarmentar,


porque dice Occidente: “toda la culpa la tienen las víctimas.


El verdugo es siempre inocente”.


Para los fines de la conquista, fue preciso, necesario y estratégico cercenar las memorias y ceremonias antiguas de los indios, porque en esos residuos de resistencia se reproducía su modo de vivir. La inversión religiosa la describe muy ben Guaman Poma de Ayala cuando señala que “les quitaron su ley antigua y les pusieron temor y culpa donde antes había justicia”. Para arrebatarles y despojarles de humanidad, no bastaba con reducirlos a la miseria sino acabar con su memoria y sus costumbres, con su historia y su cultura.


Pero lo que las armas habían pretendido terminar, sólo logró su aplazamiento, pues la memoria comenzó a renacer, una y otra vez que la amenaza del exterminio prendía sus terruños, pero también su rebeldía. Las armas jamás pudieron doblegar el espíritu de liberación que atravesó, hasta el día de hoy, todas las formas que adquirió la dominación, el despojo y el robo de su tierra sagrada.


Hoy la liberación se expresa como

restauración

. El “progresismo” no entiende que el progreso es un mito, que la alternativa ya no es aferrarse al tren del progreso sino ponerle un freno y proponerse, con mayor denuedo, despertar y

conservar

 los valores que la tradición de nuestros pueblos nos ha legado, frente al desastre y el desmoronamiento de los valores moderno-occidentales. Pero

restaurar

 no es volver sino

recrear

,

actualizar

 lo que hemos perdido: una existencia más digna, libre y justa, re-ligada a lo natural y espiritual, a la simpleza que significa vivir en plenitud; lejos del dinamismo, ritmo y la inclemencia del tiempo inhumano del capital y el mercado (una vida válida para todos, donde ya no gobierne la ambición de unos cuantos).


En el siglo XV, el Abya Yala estaba atravesando una época de esplendor civilizatorio, superior, en muchos casos, a la Cristiandad latino-occidental (porque Europa recién se estaba reconociendo como nueva entidad ontológica y geopolítica). En realidad, en 1492,

quien se descubre no es América sino Europa

 y lo hace no a partir del “encuentro” con el otro sino negando su humanidad, para afirmarse como superioridad absoluta, una vez que ha diezmado la capacidad de resistencia de los pueblos dominados. El Abya Yala no fue reducida civilizatoriamente por vivir en el atraso histórico, en la barbarie (que es una pura leyenda negra que está siendo desmentida, cada día, por los nuevos hallazgos y argumentos antropológicos, arqueológicos, demográficos, tecnológicos, etc., etc.).


No nos vencieron por astucia, inteligencia o superioridad sino por una incompatibilidad radical. La

cultura de la vida

 (en todas sus expresiones) respeta los límites éticos que manifiesta la idea del bien. Una cultura de muerte, basada en la culpa infinita, el sacrificio, la aniquilación del

humanismo del otro hombre

, no admite límite alguno. Como en la actualidad, cuando el Imperio y Occidente, en su decadencia, desatan la política del odio, desatan un poder sin límites. Salah ad-Dîn o Saladino lo expresaba así, refriéndose a los cruzados cristianos: es casi inhumano luchar contra ejércitos tan hambrientos de sangre y muerte. Si el monje Bernardo de Claraval estimulaba a los cruzados con el perdón de los pecados y el paraíso eterno, por cada moro que se aniquile, se comprende la crueldad que despierta el odio al “infiel”. Como hoy en Gaza, el Imperio y Europa jamás abandonaron esa brutalidad sin coordenadas morales. Los pueblos expulsados a ser periferia del “primer mundo”, fuera de las fronteras del

humanismo liberal-moderno excluyente y selectivo

, aun cargan con la interrogante: ¿cómo puede ser posible vivir en un mundo sin respeto por la vida?


Occidente nunca fue superior. Su moralidad los retrata en la figura de aquél que afirma que “lo único que puede detenerme es

Mi propia moral

,

Mi propio pensamiento

.

No necesito

 del derecho internacional”, Trump dixit. Occidente es el nicho de la tradición imperial, que siempre debe retornar, como dice Dostoievsky, al lugar del crimen. Es su condena y, por eso mismo, debe acallar a los vencidos, para dejar de escuchar el clamor de los muertos que deja su progreso y desarrollo.


La invasión y la …

author: Anooradha Iyer Siddiqi
title: Reading List: Anooradha Iyer Siddiqi
content:
We are taught to think of a refugee camp as an object produced in an instant, only in response to an emergency — one brought on, perhaps, by those seeking refuge. We are taught that refugee environments are provisional and abject, moreover, to be naturalized as such within the African landscape —

as

 the African landscape. We are taught to misread migrant spaces as lacking history or architectural expression. To counter these misdirections,

Architecture of Migration: The Dadaab Refugee Camps and Humanitarian Settlement

 looks closely at the complex settlements, ecologies, domesticities, archives, and material aesthetics. In Ifo, Dagahaley, and Hagadera camps, established in 1991 by the Kenyan government and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees at Dadaab, Kenya, in lands shared with Somalia and Ethiopia, the book finds African, Muslim, and Afro-Asian aesthetic worlds and a historical repository of partition, sedentarization, and migration. Dadaab forms a material afterlife of events long unfolding, through colonial and postcolonial time and space, and in multiple registers, aesthetic as well as social.

My book is grounded in 14 years of feminist and critical collective practice and research (see

Cohabitations

,

Dadaab Commons

,

Feminist Architectural Histories of Migration

,

Insurgent Domesticities

, and

Settlement

). While researching in dozens of archives and libraries in Africa, Asia, and Europe, and interviewing hundreds of women practicing architecture and art, representing governments, cultural institutions, and nongovernmental agencies, or living life in refugee camps, I read many books! If the anticolonial thought in Frantz Fanon’s

Black Skin, White Masks

 and Walter Rodney’s

How Europe Underdeveloped Africa

 anchored my work, its everyday tugs and buoying came from feminists.

Ifo camp Chairlady Isnina Ali Rage. Photo by author, 2011.

My study of the handcrafted acacia camp environments and interviews with many of their builders — including Ifo Chairlady Isnina Ali Rage and shopowner Shamso Abdullahi Farah, and Dagahaley farmer Maganai Saddiq Hassan — gave shape to a consciousness rooted in the social and ecological worldmaking of African, Muslim, and Global South feminists. Let me begin with three. Sylvia Tamale not only insists on decolonizing master narratives that suppress multiplicity in

Decolonization and Afro-Feminism

, but through her years of activism in Uganda and beyond, plants the working and thinking of African feminists on the ground, in the natural environment. This perspective is hardly limited to African feminists, as Radha D’Souza demonstrates in the

Court for Intergenerational Climate Crimes

 — based on her book

What’s Wrong with Rights?: Social Movements, Law and Liberal Imaginations

 — which foregrounds the workhorse labor and the place of the indigo plant (Comrade Indigo) within majority-world feminist intellectual commitment; she dispenses with reductive “West versus Rest” critiques through the perspectives of European underground and Third World intellectuals in the co-edited

Decolonizing Knowledge: Looking Back, Moving Forward

 (

open access

). Further articulating the vitality of social difference to inform constructions of knowledge, Saba Mahmood argues that those constructions must assert against universalizing epistemes, secular as well as religious, in her foundational work on Cairo’s women,

Politics of Piety: The Islamic Revival and the Feminist Subject

.

Store and shelters designed and built by Shamso Abdullahi Farah, Ifo camp. Photo by author, 2011.

From there, global Black feminisms were my north star. Yvonne Adhiambo Owuor’s

Dust

 dwelt within the landscapes of Kenya’s Northeast, the erstwhile colonial “frontier” constituted of migratory lifeways and marabou storks; her habitations haunt my book’s histories of land, emergency territory, and sedentarized pastoralists.

Lose Your Mother: A Journey Along the Atlantic Slave Route

, Saidiya Hartman’s attempt to fill in the blank slate of the historical record and her own life, helped me think with the stories of enslaved children freed from Indian Ocean

dhows

, raised near Bombay, and resettled near Mombasa: the negotiation between rescuer and rescued in the East African abolitionist settlement of Freretown that forms Dadaab’s prehistory. My book stands on the shoulders of Mabel O. Wilson’s work on: (1) spatial agency, as rooted in the bodies of builders and the physical labor …

author: Anne Marxze Umil
title: Int’l solidarity vs Pax Silica
content:
At the Shut the Pax Down: Resistance and Solidarity Against Imperialist Plunder workshop in Bangkok, Thailand on October 14, 2026. (Photo from ILPS Philippines Facebook page)

Despite the advancements of AI technology, there is also the growing resistance.

BANGKOK – Organizations from different parts of the world are now united against the Pax Silica Initiative to be signed by the United States and the Philippines in November. US President Donald Trump reportedly will visit the Philippines to sign the agreement.

“We are in a period of extreme conflict between two very powerful and imperialist countries and the US is trembling and shaking. We have to maintain that fervor of revolution, that ability to throw stones at them, to bring them down and to make sure that the US imperialist power is no more,” said Azra Sayeed, secretary-general of the International League of Peoples Struggles (ILPS) during an activity in Bangkok, Thailand dubbed “Shut the Pax Down: Resistance and Solidarity Against Imperialist Plunder” on October 14.

The International Monetary Fund and the World Bank (IMF-WB) held its annual meeting in Bangkok from October 12 to 18. Participants included central bank governors, economic policy makers and business leaders.

In a statement, the Campaigners of the Peoples Global Campaign (PGC) Against IMF and World expressed concern over IMF-WB’s push for new technologies, including the widespread adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in Global South economies.

The group said that the “frantic race” for AI dominance intensified mining and extraction in resource-rich countries in the Global South. Transnational corporations are extracting rare earth elements (REEs) and other critical minerals to meet the growing demand for AI infrastructure. To secure control over the AI supply chain, countries like the US initiated the formation of Pax Silica and other similar formations.

“We know that imperialism is about world domination and control over resources. In the previous century, the rivalry among imperialist powers centered on oil because whoever controlled oil could wield significant influence over the military and the economy,” Arnold Padilla, secretary-general of ILPS-Philippines said during the event.

Now, he stressed, the battle is over critical minerals as whoever controls AI and the critical minerals needed to build its infrastructure could gain a significant advantage in dominating the world. “Essentially, that’s the battle now between the US and China. So, who will control this critical sector?”

This is why, Padilla said, the Philippines is up for a major battle to halt the signing of the US-led Pax Silica Initiative this year in time for the Asean Summit from November 16 to 18.

He said that AI is not just about the software that people use but also about weapons like drones “that can make decisions in actual battles without any human intervention.” He added that these sophisticated weapons will be made of minerals to be extracted from the Philippines.

Read: Critical minerals policy framework linked to Pax Silica? Read: War and plunder: US imperialism in the Philippines

“Pax Silica is made up of 24 countries, of course, led by the US. And it’s a special coalition. Specifically chosen by the US because countries that belong to Pax Silica perform a specific specialized role because it’s about controlling the supply chain,” Padilla said. “We don’t have high technology, we don’t have the logistic network, we don’t have capital or energy. But what do we have? We have the critical minerals. So for us in the Philippines, this is all about plunder.”

Donna Denina, secretary-general of International Women’s Alliance (IWA), said that US Undersecretary of State for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg, former tech executive and adviser tied to the controversial software firm Palantir, designed Pax Silica to give the US control over the global technology supply chain.

Palantir is a technology firm with clients from the Pentagon and foreign militaries including the Israeli government. But Denina said that Palantir is now expanding its influence beyond military tech into the health care sector.

In the US, she said that Palantir’s AI software is being used to manage hospital staffing and scheduling. This raised concerns among healthcare workers and prompted protests.

She said that more than 1,000 nurses from the National Nurses United union protested against healthcare institutions’ contracts with Palantir …

author: LCM-Redaktion
title: Heilige Drecksarbeit – Die deutsch-israelischen Militärbeziehungen und die Staatsräson
content:
Der vorliegende Text ist eine gekürzte Fassung des gleichnamigen Beitrags aus dem Sammelband „

Trümmer auf Trümmer. Zur Kritik der deutschen Staatsräson

“, erschienen bei der Buchmacherei. Das Autor:innenkollektiv beschäftigt sich hier ausführlich mit der historischen Genese der militärischen Beziehungen zwischen der Bundesrepublik und dem zionistischen Staatsprojekt sowie der Geschichte des Existenzrechts Israels als deutsche Staatsräson. Neben diesem Beitrag finden sich im Sammelband zahlreiche weitere Texte, die sich aus historischer, juristischer und politischer Perspektive mit dem Thema der „Staatsräson“, deren Bedeutung für einen neuen deutschen Nationalismus, dem Phänomen der „Antideutschen“, kolonialen und antikommunistischen Kontinuitäten und der aktuellen Bedeutung im Bezug auf den Genozid in Gaza auseinander setzen.

von

AK Beau Séjour


Wirft man einen vergleichenden Blick auf die Zahlen der deutschen Waffengeschäfte im Jahr 2024, so fällt auf, dass Israel mit 161 Mio. Euro nur an sechster Stelle steht. An erster Stelle stand im Jahr 2024 die Ukraine mit 8,1 Milliarden Euro, gefolgt von Singapur (1,21 Mrd. Euro), Algerien (558,7 Mio. Euro), den USA (319,9 Mio. Euro) und der Türkei (230,8 Mio. Euro). Es gehe, so wird immer wieder zu Recht angemerkt, den Herren Rheinmetall und Thyssenkrupp nicht um die konkrete Tötung palästinensischer Kinder, sondern um das allgemeine Geschäft mit dem Tod. Die militärischen Beziehungen zwischen Deutschland und Israel müssen, das ist fraglos richtig, auch als gewöhnliche deutsche Handelsbeziehungen zwischen handelsüblichen Schurkenstaaten betrachtet werden. Doch dieses profane globale Geschäft mit dem Tod braucht, insbesondere in Deutschland, einen robusteren Überbau als das Geschäft mit Autos oder Kosmetikartikeln. Laut Marx spricht die »scheinheilige und heuchlerische Ideologie der Bourgeoisie ihre aparten Interessen als allgemeine Interessen« aus.

1

 Und in Bezug auf Wirklichkeit und Ideologie der bürgerlichen Familie schreibt er weiter, dass »[i]hrer schmutzigen Existenz […] der heilige Begriff in offiziellen Redensarten und in der allgemeinen Heuchelei« entspricht.

2

 Die schmutzige wirkliche Existenz deutscher Außen- und Handelspolitik muss in vergleichbarer Weise sakralisiert und den Deutschen als ihr allgemeines und moralisches Interesse verkauft werden, insbesondere deshalb, da sich nach 1945 jedes deutsche Großmachtstreben verbot. Gerade hierbei spielt Israel eine zentrale Rolle. Die umfassende und bedingungslose Unterstützung Israels wird in einen Akt höchster Sakralität verwandelt – eine sakralisierte Beziehung, hinter der sich, wie noch zu zeigen ist, die aparten Interessen der deutschen Bourgeoisie verbergen.


Diese Sakralisierung staatlicher Gewalt drückt sich in zahlreichen Reden deutscher Politiker:innen aus. So verkündete Angela Merkel in ihrer berühmten Staatsräson-Rede von 2008: »Deutschland und Israel sind und bleiben – und zwar für immer – auf besondere Weise durch die Erinnerung an die Shoah verbunden«. Die ehemalige deutsche Außenministerin Annalena Baerbock leitete aus dieser Erinnerung zum ersten Jahrestag des 7. Oktober im deutschen Bundestag die Legitimität von Gewalt ab: »Die Sicherheit Israels ist deutsche Staatsräson, unabhängig davon wer regiert, unabhängig davon, wer Außenpolitik macht […] Das Selbstverteidigungsrecht Israels ist auch unsere Verantwortung. Dazu stehen wir nicht nur mit Worten, sondern auch mit Taten, und zwar jeden Tag.« Zwar gehören, so Baerbock, laut deutscher Staatsräson »das humanitäre Völkerrecht und das Existenzrecht Israels auf das Engste zusammen«, doch Selbstverteidigung bedeute selbst verständlich auch die vollständige Zerstörung des Gegners und »wenn sich Hamas-Terroristen hinter Menschen, hinter Schulen verschanzen, dann kommen wir in ganz schwierige Bereiche. Aber wir ducken uns davor nicht weg. Deswegen habe ich vor den Vereinten Nationen auch deutlich gemacht: Dann können auch zivile Orte ihren Schutzstatus verlieren; weil Terroristen diese missbrauchen. Dazu steht Deutschland, das bedeutet für uns Sicherheit Israels.« Die mobile deutsche Artillerie von Rheinmetall, die Sa’ar 6 Korvetten von Thyssenkrupp, die Motoren in den Merkava-Panzern vom Bodensee und die 120mm-Panzermunition aus Niedersachsen sind, nimmt man Baerbock beim Wort, der materielle Ausdruck des »Versprechens ›Nie wieder!‹, das wir in der Vergangenheit gegeben haben«, denn »›Nie wieder!‹ heißt, jeden Tag das Richtige und nicht das …

author: Unknown
title: Jugendstreik Basel
content:
Aufruf zum Jugendstreik am 20.11. in Basel


Als Jugendorganisationen aus ganz Europa, und darüber hinaus, rufen wir Unter dem Motto «FIGHT FOR OUR FUTURE, NOT THEIR WARS» zum Internationalen Jugendstreik auf.


Auch in Basel gehen wir am 20. November auf die Strasse.


Demo: 14:00 De-Wette Park


Fest: ab 17:00 (Genauere Infos werden über die Instagramkanäle bekanntgegeben)


Wieso streiken wir?


Unsere Staaten rüsten auf. Die Jugend wird darauf vorbereitet, in den Krieg zu ziehen. Während die Regierungen Milliarden in Aufrüstung investieren, wird der Sozialstaat kaputt gesparrt.


Auch die Schweiz macht mit. So plant der Bund zum Beispiel einen Rüstungsfonds in der Grösse von 24 Milliarden Franken. Das Budget für die Armee für den Zeitraum 2025–2028 wurde bereits um 4 Milliarden Franken erhöht. Gleichzeitig wird mit dem Entlastungspaket 27 in über 60 Bereichen gespart, unter anderem bei der Bildung, der Gesundheit und beim Klimaschutz.


Es zeigt die Priorität dieses Systems: Die fortlaufende Erweiterung des Kapitals.


Der Kapitalismus kann der Jugend keine Zukunft garantieren!


Die Armee dient der Interessen der herrschenden Klasse. Die neuen militärischen Kapazitäten erweitern dabei den Handlungsspielraum zur Durchsetzung dieser Interessen.


Beispiele dafür sind der Einsatz des Militärs an der Demonstration gegen den G7 Gipfel, die laufende Grenzmilitarisierung oder die Waffenexporte nach Israel.


Wir sterben nicht für ihre Kriege!

author: Tom Bramble
title: US imperialism in the 21st century
content:
At the start of this century, US imperialism was at its peak. It had been a decade since its chief adversary, the Soviet Union, had crumbled; the country was now the unchallenged global superpower. Washington was bringing countries into the North Atlantic Treaty Organization that had been the USSR’s satellites in Europe, and it could rely on its allies to extend US influence into every corner of the world.

The US dominated the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund and was the most powerful nation in the United Nations. Its economy was booming, and the federal government ran surpluses. US multinationals found new markets and investment outlets worldwide. It was the heyday of “globalisation”. The US ruling class boasted that the country was a beacon to the world. As Democratic candidate Al Gore put it in one of the presidential debates in 2000:

“It is a great tribute to our founders that 224 years later this nation is now looked to by the peoples on every other continent and the peoples from every part of this Earth as a kind of model for what their future could be … The power of example is America’s greatest power in the world.”

Twenty-five years later, US rulers are not so assured. The country has suffered a series of crises, and the global balance of power has shifted. The US remains the world’s leading power, but it is wracked by dysfunction on a series of fronts. Its allies are increasingly estranged. Wars in the Middle East have exposed its diminished military power. Its tech sector and banks still lead, but its industrial base is now much weaker. Its political system is seen not as a model for what to do, but what to avoid. 

The decay of US power can be understood as the result of four interrelated phenomena: an imperial crisis in the Middle East, an economic crisis that crashed the world, the challenge from China and a political crisis that reflects and exacerbates these three trends.

The imperial crisis

The 9/11 attack on the World Trade Center in 2001 was a devastating blow to America’s sense of invulnerability. But US strategists also recognised the attack as an opportunity to advance US power—justification for a new round of wars that would intimidate the country’s rivals and allies alike and overcome the Vietnam-era legacy of widespread domestic opposition to far-flung and lengthy land wars. 

The idea of an aggressive revival of US military interventionism had been germinating in the ranks of the Republican Party for some years in its “neoconservative” wing. The leading think tank was the Project for a New American Century, founded by William Kristol and Robert Kagan. Its supporters and associates included Dick Cheney, Donald Rumsfeld, Paul Wolfowitz and John Bolton, all of whom held senior positions in the George W. Bush administration, which had won the 2000 election. 

The October 2001 invasion of Afghanistan was the first step in this wider project. Bush’s cabinet believed that the US would topple the ruling Taliban in Kabul and then lead a triumphal march through the capitals of its defeated enemies. Iraq, Iran and Syria were the main targets and, further afield, North Korea. Regime change was the objective.

In the short term, the invasion of Afghanistan was a stunning success. The Taliban were overthrown within two months. Domestic support for the war was overwhelming. It seemed US imperialism was back. Next was Iraq. The Bush administration justified its invasion by associating the country’s president, Saddam Hussein, with the 9/11 attacks and claiming that he had built an arsenal of weapons of mass destruction to threaten the West. On 19 March 2003, the US and its allies invaded Iraq. Within three weeks, US forces had taken Baghdad, and on 1 May Bush appeared on the deck of the

USS Abraham Lincoln

 to declare “mission accomplished”. 

Yet things turned bad for the US in both countries. In Iraq, local resistance to the occupation soon emerged. By the following year, it was raging. The US responded by flattening whole neighbourhoods, deploying white phosphorus and uranium-tipped weapons. Regular sweeps of suspected resistance activists terrified neighbourhoods and filled the jails. The US destroyed civilian infrastructure providing clean water, power and health care. And it sacked more than 100,000 government employees, creating mass unemployment and impoverishing millions. The death toll rose steadily. A study by the

Lancet

 journal in 2006 estimated 655,000 excess deaths in …

author: ROAPE
title: Eusi Kwayana (1925-2026)
content:
Eusi Kwayana was born Sydney King, as he was known initially for his first, more than two decades in public life. In 1968 he took on his African name which in Swahili means ‘Black man of Guyana.’


Eusi Kwayana was a founding father of post-colonial independence Guyana and Caribbean politics and was associated with the triumvirate of personalities that shaped them: Cheddi Jagan, Forbes Burnham, and Walter Rodney. He came to write the anthems of the three parties they led. Yet his own contributions to the Black and global radical traditions are still being recognized and recorded. This will be challenging in an environment where he receives national and regional honors for being a mere educator, writer, and cultural activist. It’s undeniable; he was a revolutionary.


What does it mean that Eusi Kwayana was a revolutionary? He was a campaigner against white supremacy, empire, capitalism, patriarchy, and ecological destruction. More than that, where he led breakthroughs against colonialism that denied Guyana, the Caribbean, and the Global South self-government, at the post-colonial independence moment he continued to confront the African and Caribbean political class, whether aristocratic or progressive. As historian and political activist, he always wished for everyday people to directly hold the reins of society. Of course, it was a matter of positioning ourselves to bring this about. His strategies of what to do and how to do it, must be revisited.


Detained When Guyana was Occupied by Anglo-American Imperialism


Eusi was detained when the Cheddi Jagan-led People’s Progressive Party (PPP) was overthrown by Anglo-American empire after winning election to Guyana’s colonial legislature in 1953. The country was occupied for 133 days. Before the Cuban Revolution of 1959, the PPP of Guyana was seen as a major threat to US and British hegemony during the Cold War in the Western hemisphere.


Eusi, with Rory Westmaas and Martin Carter, were perceived as the ‘ultra-left’ of the PPP.  In 1956, the split with Cheddi Jagan came, not over disagreements about commitments to a multi-racial party or movement. Rather, when Eusi and others advanced and defended the inclusion of Guyana in the movement for West Indian Federation. It was a permanent concern.


Multi-Racial Unity, Black Autonomy, and Caribbean Federation


This was part of an unfolding process of awareness. Cheddi Jagan was a socialist cosmopolitan when he faced the wider public. But he was also an ethnic leader of the Indo-Guyanese. Eusi concluded that it was no creative conflict to be an advocate for Afro-Guyanese as well. And it was important to address his Afro-Guyanese constituency

within the hearing

 of the Indo-Guyanese.


In 1959, Eusi became friendly with CLR James and Selma James in Trinidad at the height of the movement for colonial freedom led by Eric Williams’s People’s National Movement (PNM). He learned some important things about political journalism and activism in dialogue with CLR as he was editing

The Nation,

and Eusi was responsible for the People’s National Congress’s (PNC)

The New Nation

in Guyana.


Making Guyana a Global Refuge


In 1961, Eusi founded African Society for Racial Equality (ASRE) with the scientist H.H. Nicholson, known as ‘Vigilance’, and in 1964, co-founded African Society for Cultural Relations with Independent Africa (ASCRIA). With his wife

Tchaiko Kwayana

, an African American from Georgia in the US, who made her own mark as a teacher in New York and California, and her own sojourns to Nigeria, Ghana, and Latin America, Eusi pioneered the African cultural revolution in the Western Hemisphere, and was a transmission belt for African Americans and continental Africans finding a refuge from white supremacy and empire in Guyana as they pursued self-reliance and cooperative living. He was instrumental in making powerful ties between Ghana and Guyana.


It was Eusi that in 1966 gave Forbes Burnham the idea for Guyana being known as the ‘cooperative republic’ at official independence. In the early 1970s, Eusi was a supporter of the most dedicated cooperatives in the hinterland, such as the one at Marudi led by Joe Maxwell. The most dynamic cooperatives would be repressed by the state before the famous Jonestown fiasco.


An Original Educator of the African World


Eusi’s travels in Africa in 1964-65 and 1969 brought him to Nigeria, Mali, Sierra Leone, Liberia, Kenya, Tanzania, Zambia, Ghana, and Guinea-Conakry.  As a leader …

author: Monthly Review Press
title: The latest on Gabriel Rockhill’s “Who Paid the Pipers of Western Marxism?”
content:
Controversy, controversy…it’s no surprise that this book is selling very well. See more on this from

Bisharat Abbasi

, in his post: “

In Defence Of Gabriel Rockhill’s

Who Paid the Pipers of Western Marxism: Anti-Imperialist Marxism Versus The Imperial Theory Industry

.

“


DIGEST: Reviews, interviews, appearances


Marx Memorial Library

in London hosted a dual book launch for

Requiem for French Theory

 and

Who Paid the Pipers of Western Marxism?

with Gabriel Rockhill, Aymeric Monville, and Jennifer Ponce de León, who engaged in a discussion regarding the effects of imperialism on the production and dissemination of knowledge. Far from simply engaging in a critique of the faux radicalism of the prominent discourses within the imperial theory industry, the discussion was grounded in a reasoned defense of the vibrant international tradition of anti-imperialist Marxism. Topics included the imperial promotion of Western Marxism and postmodern French Theory, the international war of ideas, the failed efforts to discredit anti-imperialist Marxism, culturalism and identity politics vs. a materialist analysis of the colonial question, fascism past and present, the dialectics of actually existing socialism, and the current state of global class struggle in theory and practice.

Watch here

or below


The Left Chapter

, reviewed by Leo Schwarz:


“Shortly before his death, Herbert Marcuse wrote an essay on Rudolf Bahro’s book

The Alternative in Eastern Europe

. In the essay, Marcuse hailed Bahro’s ‘critique of actually existing socialism’ as ‘the most important contribution to Marxist theory and practice in decades.’ This statement was part of a coordinated campaign for the book and for Bahro that swept through the major media outlets of the Western world between 1977 and 1979–80. As we now know (or can know), a striking number of the key figures in this campaign maintained connections in the postwar decades to the Central Intelligence Agency or to various institutions and organizations that were either controlled, funded, or considered ‘friendly’ by the CIA or the U.S. State Department. In the first volume of his three-volume reconstruction of the ‘intellectual world war’ against actually existing socialism, Gabriel Rockhill examines the history and specific function of these networks of the ‘imperial theory industry’ that emerged after 1945, with his interest focused primarily on the Frankfurt School and the academic “Marxisms” of the Western world, which are usually categorized as ‘Western Marxism’…..”

 Read more….

“…I was among those who criticized the Soviet system in its post-Stalin decades, and the lesson learned was that the greatest losers were the peripheral countries, especially the Arab nation, since the Soviets had long acted as a force restraining the imperialist beast. More importantly, this collapse was, in historical-materialist terms, a setback—an exception—because history fundamentally advances upward. Though our wounds were deep, the class enemy emerged victorious but also wounded, most notably by becoming the sole superpower, exposing its flaws and unleashing its brutality. In this brief context, I attempt to summarize Gabriel Rockhill’s book—a painstaking and rigorously documented scholarly work. Yet its timing is no less important than the work itself, for it constitutes a bold revolutionary confrontation that demonstrates the author’s profound communist commitment in an era when loyalty to communism has become rare and the fungi of internalized defeat have spread everywhere, filling the burrows with fleeing rats….”
