author: Brian Hioe
title: Animal Rights Advocates Call for Referendum on Snare Traps
content:
ANIMAL RIGHTS ADVOCATES are currently campaigning for a referendum to be held on the use of wild boar snares.

In particular, animal rights advocates have long criticized wild boar snares as overly cruel. Such traps use spring-loaded mechanisms to tighten around animals’ limbs when triggered.

Nevertheless, such traps have also been criticized for ensnaring other species, as they do not distinguish. Endangered species such as Formosan black bears and leopard cats had also been killed by such traps, as have cats and dogs, sometimes resulting in their losing limbs if they survive.

Though claims had been made that Indigenous hunters used such traps as part of traditional hunting rights, animal rights groups have generally cited that this was rarely the case, in that Indigenous hunters generally do not use such traps. By contrast, such animal rights advocates state that Indigenous hunters more commonly use traps made from wood, bamboo and vines, and other natural materials. In the past, the Central Election Commission turned down calls for a referendum on the use of wild boar snares on the basis that the referendum was unclear as to whether it pertained to traps used by Indigenous hunters.

Otherwise, such traps are sometimes used by farmers as a means of preventing damage to their crops. Animal rights advocates have called on the government to provide electric fencing, protective netting, or other means for farmers to protect their livestock and crops.

The proposals called for by animal rights advocates are relevant to the use, display, and sale of wild boar snares, as well as their import and export. It is thought that China is a major source of some of the wild boar snares used in Taiwan.

It is unclear as to whether the Central Election Commission will approve the referendum currently called for by animal rights advocates. At the same time, without a major political party endorsing it as an issue, such a referendum is unlikely to gain traction. It is to be seen if either the DPP or KMT, or perhaps even both parties, throw their weight behind the proposal.

One notes that there have been cases of political bipartisanship between both major parties on the issue of animal rights in past years, as seen with politicians of both parties supporting enshrining animal rights in the constitution. Even so, such politicians ultimately did not prove serious about such promises outside of election campaigning, as a result of which neither the KMT nor DPP acted on claims in past election cycles that animal rights would see constitutional protection.

author: Sophie Lemcke
title: So ist es, als weibliches Rind in der Milchindustrie zu leben
content:
Die Milchindustrie ist ein grausamer Kreislauf des Leids und endet mit einem gewaltvollen Tod.


Wie fühlt es sich an, in dieses System hineingeboren zu werden, ohne die Möglichkeit, dem zu entkommen?


Der einzige Grund, weshalb die Industrie dich „produziert“ hat: Auch du sollst Kinder gebären, immer wieder, damit du Milch produzierst. Milch, die dann von Menschen, statt von deinem Kalb konsumiert werden kann.


Du wirst fixiert, während jemand das Besamungsgerät in deine Vagina sowie seinen Arm in deinen Anus einführt. Wenn die Zwangsbefruchtung nicht beim ersten Mal zur Trächtigkeit führt – was oft der Fall ist –, wird dieser Vorgang mehrfach wiederholt.


Neun Monate – wie bei uns Menschen – wächst dein Kalb in dir heran. Du spürst eine Verbindung, merkst, wie es sich bewegt und immer größer wird. Je schwerer du selbst wirst, umso stärker werden deine Gelenkprobleme. Die rutschigen und harten Spaltenböden, auf denen du fast dein ganzes Leben verbringst, führen oft zu Verletzungen.


Dann bringst du dein Kalb zur Welt. Um dich herum riecht es extrem nach Kot und Ammoniak, von den Ausscheidungen der Tiere.


Endlich ist es da, noch ganz nass und schwach. Du leckst ihm über das Fell, um es zu wärmen. Es sucht deine Nähe und will an deinem Euter die für ihn so wichtige Erstmilch trinken. Sie stärkt sein noch schwaches Immunsystem und gibt ihm Kraft. Doch dann kommen die Arbeiter*innen.


Sie zerren dein noch ganz wackelig stehendes Kalb weg von dir. Es ruft nach dir. Du versuchst, bei ihm zu bleiben, aber du hast keine Chance. Die Menschen haben es weggebracht – du wirst es wahrscheinlich nie wiedersehen und nach nur zwei Monaten direkt wieder gewaltvoll befruchtet.


Du wirst nach der Geburt monatelang mehrmals täglich in den Melkstand getrieben – und die meiste Zeit davon bist du bereits wieder schwanger. Dein Körper muss gleichzeitig ein neues Kalb versorgen, das in dir heranwächst, und täglich über 22 Liter Milch produzieren. Dein Euter und deine Zitzen schmerzen. Aufgrund der extremen Überzüchtung produzierst du viermal so viel Milch, wie du es natürlicherweise für dein Kind tun würdest.


Die Prozeduren und Haltungsbedingungen zehren stark an deinem Körper. Dein Euter ist entzündet und schmerzt bei jeder Berührung. Andere Tiere humpeln, weil ihnen jeder Schritt wehtut. Viele sind schwach und ausgelaugt.


Wenn du nicht schon vorher stirbst oder getötet wirst, weil dein Körper nicht mehr kann, dann wirst du voraussichtlich nach nur fünf Jahren getötet – obwohl du unter natürlichen Bedingungen 25 Jahre alt werden könntest.


Dann kommt der Tag, an dem du als nicht mehr profitabel giltst. Du wirst aus dem Stall getrieben – das erste Mal nach Jahren verlässt du ihn, aber das ist kein Grund zur Freude.


Zusammen mit anderen erschöpften „ausgedienten Milchkühen“ wirst du auf einen Transporter verladen. Du hast Mühe, über die Rampe zu gehen. Deine Gelenke schmerzen vom jahrelangen Stehen auf Spaltenböden. Im engen Transporter stehst du dicht an dicht mit den anderen Tieren, der Lkw wackelt. Manche fallen hin und werden versehentlich getreten. Eure Fahrt in den Schlachthof dauert mehrere Stunden, ohne Wasser, ohne Nahrung, ohne Pause.


Angekommen erwartet dich ein brutaler Tod. Überall riecht es nach Blut, du bekommst Panik, aber es gibt keinen Ausweg. Dann ein Bolzenschuss in deinen Kopf. Wenn die Betäubung korrekt durchgeführt wurde und wirkt, brichst du zusammen. Wenn nicht, kann es sein, dass du bei Bewusstsein und unter extremen Schmerzen erlebst, wie dir deine Kehle aufgeschnitten wird und du verblutest.


Es ist unvorstellbar, was Mutterrinder in der Milchindustrie erleiden müssen.


Der wahre Preis von Milch


Ein Ermittler von Animal Equality hat mehrere Monate undercover in einem deutschen Milchgewinnungsbetrieb gearbeitet und den Alltag der Tiere dokumentiert. Was unsere Undercover-Recherche zeigt, ist der wahre Preis von Milch: Ausbeutung, Gewalt, Schmerz, Leid und Tod.


Auf unserer Webseite erfährst du mehr und kannst die Stellungnahme des Betriebs nachlesen:


Zur Undercover-Recherche


Unterstütze dieses grausame System nicht!


Entscheide dich konsequent für pflanzliche Lebensmittel. Im Supermarkt findest du zahlreiche Alternativen zu Milch, wie:


Hafermilch – mild, cremig, perfekt für Kaffee und Müsli (oft die günstigste Option!)


Sojamilch – proteinreich, ideal zum Kochen und Backen


Mandelmilch – leicht nussig, besonders lecker in Smoothies


Reismilch – süßlich und gut verträglich …

author: admin
title: Solidarität mit nichtmenschlichen Tieren im Klimakollaps
content:
Am 2. November ist Friederike Schmitz zu Gast in Leipzig. Ihr Vortrag beschäftigt sich mit der Frage von Solidarität mit nichtmenschlichen Tieren im Klimakollaps.

Plaque, Industriestraße 101, Leipzig

Orga: tierbefreier*innen Leipzig

Die Erderhitzung schreitet voran und wir müssen damit rechnen, dass Wetterextreme und Katastrophen unsere Gesellschaften massiv unter Druck setzen werden. Es ist daher realistisch, von Kollapsszenarien auszugehen – das bedeutet nicht zwingend ein einmaliges Ereignis, das plötzlich alles verändert. Es kann auch bedeuten, dass etablierte Systeme und Sicherheiten zunehmend instabil und unverlässlich werden.>

Die Kollapsbewegung fordert, dass wir uns gemeinsam darauf vorbereiten und solidarische Strukturen aufbauen, denn wer gegen Umweltzerstörung und Faschismus kämpft, kann sich auf den Staat nicht verlassen. Doch inwieweit sind nichtmenschliche Tiere dabei eingeschlossen? Und wie könnte es aussehen, wenn die Solidarität nicht an der Speziesgrenze haltmacht? Der Vortrag liefert einen Einstieg in diese Fragen und lädt zu Austausch und Diskussion ein.

Friederike Schmitz ist eine deutsche Philosophin und Publizistin mit dem Schwerpunkt Ethik und Politik der Mensch-Tier-Beziehung. Zu ihrem Schwerpunkt gehört die Klimagerechte Transformation von Landwirtschaft und Ernährung. In dem Podcast “Was zu retten ist?” thematisiert sie zusammen mit Annemarie Botzki (Campaignerin und Aktivistin) Klima, Kollaps und Ernährung.

author: Animal Rising Press
title: Guilty Verdict For King’s Sheep Rescuers In Theft Trial
content:
After a four-day trial at Norwich Crown Court, Rose Patterson, Sarah Foy, and Rosa Sharkey have all been found guilty of theft after the rescue of three lambs from King Charles III’s Sandringham Estate in May 2023. Sentencing to follow today.

Despite the verdict, Animal Rising claims that the rescue and subsequent trial have helped to put a spotlight on the reality behind animal farming in the UK, with over 10 million sheep being slaughtered yearly [1].

The controversial rescue made front-page news across the UK and headlines around the world [2]. It captured the attention of the British public, questioning how we relate to animals in the food system and if it’s a rescue or a theft to take them from farms.

Animal Rising director Rose Patterson, alongside Rosa Sharkey and Sarah Foy, rescued the lambs - Sammy, Sunny and Sooty - before informing police the following day. The women held signs outside Windsor Castle reading “I rescued the King’s sheep” before reporting what they had done to police. They each face up to 7 years' imprisonment.

Earlier this year, Patterson was found not guilty by a jury over another Animal Rising open rescue, after helping to rescue beagle puppies from MBR Acres, a facility breeding animals for testing [3].

Animal Rising director Rose Patterson, one of the three defendants found guilty today, said:

Sammy, Sunny and Sooty remain safe and are now fully grown.

The trial followed a series of open-rescue trials relating to Animal Rising’s rescue of beagles from MBR Acres. In January this year, Animal Rising made history by securing the UK’s first-ever not-guilty verdict in an open-rescue case [4]. The lambs were rescued from Appleton Farm, which forms part of the Sandringham estate.

Defendants Patterson and Foy are available for comment or broadcast interview upon request.

For further information, comment, or to arrange an interview, please email press@animalrising.org or call +44 1225 29 6691

Rose Patterson, 37, is the Director of Animal Rising. An advocate for animals since 2012, she holds an MSc in Animal Welfare Science, Ethics, and Law and previously worked with World Animal Protection before joining Animal Rising in 2020.

Sarah Foy, 26, has been involved in a range of campaigns advocating for a just and sustainable food system that works for animals, farmers, and the planet. She brings a practical, hands-on approach to her advocacy, with real-world experience caring for rescued farm animals at sanctuaries and protesting alongside farmers.

Rosa Sharkey, 26, is a food charity worker. She is passionately committed to reducing the impact of our food system on the climate crisis, community action, and animal rights.

Animal Rising is a nonviolent campaign group working to fundamentally transform our relationship with animals and nature, and build a more sustainable future for animals, people and the planet. Animal Rising is calling on the Government to end factory farming by 2040 and support a transition to a sustainable plant-based food system.

title: Smokescreen Saturday Exposed: Chris Packham Blasts The Quorn Hunt Over Sickening Fox Cruelty That Blows Apart Trail Hunting’s Biggest Lie
content:
When we showed wildlife campaigner Chris Packham the sickening footage of the Quorn Hunt, his response was damning:


“Another bloody year, another bloodied body, another animal tortured and torn to pieces to gratify the bloodlust of savages. Where is the damned consultation and where is the damned ban?”


Chris Packham condemns the Quorn Hunt footage.


The footage lays bare the brutal reality of cub hunting – the practice of using foxes to train young hounds to hunt and kill.


WARNING: DISTURBING FOOTAGE


Cub hunting is not some isolated activity. It is the preparation for the hunting season ahead. Throughout the autumn, young hounds are taught what to chase, what to kill and how to respond to the huntsman’s commands. What they learn – or fail to learn – during these crucial weeks sets the tone for the entire season.


This is what makes the Quorn Hunt footage so damning. It shows hounds being deliberately encouraged to seize and tear at a fox, with hunt staff repeatedly intervening to reinforce that behaviour.


On the eve of National Trail Hunting Day aka Smokescreen Saturday – as the British Hound Sports Association (BHSA) and the Countryside Alliance prepared to showcase so-called ‘trail hunting’, the Quorn Hunt provided a horrifying glimpse of the reality behind the myth of trail laying.


On Friday 16 October, 2026 Northants Hunt Saboteurs visited The Quorn Hunt’s kennel meet at Kirby Bellars, near Melton Mowbray, Leicestershire.


The Quorn has a long history of royal connections. King Charles regularly rode with the hunt when he was Prince of Wales. His association with the Quorn came to an end following the emergence of footage showing

hunt members pulling a fox cub from its den

 and throwing them to the hounds to be torn apart.


The footage begins with the saboteurs’ drone approaching a group of barns stacked with bales. Mounted riders are positioned around the outside of the covert – a classic cub hunting tactic designed to frighten fleeing foxes back into cover, where the hounds can kill them.


Riders surround the covert which forces the fox back towards the barns.


As the drone circles to the far side of the barns, a group of hounds comes into view. A quad bike can be seen approaching, alongside another rider. More hounds appear on the track, along with a riderless horse.


Two terriermen jump off the quad bike and run towards the hounds, which have gathered in a narrow passageway between two barns.


Trapped. The fox is between the two barns.


What the drone captures next is utterly horrific – and exposes the brutal reality behind the hunting industry’s claims about scent trails.


The huntsman is already on foot, surrounded by excited hounds. He is swinging something towards them, encouraging them to grab hold. As the footage unfolds, it becomes clear that he is swinging a fox.


First the huntsman is alone shaking the fox to excite the hounds.


The hounds are repeatedly encouraged to seize the fox. Eventually, several begin to grab hold, and the huntsman encourages them further, pulling and tugging against them as though playing a game.


The huntsman blows on his horn over the hounds reinforcing the sound of the horn call with the kill.


When the hounds finally take the fox from him, he bends over them as they tear at it and then blows his hunting horn – most likely sounding the traditional call for a kill, reinforcing the hounds’ association between the horn and their quarry.


He then gives one of the terriermen a thumbs-up.


Thumbs-up.


When the hounds begin to lose interest again, the terrierman picks up the fox’s body and repeatedly shakes it in front of them, encouraging them to take hold once more. He appears to push the fox towards the hounds jaws.


The terrierman also has a go with the fox – shaking the body into the hounds jaws.


When the dogs finally grip it, he pulls against them in a grotesque tug-of-war. Once the hounds take the fox from the terrierman, the huntsman again blows his horn over them.


As more hounds join in, the terrierman pats one of the dogs. But as he does so he appears to hear the drone and looks up.


The terrierman suddenly notices the drone. Too late.


Suddenly everything changes.


The fox’s body is hurriedly retrieved from the hounds, and the two terriermen scramble to stuff it beneath the hay bales.

author: Zeit Online
title: Warum die Deutschen nicht ausrasten?
content:
Während in Frankreich Barrikaden brennen, bleibt es hierzulande ziemlich ruhig. Geht’s den Deutschen so viel besser? Nein, sie sind nur die Summe ihrer Ängste.


Verschwitzte Gesichter hinter Sturmhauben, ein Rathaus, das lichterloh in Flammen steht, Ascheberge am Straßenrand. Die Bilder der Ausschreitungen in Frankreich, die in diesen Tagen zu uns herüberschwappen, können bei deutschen Betrachtern für gemischte Gefühle sorgen. Im ersten Moment kann man erschrecken; die Franzosen, meine Güte! Oder aber man macht einen Schritt zur Seite. Und fragt: Warum blieben wir in Deutschland von solchen Ausschreitungen bislang verschont? Warum rasten die Deutschen nicht aus, wie Menschen in anderen Ländern der Welt, zumindest nicht in diesen Massen? Und das, obwohl radikale Einstellungen auch hierzulande zunehmen?


Beobachtet man die Protestkultur in Deutschland in den vergangenen Jahren, kann man sich fühlen wie in einer düsteren Variante von Samuel Becketts Warten auf Godot. Man spürt, da baut sich etwas auf, der Unmut, so erwartet man, muss bald eskalieren, das Aufbegehren steht vor der Tür. Und alle fürchten es schon. Doch dann? Bleibt es aus.


So war es, als die Gelbwesten in Frankreich durch die Straßen zogen und die Zeitungen ein baldiges deutsches Pendant prophezeiten. So war es, als die Klimaaktivisten ihre Hände auf die Autobahn klebten; CSU-Politiker Alexander Dobrindt sah damals gar die Entstehung einer »Klima-RAF« voraus. Und auch auf die Pegida-Demonstrationen und die Bauernproteste schaute die Öffentlichkeit voller Angst vor flächendeckender Eskalation. Nur kam diese nie. In Deutschland gibt es den Zorn der Masse. Aber er kocht selten über.


Bevor sich jetzt jemand wütend in die Kommentarspalte verabschiedet: Ja, auch hierzulande kommt es zu Gewalt bei Protesten. Linksradikale schmissen in den vergangenen Jahren Steine auf Polizisten, Rechtsradikale griffen Gegendemonstranten an, Corona-Demonstrierende kletterten über das Gitter zum Reichstag, Pro-Palästina-Demos endeten mit Verhaftungen. Aber im Vergleich zu Frankreich etwa rasteten die Deutschen zuletzt selten richtig aus, zumindest nicht in Gestalt einer gewaltbereiten Masse, die landesweit durch die Straßen zieht, öffentliche Gebäude in Brand steckt und Läden plündert.


Das vielleicht bekannteste Beispiel für gewaltsame Ausschreitungen bei Demonstrationen der letzten Jahre sind die linksradikalen Proteste rund um den G20-Gipfel 2017. Aber auch diese blieben auf einen Ort und den Anlass beschränkt. Und es war kein allein deutscher Protest, er war international. Aus ganz Europa reisten Demonstrierende an, um ihrer Wut Ausdruck zu verleihen.


Was also passiert mit der deutschen Wut auf der Straße? Unmut gibt es hier schließlich auch. Die AfD macht längst mit der mangelhaften Infrastruktur, der übertriebenen Bürokratie, dem Aussterben von Kleinstädten und der Verelendung von Großstädten Politik.


Wenn man in die Zahlen schaut, gibt es viele der Probleme, die in Frankreich beklagt werden, auch hier: Der Anteil derer, die armutsgefährdet sind, liegt hier wie dort bei 16 Prozent. Die Preise für die Verbraucher sind in beiden Ländern um ziemlich genau drei Prozent gestiegen. Die hohen Mieten sind in Deutschland sogar ein größeres Problem als in Frankreich. Beim letzten Pisa-Test schnitt Deutschland so schlecht ab wie noch nie. Die Jugendarbeitslosigkeit ist in Frankreich zwar deutlich höher, aber auch hierzulande haben Jugendliche, was ihre Zukunftsaussichten angeht, allen Grund, die Fassung zu verlieren. Steht uns der Kipppunkt also vielleicht doch nur noch bevor?


Telefoniert man Protestforscher im Land ab, rechnet keiner von ihnen damit, dass Ausschreitungen, wie wir sie in Frankreich sehen, in nächster Zeit bei uns drohen könnten. Strukturelle Gründe werden da genannt. Die Tatsache, dass hierzulande Gewerkschaften regelmäßig mit Unternehmern am Tisch sitzen und Kompromisse aushandeln, bevor alles eskaliert. In Frankreich gehe die Polizei viel härter gegen Demonstrierende vor, auch das befördere die Eskalation eher, als dass es sie verhindere. Der vielleicht größte strukturelle Unterschied ist, dass es in Deutschland keine Zentralregierung gibt, die von oben alles entscheidet und auf die sich die geballte Wut einer ganzen Bewegung entladen kann. Im föderalen System bleibt der Protest eher lokal, statt sich im Land auszubreiten.


Oft erstickt die Wut aber auch in der Frustration. Der Protestforscher Simon Teune von der FU Berlin sagt: »Die Deutschen haben …

author: Kenny Bruno
title: Mafia Diplomacy Will Continue After Kimberly Guilfoyle
content:
Guilfoyle’s mission in Greece — to push fossil fuels — is also playing out in the US with a permitting reform bill.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Kimberly Guilfoyle is out as U.S. ambassador to Greece. Mainstream media focused on Donald Trump Jr.’s former fiancée’s credit card bill and her penchant for extravagant partying and fashion. The next ambassador might not share those particular foibles, but the real significance of Guilfoyle’s appointment will last. She was what Dexter Filkins, writing in The New Yorker, calls “a new kind of Washington figure, for whom public office serves as a means to extraordinary wealth.” Donald Trump’s almost daughter-in-law was following in the footsteps of his son-in-law.

Jared Kushner does diplomacy and business simultaneously, and he’s getting really rich from it. While Kushner is dispatched to work on Iran and Ukraine, with meetings on the side to recruit billions to his investment funds, Guilfoyle was sent to Greece as the de facto ambassador for liquefied natural gas (LNG). In other words, her job was to shove LNG down the throats of Southeastern and Central European countries. Her refrain was U.S. energy dominance.

A more diplomatic diplomat might have noticed that one country’s dominance means, logically, another’s subservience. But tact was not Guilfoyle’s strong suit, and, according to the Wall Street Journal, another of her gaffes was not-so-subtly telling Greece’s energy minister that the U.S. could change the government of any country it wants.

Guilfoyle denies any intimidation took place, but threatening or forcing regime change for the sake of oil is not far-fetched. (See: Venezuela.)

In Southeast and Central Europe, the U.S. government is pushing something called the Vertical Gas Corridor (VGC), an opaque infrastructure initiative stretching from Greece through Bulgaria, Romania, Hungary, Slovakia, Moldova, and ultimately Ukraine. As stated by the U.S. Energy Association, the VGC “opens access to Europe’s largest underground gas storage system, located in Ukraine.”

Publicly, the U.S. is framing the project as a strategic corridor that strengthens regional energy security and reduces Russian influence. In practice, it is becoming a way to trade dependence on Russia for dependence on the U.S. Greece will be the entry point and collaborator in the plan. U.S. LNG exporters stand to make huge profits, especially when there are high prices, as has been the case during the Iran War.

Why is the U.S. going to the mat for the Vertical Gas Corridor? The fossil fuel industry sees LNG exports as the lifeboat for the sinking ship of the conventional oil industry. For U.S. LNG, as with crude oil, it’s export or die. Those were Ambassador Guilfoyle’s marching orders.

An inconvenient reality for the industry is that market enthusiasm for the VGC appears remarkably weak. Repeated capacity auctions linked to the corridor, in which gas companies bid for the right to use pipelines and other infrastructure, have attracted limited commercial interest. Several auctions failed outright, while others generated only modest bookings concentrated in specific segments of the network.

Infrastructure projects backed by robust commercial fundamentals typically attract customers on their own merits, without the need for lobbying and strong-arming. Massive terminals require long-term contracts, and the U.S. is determined to get both — whether or not it makes any economic sense.

For Greece, the stakes are particularly high.

The country is being positioned as the southern gateway for American LNG entering Southeast Europe. While this positioning promises geopolitical visibility, it also risks tying the Greek economy to fossil fuel infrastructure whose long-term viability remains deeply uncertain. Investments in LNG terminals, pipelines, and associated facilities are dependent on future gas demand that may never materialize as Europe accelerates its clean-energy transition.

At the same time, communities and ecosystems in Greece bear the environmental costs, just as surely as the Texas and Louisiana communities where the methane gas originates. From the Sea of Thrace to other sensitive marine areas, new infrastructure developments are proceeding despite growing concerns over climate impacts, methane emissions, and ecological damage.

title: Resistance against solar power plant project kicks off in Amed
content:
Resistance against the planned “Zenkar 2 Solar Power Plant and Energy Storage Facility” project in Amed’s Arzoxlî neighborhood entered its second day. While legal proceedings against the project’s “Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) Positive” decision are ongoing, company employees entered the construction site accompanied by the gendarmerie and riot police.


In response, neighborhood residents, representatives of political parties and civil society organizations, and environmental activists marched to the project site. A banner reading “Our ancient city of Ğırap and our village must not be sacrificed to capital” was unfurled, while protesters chanted, “Our land, our water, our existence.”


Prevented from accessing fields


Residents encountered a gendarmerie blockade near the project site and demanded an explanation of the legal basis for the work being carried out in the area. Lawyer Ahmet İnan, chair of the Environment and Urban Affairs Commission of the Amed Bar Association, said the restrictions were not limited to the project site and that access to fields outside the construction area was also being blocked.


Berdan Öztürk, a DEM Party member of parliament for Amed, said they opposed the project, stating that villagers were being deprived of their right to life and that people were being forced to leave the places where they lived.


Neighborhood residents emphasized that they earn their livelihoods through agriculture and livestock farming, saying the power plant threatened their health, livestock farming, and future. Residents stated that they would defend their land and pastures against the company’s activities and reiterated that they did not want the project.


Legal struggle and tent vigil


Ahmet İnan, chair of the Environment and Urban Affairs Commission of the Amed Bar Association, said lawsuits had been filed against the pasture allocation permit, the zoning plan, and the EIA report, and that legal proceedings were ongoing. İnan said they would continue all legal efforts and called on democratic organizations and environmental defenders to show solidarity and help expand the tent vigil.


Following the statements, neighborhood residents began a tent vigil at the project site. They stressed that they would continue their resistance to protect their land and living spaces.

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: Farmers decry government’s lack of preparation for Super El Niño
content:
Farmers, scientists and environmentalists, held a forum, October 18 on the impacts of Super El Niño on farmers and fisherfolk and the government’s lack of preparations for it.

A Super El Niño is a stronger El Niño where the temperature of the Pacific Ocean increases to 2C above the average. In the Philippines, it leads to the extreme shifting of weather conditions, bringing in severe drought, or stronger rainfall events. For farmers, it is the government’s unpreparedness that turns it into an even greater calamity, made even worse by the climate crisis.

Farmers Geraldine Patriarca and Ginny Nabia from Bicol and Negros expressed how their communities are already experiencing extreme drought, and are unable to sustain themselves and their families. They demanded Marcos Jr. to give genuine solutions to farmers’ struggles, not his proposed buckets that they say “will barely even catch any rain.”

Irish Cuaresma of Advocates of Science and Technology for the People (Agham), added that farmers and Indigenous peoples are further undermined by “disaster capitalism,” where corporations benefit from humanitarian crises.

Sharl Lopez of Philippine Network of Food Security Programs (PNFSP) meanwhile, criticized the government for not upholding their obligation to uphold the people’s right to food security, and advocated for the passing of the Right to Adequate Food Bill.

After the forum, farmers held a flash mob calling for national industrialization, genuine agrarian reform. (RVO)

author: Taylor Noakes
title: ‘Snipped And Posted’: How Pro-Oil Groups Generate Viral Content Online
content:
In December 2025, former B.C. Premier Christy Clark gave an interview on Global News where she described Canada’s west coast ban on oil tankers as a “ridiculous” constraint on the Canadian economy.


A clip of Clark’s interview then began to circulate online, where it was shared by several Canadian conservative influencers and aggregator accounts on platforms including X and Facebook with captions including “reality check,” “huge truth bomb” and “economic self-sabotage.”


Within days, the interview clip was spreading across the social media feeds of people in B.C. and beyond, eventually surpassing 1.6 million views.


But this was not necessarily a case of west coast residents suddenly deciding organically they wanted to overturn the ban on coastal oil tanker traffic brought in by former Liberal Prime Minister Justin Trudeau.


The digital media amplification of Clark’s comments was orchestrated in part by Canada Action, a pro-oil industry advocacy organization partly funded by

Cenovus Energy

, Canada’s third-largest oil and gas company.


It was one example of “showcasing Canada Action’s content leadership influencing the public discussion,” according to an internal slidedeck from the Calgary-based group. That slidedeck, which hasn’t yet been reported on, was obtained by Greenpeace Canada and published in its October 2026 report

Manufacturing Petro-Populism

.


Screenshot from a Canada Action Slidedeck called “Extended Third Party Reach: Showcasing Canada Action’s content leadership influencing the public discussion”.


These and other presentation slides from Canada Action demonstrate how fossil fuel interests manufacture the appearance of consent for increased oil and gas production in Canada, according to experts who study the spread of climate disinformation online.


“Most people can pretty easily see through messages coming directly from the Canadian Association of Petroleum Producers (CAPP) or industry CEOs,” said Shane Gunster, a professor at Simon Fraser University’s School of Communications, in a statement to DeSmog. 


“But when the message comes from people in their social network, local business leaders, their family and friends, they’re far more likely to engage with it and maybe even be persuaded by it. And this is especially true for growing segments of the public that don’t consume a lot of news.”


Canada Action didn’t respond to DeSmog’s questions about the slidedeck.

According to the Greenpeace report, Energy in Action is an oil-industry backed network of thirty organizations that advocate for the fossil fuel sector, including front groups, charitable organizations, companies, media organizations and lobby groups. title: Fosil yakıtın Türkiye'ye faturası: Yılda 26 bin 500 ölüm, 55 milyar dolar kayıp
content:
Birleşmiş Milletler'in Kasım'da Antalya’da düzenlenecek COP31 zirvesi öncesinde Enerji ve Temiz Hava Araştırma Merkezi (CREA) ile Temiz Hava Hakkı Platformu (THHP), fosil yakıtların yarattığı ekonomik kaybı gözler önüne seren bir rapor yayınladı. 

Fosil Yakıtların Türkiye’ye Ağır Faturası: Sağlık Yükü ve Ekonomik Maliyeti

 raporunun sonuçları, bugün İstanbul’da düzenlenen basın toplantısında açıklandı. 


Rapora göre Türkiye’de hava kirliliğinin (PM₂.₅) yüzde 52’si, kömür, petrol ve gaz gibi fosil yakıtlardan kaynaklanıyor. Bu kirliliğin sağlık üzerindeki etkileri, Türkiye ekonomisine bir yılda yaklaşık 55 milyar dolara mal oluyor. Bu tutar, ülkenin 2024 yılı gayrisafi yurt içi hasılasının yüzde 4,1’ine karşılık geliyor.


Fosil yakıt kirliliğinin yıllık ekonomik maliyeti, Sağlık Bakanlığı’nın tüm 2024 bütçesinin yaklaşık 2,5 katı. Fosil yakıt kaynaklı hava kirliliği, kalp ve damar hastalıkları, solunum yolu hastalıkları, akciğer kanseri, inme ve diyabet nedeniyle gerçekleşen ölümler dahil, Türkiye’de yılda yaklaşık 26 bin 500 ölüme yol açıyor.


Kaynak:  

Fosil Yakıtların Türkiye’ye Ağır Faturası: Sağlık Yükü ve Ekonomik Maliyeti

 raporu


Raporda öne çıkan bulgular şöyle:


Bir yılda İstanbul’da 8 bin 100, Ankara’da 2 bin 500, İzmir’de 2 bin 400, ülke genelinde ise toplam 26 bin 500 erken ölüme yol açan hava kirliliği, Yunanistan’dan Mısır’a uzanan bir coğrafyada da ölümlere neden oluyor. 


COP31’in ev sahibi Türkiye, fosil yakıtlara bağımlılığını azaltacak somut adımlarla hava kirliliğinin sağlık ve ekonomi üzerindeki yükünü hafifletebilir, uluslararası arenada iklim alanında liderliğini ortaya koyabilir. 


Türkiye, Kasım ayında COP31’e ev sahipliği yapmaya hazırlanırken fosil yakıtlara bağımlılığın hem ülke içinde hem de Doğu Akdeniz genelinde yol açtığı sağlık sorunları büyük bir ekonomik yük oluşturuyor.


HALKLARIN İKLİM ZİRVESİ


COP31 için “yeşil aklama” itirazı: Sinpaş’a karşı uluslararası kampanya başlatılacak


19 Ekim 2026


"Yakıt emisyonları binlerce ölüme ve ekonomik kayba yol açıyor"


Fosil yakıtlara bağımlılık, Türkiye’nin ekonomik yükünü de katlayarak artırıyor. Fosil yakıtlarda büyük ölçüde ithalata bağımlı olan Türkiye, uluslararası fiyat şoklarına açık hale geliyor. Nitekim Türkiye İstatistik Kurumu’nun açıkladığı verilere göre Hürmüz krizi sırasında enerji ithalat faturası 2026’nın Ağustos ayında, bir önceki yılın aynı ayına kıyasla yüzde 33,8 arttı. Bununla birlikte PM₂.₅ kirliliği, çalışanların sağlığını ve iş gücü verimliliğini de etkiliyor.


Karbon emisyonlarının da en büyük kaynağı fosil yakıtlar. 2024 verilerine göre kömür, Türkiye’nin elektrik üretiminin yüzde 35’ini, doğal gaz ise yüzde 19’unu karşılıyor. Karayolu ulaşımında tüketilen enerjinin yüzde 66’sı dizelden, yüzde 17’si LPG’den ve yüzde 16’sı benzinden geliyor. Elektriğin payı yüzde 0,2 düzeyinde kalıyor. Sanayide ise fosil yakıtlar nihai enerji tüketiminin yaklaşık yüzde 60’ını oluşturuyor.


CREA Analisti ve raporun başyazarı Vera Tattari, araştırmanın Türkiye'nin fosil yakıt kaynaklı hava kirliliğinin ülke sınırlarını aştığını gösterdiğini belirterek şunları aktardı:


Kara kaynaklı fosil yakıt emisyonları hem Batı Asya’da hem de Avrupa’da binlerce ölüme ve milyarlarca dolarlık ekonomik kayba yol açıyor. Bu rakamların arkasında, kirli havanın sonuçlarıyla yaşayan insanlar ve aileler var. COP31 yaklaşırken Türkiye, bölge halkının sağlığını ve ekonomik refahını korumak için fosil yakıtlara bağımlılığını azaltma taahhüdünde bulunarak iklim liderliğini somut adımlarla ortaya koyabilir.


"Adil, düzenli ve eşitlikçi biçimde uzaklaşılması gerekiyor"


Rapora göre; Türkiye’de kara kaynaklı fosil yakıt emisyonlarının neden olduğu sınır ötesi hava kirliliği, bölgedeki beş ülkede de binlerce ölüme yol açıyor. Buna göre 2024 itibarıyla hesaplanan yıllık ekonomik yük; Mısır’da 2,1 milyar dolar, Suriye’de 200 milyon dolar, Irak’ta 800 milyon dolar, İsrail’de 4,5 milyar dolar ve Yunanistan’da 1,5 milyar dolar.


THHP Koordinatörü Deniz Gümüşel, Türkiye'nin fosil yakıtlardan çıkış için bir yol haritası hazırlayarak ve uygulamaya geçirerek, bu enerji türünün sağlık ve ekonomi üzerindeki yükünü azaltmayı başarabileceğini belirtiyor. Gümüşel, atılacak somut adımların ilkinin, elektrik üretiminde Afşin Elbistan A ve Cenal santrallerindeki genişletme projeleri gibi yeni kömürlü santrallere izin verilmemesi olduğunu belirtiyor.

title: Scotland: Anti-Data Centre Movement Gathers Momentum
content:
“Every time you ask ChatGPT a question, read a Google summary or make an online bank payment, a data centre is working behind the scenes. Now Scotland is part of a global race to build many more of them – on a massive scale. The explosion in artificial intelligence (AI) over the past few years has seen tech firms scrambling to build new “hyperscale” data centres, including some which would rank among the biggest in the world. Plans are in place to build at least 23 giant AI-powered data centres” (

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6qxv55882z1o

).


AI has insinuated itself into all areas of life and society. For example in education, it has managed to secure huge contracts with universities and schools, leading to the forcing of AI on teachers and students.


AI is controlled by Big Tech capitalists and by heads of state. It hopes to create huge dividends for shareholders and profits for its owners while claiming to be good for society.


AI has not stopped war. It is developing techniques to destroy cities and kill people remotely. It has not created better working conditions, the end of unemployment, and an improvement in living standards. It has done the opposite. It has not led to a solution to climate change. In fact, the mass development of data centres will accelerate climate change. It has not led to social progress. In fact, the plutocrats are increasingly taking over and controlling the media, political and social power and moving towards increasingly more authoritarian forms of rule, in order to preserve and regenerate a failing capitalism.


The uprising against data centres is therefore also a revolt against AI and against a system that puts profits before people and the planet.


Where are the Data Centres


The map, produce by the Action for the Protection of Rural Scotland (APRS), shows the extent of proposed data centres (

https://aprs.scot/data-centres-campaign/

).


Some of the biggest ones planned are:


Chapel Stile Data Centre (Dumfriesshire)


The Ferret, well-known for its hard-hitting, independent and thoroughly-researched journalism says:


“CX Tech Limited has lodged plans for a 1,000 megawatt (MW) data centre at the site of the former Chapelcross nuclear plant in Dumfriesshire, which could benefit from up to £23m in taxpayer support. Company records show CX Tech’s controlling shareholder is Wpgss Limited, which is owned by property mogul and Tory treasurer Graham Edwards through a holding company registered in the British Virgin Islands (BVI) – a notorious tax and secrecy haven.” (https://www.theferret.scot/scotland-data-centre-graham-edwards/)


Auchertool: Fife


The site would span 60 hectares, about the size of 84 football pitches. It would be bigger than the village itself, completely transforming the life of the village. People are concerned at the noise and pollution, the impact on health and the sheer size of the development. As one villager said: “The village will be left in the shadows of the data centre. It’s huge. It is like having a tower block laid on its side plonked in the middle of the countryside.” (https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cddle43jr1go)


‘Green’ Data Centres


The applications for the big data centres are claiming to be ‘green’. This way they can be considered to be part of “National Development 12”. It is up to the planning authority to interpret and apply the guidelines. According to Action for the Protection of Rural Scotland: “We believe that there will be serious unintended consequences of this policy until a strict definition of a green data centre is established, combined with an overall limit to the amount of energy that Scotland intends to divert to data centres. We have looked at data centres in development around Scotland and have seen that, in many planning application documents, or pre-application consultations, they are describing themselves as ‘green’ data centres. This can range from claiming to be green because they have solar panels on the roof to claiming the fact they use grid electricity in Scotland makes them green, some mention using waste heat in heat networks.”

author: Publicación Abierta
title: E INICIO EL PROCESO DE CONSULTAS A COMUNIDADES INDIGENAS SOBRE EL PLAN DE MANEJO DEL HUMEDAL LAGUNA MELINCUE (Santa Fe)
content:
Melincué, 22 de octubre de 2026 (por Centro Mocovi)


 El 20/10/2026 desde las 9 a 17 horas se realizaron los Talleres para iniciar el Proceso de Consulta Previa del Plan de Manejo del Sitio Ramsar “Humedal Laguna Melincué”, junto con el Ministerio de Ambiente y Cambio Climático de Santa Fe (Luciana Manelli, Directora Prov. de Bosques Y Áreas Protegidas), la Dirección Provincial de Pueblos Originarios (Victor De Battista), y el IPAS (Ramón Vilafañe). Los Talleres se realizaron en las Comunidades indígenas del Pueblo Mocoví de Maicasari Iagpa (Carreras), Noagué Noa Nonot’i (Melincué) y Ñachishinaxanaxat (Carmen).


El Centro Mocoví “Ialek Lav’a”, organización indígena que representa a las Comunidades Indígenas del Pueblo Mocoví asentadas en el Sitio Ramsar “Humedal Laguna Melincué”, y como parte integrante del

Comité Intersectorial de Manejo del Sitio Ramsar Humedal Laguna de Melincué

; viene impulsando el Procedimiento de Consulta Previa, Libre e Informada de las Comunidades Indígenas asentadas en el Sitio Ramsar “Humedal Laguna Melincué” sobre el Plan de Manejo de esta Área Natural Protegida.


Debemos destacar, que de la consulta preliminar realizada a las autoridades tradicionales indígenas de las comunidades mencionadas, en relación a la zona geográfica de impacto del Proyecto, resulta que existen comunidades y familias indígenas de los Pueblos Mocovi, Mapuche, Ranquel y Querandí radicadas en la zona de influencia del mismo; por lo que resulta obligatorio la aplicación de la Ley Nacional 24.071 (Convenio 169 de la Organización Internacional del Trabajo -OIT-) respecto a la aplicación de los procedimientos del Consentimiento Previo, Libre e Informado (CPLI) de los Pueblos Indígenas, contenidos en la norma citada.


Al respecto, y dado que la propuesta y el Proyecto “Plan de Manejo del Sitio Ramsar Humedal Laguna Melincué” , realizado por el Ministerio de Ambiente y Cambio Climáticoi, no tuvo la participación y consentimiento de las Comunidades Originarias, se deberá iniciar los procesos de consultas, en el marco del Convenio 169 de la OIT (Ley Nac. 24071), la Constitución Nacional (Art. 75, inc. 15), las leyes provinciales 10.375 y 11.078; la Declaración de las Naciones Unidas sobre Derechos de los Pueblos Indígenas; y la Declaración Americana sobre Derechos de los Pueblos Indígenas (OEA), a las Comunidades Indígenas de los Pueblos Mocovi, Rankülche, Mapuche y Querandí, asentadas en el Sitio Ramsar Humedal Laguna Melincué; a fin de determinar los impactos de las acciones y actividades a ejecutar con el proyecto; o las que surjan y propongan las Comunidades y organizaciones Indígenas. La misma deberá realizarse en conjunto con las Comunidades Originarias, las Organizaciones de Pueblos Indígenas de Segundo Grado (Centro Mocoví “Ialek Lav’a”) en aplicación de las Salvaguardas Sociales y Ambientales para Pueblos Indígenas contempladas en la legislación vigente.


En este caso el procesos de Consultas debe incluir un Plan de Manejo del Sitio Ramsar Humedal Laguna Melincué con la visión de los Pueblos Indígenas (PPI), o un Capítulo de Pueblos Indígenas, que contenga lineas de acción y actividades a desarrollar por el CIM (Comité Intersectorial de Manejo del Sitio Ramsar Humedal Laguna Melincué), incluido un especialista indígena y la asistencia técnica de las propias Organizaciones de Pueblos Indígenas (OPI), en el marco determinado por la 

Convención Ramsar: “

facilitar la participación directa de las comunidades locales y pueblos indígenas en el proceso de adopción de decisiones en los planos local y nacional para el uso sostenible de los humedales, incluido el suministro de los recursos necesarios; (Art. 15); y que “los expertos técnicos y las comunidades locales y pueblos indígenas a que trabajen conjuntamente en la planificación y el manejo/gestión de los humedales a fin de asegurar que en la adopción de decisiones se tomen en consideración los mejores conocimientos científicos y conocimientos locales disponibles; (Art. 18).


En los Talleres realizados se habló sobre la Visión Indígena del Humedal y la relación de las Comunidades con el Area Protegida, incluido los usos tradicionales dado por las Comunidadesa la biodiversidad del Humedal, y los proyectos que tienen en dicha Area Protegida, Territorio Ancestral y Sagrado Indígena….


ARIEL ARAUJO- Coordinador Centro Mocovi “Ialek Lav’a”

author: Unknown
title: Where are the Zapatistas 30 years later?
content:
The Zapatista Army of National Liberation (EZLN – Ejército Zapatista de Liberación Nacional), which emerged in Chiapas in the first days of 1994, came to the world's attention through an armed uprising in a region of Mexico marked by widespread poverty and inequality, where Indigenous people make up a significant proportion of the population. However, it was not only the uprising that made the Zapatista experience distinctive.


In the years that followed, the movement moved away from the goal of seizing state power and developed a practice of autonomy centred on the right of Indigenous communities to govern themselves. In this direction, it established autonomous governance, education, healthcare and production structures based on local communities. Over more than thirty years, as demands for Indigenous rights and political autonomy were not sufficiently realised, the Zapatistas declared their own autonomous governance structures and reorganised them several times. Having established autonomous municipalities and regional administrative centres for a period, the movement dissolved these structures in 2023, shifting decision-making processes to a model based on smaller, local communities.


During this process, it developed its own mechanisms for education, healthcare, justice and community governance outside the official structures of the state, and prioritised the collective use of land and natural resources. We spoke with Professor Neil Harvey of New Mexico State University about the Zapatistas.


Who is Neil Harvey?


Dr Neil Harvey is Professor and Head of the Department of Government at New Mexico State University, specialising in Political Science, Public Law and Administration. Harvey, who studies social movements and struggles for democracy in Mexico and Latin America, has conducted field research in Chiapas. He is the author of The Chiapas Rebellion: The Struggle for Land and Democracy (Duke University Press, 1998) and has published numerous articles on the Zapatista movement and autonomy.


More than thirty years have passed since the 1994 Zapatista uprising. How would you describe the most significant transformation the movement has undergone in the process of moving from an armed uprising to the construction of autonomous political and social structures?


This transformation involved several important changes over time. First, there was a shift from armed uprising to a peaceful strategy based on effective communication, which gained broad support within Mexican society and internationally. Second, there was a transition from the highly centralised position of military commanders to a structure in which civilian Zapatista members in hundreds of local communities assumed stronger leadership. Finally, the language used by the movement changed. The more traditional revolutionary discourse of the Latin American left was replaced by an approach in which different goals and cultural elements, both specific to the Indigenous peoples of Chiapas and appealing to humanity as a whole in a broader sense, were continuously expressed.


Rather than seizing state power, the Zapatistas developed autonomous structures in areas such as local governance, education, healthcare and justice. Why did this path emerge, and what has enabled these structures to survive for so long?


Shortly after their uprising in 1994, the Zapatistas clearly stated that their aim was to "change the world without taking power". By this, they meant that they refused to engage in a struggle to seize state power in Mexico, preferring instead to create their own forms of self-government and autonomous decision-making mechanisms. This approach represents a different understanding of revolution, aimed at avoiding the pitfalls of centralised leadership, a single ideology and the associated pyramid-shaped organisational structure that can emerge when attempting to seize state power. It is a call to change the world by starting from the specific conditions of each place and period in which struggles for justice emerge, while doing so in alliance with one another.


The goal of autonomy initially emerged as an extremely urgent need in the rural Indigenous communities of Chiapas. In these areas, the presence of teachers, doctors and other services provided by central or local governments was very limited. In the 1970s and 1980s, while the EZLN was undergoing its own process of independent formation, community members were also working with the Catholic …

author: Kiara Green
title: Beyond Indigenous Peoples Day: The Fight to Protect Indigenous Communities
content:
The second Monday in October is federally recognized as Christopher Columbus Day, commemorating the arrival of colonizer Christopher Columbus to the Americas. It’s undeniable that Indigenous communities lived in America long before Columbus docked his ship. Why, then, is he celebrated as the man who “discovered” America?

For years, public debate has challenged this Eurocentric narrative. In response, several states have recognised the second Monday in October as Indigenous Peoples Day. The day celebrates the resilience and the vibrant cultures of Indigenous communities in America.

Despite the lack of federal recognition, Indigenous Peoples Day continues to be celebrated while bringing attention to issues that Indigenous communities face. The day has been used to advocate for the removal of Columbus memorials, the returning of Indigenous lands, and awareness about Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women (MMIW).

The Trump administration has rejected this broader recognition. In 2025, Trump declared he was “bringing Columbus Day back from the ashes,” reinforcing the federal emphasis on celebrating Columbus rather than recognizing Indigenous peoples.

Meanwhile, proposed federal funding cuts of $2.3 billion from the administration continue to impact Tribal programs especially violence related programs and services that support survivors. These reductions could undermine essential services, including programs that address violence and support survivors.

The consequences are especially serious given the rates of violence facing Indigenous communities. On September 15, the House Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Federal Government Surveillance held a hearing titled “Missing and Murdered Indigenous People: Strengthening Public Safety in Tribal Communities.” Lawmakers and witnesses discussed how the federal government can help ensure the safety of Indigenous communities as they face some of the highest homicide and missing persons rates in the country.

According to the CDC, homicide was the fourth leading cause of death for American Indian and Alaska Natives men and sixth-leading cause for women ages one to 44 in 2023. Tribal communities rely on violence prevention programs and other services to address these disparities. Funding cuts threaten their ability to sustain this work.

During the September hearing, witnesses urged members to increase the funding for tribal communities to sustain these instrumental programs. Trent Shores, former U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Oklahoma, stressed that “Resources need to reach the people and stay there.” Myron Lizer, Former Vice President of Navajo Nation, similarly warned that “we have built programs but not continuous systems,” highlighting the gap between establishing initiatives and providing the sustained resources communities need.

Legislation like Savanna’s Act and the Not Invisible Act have started to address missing and murdered Native Americans by strengthening relations between federal and tribal law enforcement. However, significant gaps remain in preventing violence, investigating cases and supporting survivors.

As Indigenous communities continue to face high levels of homicide and missing person rates, Congress must continue to act and pass the Trace Act for a concise database. Honoring Indigenous resilience goes beyond annual recognition but a continued effort to guarantee sustained resources and legislative action that protect these communities from ongoing violence and funding cuts.

author: Vivian La
title: In Michigan, 3 tribes are on a mission to bring back a fish that disappeared 100 years ago
content:
Even when they’re young, the characteristic iridescent hues of the Arctic grayling are noticeable at the right angle.


On a brisk morning in September, fish and wildlife biologist Sean Leask counted and measured hundreds of these fish, which were raised at the Grand Traverse Band of Ottawa and Chippewa Indians’ streamside rearing facility, located just outside Traverse City in northern Michigan. 


“Some of these might be catchable by the end of next year,” Leask said. “I don’t know what their growth will look like in the wild.”


That’s because Arctic grayling haven’t been seen in Michigan waters for almost a century. By the 1930s, industrial activity like logging and overfishing, along with competition from non-native fish, had decimated their numbers. But three northern Michigan tribes and the state are trying to change that by reintroducing the fish to local waters. 


“Our taking care of them and helping them to reestablish their population helps us to reestablish ourselves, our culture, and our traditions,” said Tina Frankenberger, the Grand Traverse Band’s tribal environmental resiliency lead.


Their work joins broader efforts by tribes around the country to restore native species — from

salmon

 to

oysters

 to

condors

 — that are culturally and economically important, while also strengthening the ecosystems that these species depend on against threats like climate change.


One year into raising and releasing grayling to northern Michigan waterways, biologists with the Michigan tribes are grappling with questions about whether the fish are surviving and how to adapt their efforts to extreme weather. No released grayling have been seen in the wild. Flood conditions and the small number of fish they began with are complicating survey work.


But the tribes remain optimistic that their restoration efforts will improve as they collect more data in the coming years. Biologists think it will be around six to eight years before they can tell if grayling reintroduction has been successful.


“This is an experiment,” said Dan Mays, inland policy biologist for the Grand Traverse Band. “We’re trying our best.”


Young Arctic grayling swim in holding tanks at a Grand Traverse Band of Ottawa and Chippewa Indians streamside rearing facility near Traverse City.


Vivian La / IPR News


In the summer and early fall, the Grand Traverse Band raised around 8,000 young grayling and released them into the Boardman-Ottaway River. They’re one of three northern Michigan tribes that

received grayling eggs from a state hatchery

 in 2025, along with the Little River Band of Ottawa Indians and the Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians. This was the culmination of years of planning plus millions of dollars in combined

state

,

federal

, and

private

 funding to restore ecosystems. The eggs for Michigan’s reintroduction efforts were sourced from the Chena River in Alaska, a state where Arctic grayling are plentiful and more genetically diverse than the only remaining population in the Lower 48, in

Montana’s Big Hole River

.


Mays is already feeling more optimistic about the number and the size of the grayling that the Grand Traverse Band raised compared to last year, when a power outage at the tribe’s rearing facility killed a majority of the grayling.


“Overall, four times as many grayling,” he said. “We’re also stocking a higher proportion of bigger grayling this year. Greater size, greater survival.”


Raising the grayling is one challenge. Tracking the fish to see whether they’ve survived is another. None of the three northern Michigan tribes have recaptured a grayling yet.


“It’s like looking for a needle in a haystack, and the haystack is the size of a river,” said Alex Ontkos, an inland fisheries biologist with the Little River Band of Ottawa Indians. Earlier this year, this tribe stocked 391,000 grayling eggs using in-stream incubators on the Manistee River near Kalkaska. Not all of those eggs hatched, with viability rates estimated around 50 to 60 percent, Ontkos said.


Unlike the Grand Traverse Band, the Little River Band let larvae hatch directly into the incubators, grow into tiny fry, then leave the incubator. While biologists observed tens of thousands of fry leaving the incubators, they have yet to see or recapture a grayling. 


“I don’t think that that’s because they’re not out there,” Ontkos said. “It’s just a matter of being in the right place at the right time.” The team with the Little River …

author: Sara Luterman
title: Nursing Home Residents Have a Right to Vote — Despite What Trump CMS Agency Says
content:
The Nursing Home Reform Act of 1987 requires facilities to support their residents in exercising their rights.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Cindy Napolitan and her daughter Melissa have multiple sclerosis, a degenerative condition in which the immune system attacks the brain, spinal cord and nerves. They have lived together at a nursing home in Mesquite, Texas, for nine years. In previous elections, Cindy and Melissa Napolitan voted by mail, but this year they took an unusual step: They voted in person. They worried their mail-in ballots — and even their in-person votes — may not be counted.

“I’ve never worried like this before. I’ve never worried that I don’t have the proper ID. I’ve never worried that somebody is going to intimidate me. Will I encounter somebody that’s going to threaten me or make me feel less than? So yeah, I’m very worried, and I shouldn’t be,” Cindy Napolitan said. “I shouldn’t have to be worried about stuff like that. This is the 19th Amendment. I’m allowed to vote.”

Nursing home residents are guaranteed the right to vote. Around two-thirds of all nursing home residents in the United States are women, making aging and long-term care gendered issues.

There is no data on how many nursing home residents exercise that right. Cindy, 70, and Melissa Napolitan, 48, at least, feel like they’ve had good experiences with voting at their facility. Cindy Napolitan, in particular, has worked with the activities coordinator to organize rides to the polls for her, her daughter and other interested residents.

“We are scheduled to go on the first day of early voting. So in case there are any issues that we come across, we still have time to rectify the situation and be allowed to vote,” Cindy Napolitan said.

Cindy and Melissa Napolitan are more concerned this year than in previous years about government interference and voter suppression. Their fears are not unfounded: Experts and advocates for the rights of nursing home residents, older adults and people with disabilities are worried too.

In July, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services rescinded previous guidance affirming that nursing home residents have the right to vote.

“The memo does not alter the underlying law. Nursing homes are governed by the Nursing Home Reform Act of 1987 and its implementing regulations,” said Nina Kohn, a professor at Syracuse University and expert on elder law. “That law still requires facilities to support their residents in exercising their rights as Americans.”

The memo also emphasized voter fraud in nursing homes, specifically around mail-in ballots. For years, President Trump has disparaged mail-in ballots, insisting without evidence that fraudulent votes by mail had a role in his loss during the 2020 presidential election. His comments have led to some states restricting who can use a mail-in ballot and in what contexts.

According to experts, including Kohn, there is no evidence that voter fraud is a serious or widespread problem in nursing homes. Instead, Kohn is concerned about the chilling effect that it may have on residents’ rights.

“The language in the memo itself is intimidating, and it may understandably make staff think that they could face criminal prosecution or be in some other form of legal trouble if they help residents vote,” Kohn said.

Cindy and Melissa Napolitan do everything together — and on Monday, they voted together. They are also roommates at the facility; most people living in nursing homes are assigned roommates who are strangers.

“Unlike other people that have roommates that don’t get along, I’m very lucky and fortunate that I have somebody that loves me and I love her,” Cindy Napolitan said.

This is the second time Cindy and Melissa Napolitan have voted in person since entering a nursing home. The first time was during the 2024 presidential election.

“I’ve been checking my status weekly to make sure that I haven’t been dropped off the voter rolls, making sure my daughter and I don’t have some sort of issue that says that we can’t vote,” Cindy Napolitan said.

People living in nursing homes and other long-term care facilities face specific barriers. Some residents may need assistance filling out their ballots because they lack the movement or dexterity to hold a pen or press buttons on a computer screen. People with dexterity or coordination issues may also be unable to produce the same signature twice …

author: Mostafa Hosny
title: ‘Citizens’ health’ session at Egypt Forum 2026 boasts spending success with no mention of declining hospital bed numbers
content:
On Tuesday, the second day of Egypt Forum 2026, Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar described the political leadership’s support for the healthcare sector as unprecedented.


Speaking at the “citizen’s health”

session

 of Egypt Forum 2026, he said the approach dated back to the beginning of President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi’s presidency in 2014, when, he

said,

 Egypt faced a massive “disease burden,” with a lack of data and years of inadequate budget allocations that had failed to meet developmental ambitions for the system, particularly as population growth accelerated.


The minister said the state’s development plan had delivered gains in the sector, citing 16 presidential initiatives that had benefited 95 million citizens at a cost of LE44 billion. 


Abdel Ghaffar stressed that success in healthcare should not be measured by spending levels, but by the results citizens ultimately experience.


Mada Masr looked into some of those results, drawing from government

data

 published by the Central Agency for Public Mobilization and Statistics (CAPMAS).


One clear result over the time period is the notable decline in the number of beds in public hospitals between 2013 and 2024, with a drop from around 98,291 to 84,225. 


Over the same period, the number of beds in private hospitals rose from 26,009 to 36,014. 


Still, the combined total of beds in public and private hospitals fell from 124,300 in 2013 to 120,239 in 2024.


While Abdel Ghaffar portrayed inadequate budget allocations as a problem of the past, the state

has consistently fallen short

 of the constitutionally mandated minimum for healthcare spending.

 Article 18 of the Constitution requires the state to allocate at least three percent of gross national product to public healthcare starting in FY 2016/17 and gradually increase spending over time. The state has not met this threshold since the Constitution was adopted in 2014. Since then, healthcare spending has not exceeded 1.7 percent of GNP in most years.


The government allocated 1.51 percent of GNP to healthcare in the current fiscal year’s budget, half the constitutional minimum. 


Meanwhile, the government has

introduced

 a different method for calculating budget allocations that allows it to claim it is meeting the minimum spending threshold.

 


Rather than using its previous classification, which was based on the Health Ministry’s expenditure, the government now uses a “broader and more comprehensive” definition. Under this new definition, healthcare expenditure also encompasses spending by a number of off-budget economic authorities and companies as well as “any other entities providing healthcare services, such as police and military hospitals, Al-Azhar hospitals, the comprehensive health insurance system and its associated programs,” a Finance Ministry source previously told Mada Masr. Without publicly available data on these entities’ healthcare spending, it is impossible to verify whether they bring total annual healthcare spending to the constitutionally mandated minimum.


The same expansion of what constitutes annual “health spending” also allows the government to include the budgetary allocation for these entities’ debt repayments as investment in the sector, according to the same source.


The president

confessed

 three years ago that the state is not meeting the constitutional requirements, saying in a public address that “the required numbers aren’t available, folks.”

 His comment came days after the government’s assertion that it was meeting the required spending levels.


Aside from its commentary on expenditure, the government’s Egypt Forum 2026 also highlighted the Universal Health Insurance System, one of the leading presidential health initiatives.


Egypt’s Healthcare Authority head, Ahmed al-Sobky,

described

 the system as a comprehensive reform of Egypt’s healthcare sector, capping an “enormous leap forward” under Sisi, following earlier historic transformations under King Fouad I and former President Gamal Abdel Nasser.


Shortly before the forum, the government began promoting the second phase of the Universal Health Insurance System, launching a pilot phase in Minya Governorate. 


The first phase launch in the governorates of Port Said, Ismailia, Suez, South Sinai, Luxor and Aswan began in 2018 and was

completed

 in 2025.

 


Sobky said the system had achieved its objectives by strengthening social justice and reducing poverty by lowering …

author: Matthew McWade
title: The False Promise of Patient Rights in Psychiatric Units
content:
I

 have been aware of patient rights since I began working as a Certified Peer Specialist in 2006. I had the privilege of serving as emcee at an M-POWERed event at the statehouse in 2009, and participated in testimony related to Massachusetts’ Restraint and Seclusion Initiative around the same time. I worked for a year at The Transformation Center, a wing of M-POWER, the now-defunct grassroots political organization that secured Massachusetts mental health patients their six fundamental rights on psych units. I knew each of the six fundamental rights by heart (humane environment, daily private visitors, professional communications, uncensored mail, phone access, and outdoor access), but after becoming a peer specialist, I rarely experienced psychiatric hospitalization myself and had little opportunity to see how well those rights were upheld.


During a manic episode in late 2025, I felt little fear about voluntarily admitting myself to my local psych hospital because I assumed my rights would be respected. After a single weekend, I was astonished by the poor implementation of the six fundamental rights, and my mental state deteriorated as a direct result of the psych unit’s inability to uphold even the most basic of those rights.


Feeling sure that I could manage my mania and medication on my own, I asked for an immediate discharge, which was not granted (I signed a three-day but was told I would be taken before a judge — recalling my commitment in 2002 where the judge took one look at me and committed me without asking me a single question or providing me an opportunity for defense, I was hesitant to trust the local courts). Reviewing the rights board in the hallway, I vocally indicated to the staff where their policy deviated from state law, and I was met with disregard that devolved to disdain. Trapped and contemplating how to either exercise my rights or win my freedom to return to the community, I took comfort in the fact that at least the newest of the six fundamental rights, the right to fresh air, was being honored (though without access to cigarettes, which continually annoyed the other patients).


My first effort towards garnering assistance was to speak privately with my parents about my concerns, including the psych doctor’s stubborn refusal to discuss my discharge, but I was met with deprivation as my right to receive daily visitors of my own choosing, in private and at reasonable times, was immediately trampled. My elderly parents, who have vision problems and live over an hour away from the hospital, politely requested an earlier visiting time, in the early afternoon. The established visiting hours were 6pm-8pm (after the sun has set in late-autumn New England) which prevented my parents from ever having an extended visit with me during my entire psych ward stay considering they could not drive at night. They merely dropped off clothes, my phone, and a book and then left.


My next attempt was to have a private conversation with my mother about how I might secure a discharge, but I was met with another right denied when I was told I needed a “prescription” from the psych doctor for a private phone call (which she did not grant). I was told that even if I did get the “prescription phone call,” a staff member might be required to stand in the room (no one explained how the conversation could remain private with a staff member in the room). My mother insisted on having this phone conversation, being as upset as I was that they would not let me leave. I was left with two options: I could either call my mother from the crowded cafeteria during my allotted 30 minutes of daily cell phone access (with another staff member sitting five feet away with a sign-in sheet pretending not to listen as I whispered over the other 15 local phone conversations), or I could call my mother from one of the two “very private” payphones, each about seven feet from the staff office in the “secluded” hallway that everyone needed to walk through to arrive at the cafeteria or the TV room.


Reading the patients’ rights board, I noticed an unnumbered set of rights including the “right to know why you are being held on the psych unit and the stipulations for your discharge.” Waiting the entire evening, I knew I could question my assigned psych doctor the next day. Working with this doctor became a chore. She would devote barely two minutes to speaking with me regardless of my concerns, and refused to meet with me at all one day …

author: Unknown
title: Ulus: Healthcare must be free and accessible to all
content:
Structural problems in public hospitals and shortcomings in healthcare services are making it increasingly difficult for citizens to access medical care. People struggling to secure appointments through the Central Physician Appointment System (MHRS) sometimes have to wait at least 15 days just to submit an appointment request. Patients who eventually manage to obtain appointments after considerable effort must then try to explain their health problems within limited consultation times due to overcrowding in hospitals.


Difficulties in securing appointments and restrictions on consultation times are further deepening problems concerning the quality and accessibility of healthcare services.


Mehmet Nuri Ulus, Co-Chair of the Diyarbakır (Amed) Branch of the Health and Social Service Workers’ Union (SES), spoke to ANF about the problems facing public hospitals.


‘Healthcare is not being transformed, it is going backwards’


Ulus recalled that the Justice and Development Party (AKP) government has introduced healthcare reform and transformation programmes since 2002. He said that the policies implemented in recent years have caused serious problems in healthcare services and continued: “The AKP government has announced numerous programmes under the names of healthcare reform and healthcare transformation. However, particularly over the past 10 to 15 years, what has been called healthcare transformation has, from our perspective, meant collapse and regression. We have experienced both the COVID-19 pandemic and the earthquake during this period. These major crises showed us just how inadequate the healthcare system was in responding to the problems that arose.


The healthcare system should have been prepared for these crises and should have had the capacity to meet society's healthcare needs. Healthcare is a service that must be provided within the framework of the social welfare state. Everyone must be able to receive healthcare services equally, accessibly and in their mother tongue.


However, in recent years, we have seen healthcare services increasingly turn into a system in which those who have money can access care more easily. The proliferation of private hospitals is one aspect of this. Another is the emergence of an approach in which even public hospitals link faster access to certain tests, radiological examinations, medical reports and surgical procedures to payment. This undermines the principle that healthcare services should be equal for everyone.”


‘Physical queues have been replaced by virtual queues’


Ulus addressed the appointment crisis in the healthcare system, pointing out that the queues once seen outside hospitals now continue through the Central Physician Appointment System. He said appointment systems should make healthcare more accessible, but many citizens are currently unable to secure appointments.


Ulus said: “The AKP government used to say that people had to go to hospitals early in the morning and wait in queues to see a doctor. Today, physical queues have been replaced by virtual queues. Instead of waiting for hours outside hospitals, people now try to book appointments on their phones or online. However, when you access the system, you cannot find an available appointment. The queues have therefore not disappeared; they have simply changed form. Citizens now find themselves waiting in front of digital systems to access healthcare.


People face serious difficulties securing appointments, particularly in departments such as ear, nose and throat, ophthalmology and dermatology. Citizens who cannot obtain appointments are then forced to turn to private hospitals. However, considering the economic crisis, the struggle to make ends meet and the housing problems in Turkey, not everyone has the financial means to seek treatment at private hospitals.


As a result, the inability to access healthcare has become another dimension of economic hardship. Healthcare should be free and accessible, yet citizens are forced to stretch their financial resources to obtain the medical care they need.”


‘The budget is not allocated to preventive healthcare services’


Ulus said that the problems facing the healthcare system are not limited to difficulties in securing appointments.
